The first row cost six weeks and is worth doing in full: Ganaka's week-eight slide divided 2,48,460 completions by the 3,45,000 users who had reached the screen, for 72.0 per cent, where the same numerator over the 9,60,000 mandate holders is 25.9 per cent. Rows one, two and five ask about a denominator, an owner or a unit, and cost nothing to ask. Rows three and four differ in kind: throughput after cutover needs a pilot measured over the whole recovery, and the fate of records created after it needs someone to have designed the inverse. Those are answered by work, not definition.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The forcing-function position holds that voluntary migration decays geometrically and only a credible cut-off moves the tail. Its evidence is Ganaka's series: a 14.1 per cent mean weekly decline through weeks four to seven, settling at a 14,800-a-week floor against a requirement of 88,620. For it to be wrong, decay would have to belong to the instrument rather than the population — which is what the intercept's jump from 0.354 to 0.594 shows.

The indefinite-compatibility position holds that a priced dual rail almost always beats a forced break. Its evidence is that Girivasa's seventeen-week parallel run costs a known ₹72.2 lakh while the 2025 break cost ₹27.0 lakh of invoiced damage plus two renewals nobody priced. For it to be wrong, the un-named costs of a break would have to stay small while the rail's defect surface stays flat — and parallel code paths are where the regression suite lives.

The moment-of-intent position holds that notice belongs where the user already has intent, and that saturation mostly buys alarm. Its evidence is the 8.2-fold search spike and the intercept's yield. For it to be wrong the unreachable remainder would have to be small; at Ganaka it was 1,08,340 users, 17.5 per cent of the residual, whom no intercept can touch. The dispute is whether 17.5 per cent is a rounding error or the problem.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this writes the denominator on the dashboard before the first number appears on it, and asks who physically touches the thing being changed without accepting a customer name as an answer. When there is no inverse migration they say so in the plan, not the post-mortem. They watch search queries in the first seventy-two hours and support volume in the third week, in that order. And when a programme is behind they ask which gate is holding users before asking what the screen should say — not the instinct most reviews reward.

12. The decisions

Yegneswaran reclassified Bill Box from an adoption programme to a coverage programme, moved the reported metric onto the 9,60,000 denominator, shipped the intercept and funded the ₹41.2 lakh tele-calling push. The only number worth governing, she argued, was the one the sponsor bank would read on 1 January.

Yelisetti's arithmetic is in Exhibit 3. A single February window is the cheapest plan at ₹182.0 lakh and unavailable for 61 depots. Rolling all 214 depots over fourteen wave-weeks and a three-week tail costs ₹281.9 lakh, and the extra ₹99.9 lakh buys information: it commits only its first wave — the eighteen depots nearest the Chennai training base, 520 pickers rather than the 440-picker average because trainers working from base lose no days to travel — or 874 × 520 lines, ₹19.1 lakh of dip, before it can measure the real severity. Against the single window's ₹169.3 lakh that is a ratio of 8.86, and it does not appear in the totals column. He chose the hybrid at ₹241.3 lakh, booked the ₹59.3 lakh premium as the priced cost of three change-freeze clauses, and shipped a reduced-function fallback for the 640 terminals — accepting that the dual rail he set out to retire would outlive the deadline.

Discussion questions.

1. The intercept lifts yield from 0.354 to 0.594 but cannot reach 1,08,340 mandate holders. At what cost per stranded user should Ganaka stop, and in whose budget should that sit?

2. Girivasa's ₹59.3 lakh premium is the price of three change-freeze clauses. What would it have to measure before it could quote that clause at renewal?

3. Both firms found their real problem by changing a denominator. What standing report would have surfaced it in week two?

exp20v2-qo.change.mgmt:
Change Management for Users

How do I carry users through a change they didn't ask for?

1. A Monday in September

On Monday 7 September 2026, Malini Vasudevan, head of product at Elmora, faced one decision left on a redesign her team had spent eleven months building. Elmora, based in Coimbatore, sells a billing and stock app to 2,40,000 small retailers across Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka. The new version replaced the screen on which a shopkeeper raises a GST invoice, which the company's logs showed the average shop opening some thirty times a day. Nobody had asked for it. The old screen worked; it simply could not carry the e-invoicing and WhatsApp-sharing features the roadmap required.

Engineering wanted a single cutover on Monday 12 October. Notice would go out as an in-app banner and an email on 28 September, and on the morning of the twelfth every shop would open the new screen. Mukil Venkateswaran, who ran support, observed that the date sat just ahead of the Diwali season, when his queue already doubled. Each shop paid ₹499 a month, so the base represented ₹143.7 crore a year, and the question was how much of it the change itself would cost.

2. The idea

Change management for users is the discipline of moving people who already rely on a product from the old way of using it to a new one, on a schedule the company chooses and not the user. It differs from launching a feature, which adds something; here the user's habits, data and workarounds are what is altered. Its ancestry is older than software. Kurt Lewin, writing in 1947, described change as unfreezing existing habits, moving to a new pattern, and refreezing there. Jeff Hiatt and his firm Prosci turned the individual side of this into five conditions, published as ADKAR in 2006: Awareness of why, Desire to take part, Knowledge of how, Ability to do it in practice, and Reinforcement so that it holds. Those conditions were built for employees. Product teams borrowed them because a user pushed onto a new screen meets the same five hurdles, with no manager insisting.

The model matters because the hurdles come in order, and a person stopped at one is not helped by effort spent on a later one. Malini could say it in a meeting without sounding glib: every shop we lose will have been stopped at exactly one stage, so first we find out which.

3. How it actually works

Practitioners work through six steps, and two are usually left implicit. First, list what changes for the user, which is habits and not features. For Elmora it was the position of the add-item key, the Tab shortcut regular users had memorised, and the print layout of the invoice a customer saw. Second, segment. Mahathi Vemulapalli, the analyst, split the base by invoices raised per week, because a shop raising three a week and one raising three hundred need different handling. Third, route the notice to where it is read: shopkeepers answer WhatsApp and rarely open email. Fourth, state the gain in the user's terms, "send the bill on WhatsApp in one tap", not "new architecture".

Fifth, give a way across: settings and item lists carried over automatically, a three-minute walkthrough in Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and English, and a call-back offer. Sixth, staff support for the stalled shops, not the average day. The first implicit step is measuring each stage separately. Count how many saw the notice, accepted it, knew how and finished a real invoice, because a single "migrated" figure hides where people stopped. The second is deciding when the old version dies, since a change with no end date gives nobody a reason to move. Under Plan B the opt-in did not open to everyone at once. Mahathi proposed waves by segment, lightest users first, so that the stages could be read on a small group before the heaviest invoicers arrived. That ordering is the quiet advantage of a staged change: each wave is a measurement taken before the next costly commitment. Figure 3 shows the stage-by-stage counts that Mahathi built for the two plans.

4. A worked example

Each rate in Table 1 applies only to the shops that survived the previous stage, so the figures compound. Plan A's rates multiply to 55.08 per cent, or 1,32,192 shops able to raise a real invoice on the new screen. Plan B's multiply to 77.16 per cent, or 1,85,193. Plan A's rates come from Elmora's 2024 billing-screen change; Plan B's are planning assumptions, since an August pilot of 6,000 shops was too small to estimate the last stage.

Elmora measured after 2024 that 12.5 per cent of stalled shops cancel within 60 days, support rescues already netted out. That gives 13,476 cancellations under Plan A and 6,851 under Plan B (6,850.875, rounded). A cancelled shop forgoes twelve months at ₹5,988 (₹499 times twelve), a deliberate upper bound. Plan B costs more: four weeks of running the old screen alongside, ₹38 lakh; three messages to each shop at ₹0.60, ₹4.32 lakh; and 20 temporary agents for eight weeks at ₹15,000 a week, ₹24 lakh. That totals ₹66.32 lakh against ₹3.6 lakh for Plan A's six agents for four weeks, a difference of ₹62.72 lakh, or ₹0.627 crore.

The second pass changes one input. Mukil argued that a shop stalled in the weeks before Diwali cannot invoice at all, and put the cancellation rate at 20 per cent. Plan B's opt-in window runs through the same weeks, so a shop stalled there is equally unable to invoice, and the 20 per cent applies to both. Nothing else moves: Plan A loses 21,562 shops and Plan B 10,961.

The useful figure is the break-even. Plan B has 53,001 fewer stalled shops, each worth ₹5,988 if kept, so its extra ₹62.72 lakh pays back if only 1.98 per cent of stalled shops would otherwise cancel: about one in fifty, against the 12.5 per cent observed.

5. Seven nuances

It is not release management, nor organisational change.

Release management decides when code reaches production and ends when the build is stable. Change management for users starts there and measures people. Corporate programmes such as John Kotter's eight steps of 1996 address employees who can be instructed; customers can simply leave.

Losses weigh more than equal gains.

Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky's prospect theory, from 1979, found people weigh a loss at roughly twice an equal gain. A shopkeeper loses a memorised shortcut today, while the WhatsApp feature is a promise. The benefit must be demonstrated, not announced.

Sent is not seen.

Delivery counts overstate awareness. Plan A's 85 per cent only holds if awareness is defined as an acknowledgement tap or a correct answer to "what changes on Monday?", not as emails sent.

Averages hide cohorts.

Plan B's 77.16 per cent could conceal a far lower rate among the heaviest invoicers, whose loss costs more than their count suggests. Report the funnel by segment before trusting the total.

Dual-running buys safety and needs a sunset.

Keeping the old screen alive lets users choose their moment, but with no end date nobody moves. With an end date and no way back, a bad week becomes a crisis. Elmora's ₹38 lakh bought exactly four weeks of both.

It manages the passage, not the destination.

If first-invoice success stays near 60 per cent after generous support, the fault is the design. Before relying on the method, ask which stage users stop at, what they lose, when the old way ends, and who answers the phone.

Workarounds are part of the product.

Users build habits around quirks. Maithili Vellingiri, who led customer success from Coimbatore, found shops keeping a paper tally of credit sales beside the old screen; the new layout removed the quirk that tally depended on. Logs record clicks, not the notebook on the counter, so an inventory of workarounds comes from watching shops work.

Figure 4 puts the nuances to work. The vertical axis asks what a failed session costs the user; the horizontal asks how often the changed screen is met. Elmora's invoice screen sits in the top-right quadrant, which is why a banner and an email were never going to be enough, and why a rarely used settings page in the same release could safely get one.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; small and large

ProductWho bears the costUsual routeTypical failure
ConsumerMillions of strangers, free to leaveStaged rollout, in-app promptsPublic backlash in reviews
B2BUsers, while a different person boughtBrief the admin first; contract noticeUsers learn of it from the vendor last
MarketplaceOne side, whose income depends on the toolTime changes against the other side's peaksA seller-tool change breaks buyers

Elmora is B2B in contract but consumer in behaviour: the shopkeeper is buyer and user, with no administrator to brief. In a marketplace, a change to seller tooling alters the income of one side and the experience of the other, so the same funnel needs running twice. Scale matters too. A company with 40 customers can telephone every one and need not measure stages at all. A large company cannot, so it segments, automates notices and carries legal duties such as contractual notice periods, which early-stage firms rarely face.

7. Common mistakes

Announcing at the moment of change. The symptom is a ticket spike on cutover day with the phrase "where did it go". The misunderstanding is treating notice as awareness. The cheapest diagnostic: the day before, ask 20 users to describe what will change.

Counting migrations as adoption. The dashboard is green while retention dips weeks later. The misunderstanding is that arriving on the new screen means succeeding on it. Compare first-task completion at day 7 against the old screen's rate.

Staffing support to the average. First-response time collapses in cutover week. Suppose half of Plan A's stalled shops call: 53,904 contacts against six agents' capacity of 4,800 (6 agents, 20 working days, 40 contacts a day), more than eleven times too few. Multiply stalled shops by a contact rate before hiring.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Elmora's twelfth of October is a Monday on which little happens. Shops have been told three times, on WhatsApp and in the app, each message carrying a one-line gain. A three-minute walkthrough, in their own language, waits on the new screen, and a call-back is one tap away. Support is sized for the stalled count. Each stage is counted separately and reviewed by segment, and the old screen carries a date. Mukil reads the queue daily against the contact forecast, not against last month's average. Nobody is surprised, including the shops that stalled, because someone rang them. Figure 6 marks the checkpoints.

9. Closing

Malini chose Plan B, with one amendment: if first-invoice success among the first 5,000 opt-in shops to finish the walkthrough fell below Plan B's 95 per cent ability rate in the first week, the forced date moved. She reasoned that Plan B's extra ₹62.72 lakh recovers if one stalled shop in fifty would otherwise leave, and that Mukil's 20 per cent view made the wager lopsided. The old screen would end on Monday 9 November.

Next, learn adoption and activation measurement, since the stage funnel is a cohort funnel by another name, and then post-launch monitoring, which tells you whether the support plan held. Two questions to sit with. Which of Elmora's five stages would you least trust your own data on, and why? If Plan B's last-stage rate were 85 per cent rather than 95, would your answer change, and how would you check?
exp20v2-qo.support.readiness:
Support and Operational Readiness

Is support ready for what we are about to ship?

1. The line Vyshnavi did not believe

On Monday 26 October 2026, Vyshnavi Ezhumalai, head of product operations at Larkspur Pay, studied a launch plan with one line she distrusted. Larkspur, a Bengaluru company whose app and card reader let small shops accept UPI and card payments, was due to release Instant Settlement on Tuesday 3 November. Instead of waiting until the next working day, a merchant would see a day's takings in the bank account within minutes. The plan exposed 20 per cent of the 3,00,000 active merchants in week one, or 60,000 shops. Beside "Support" the plan said: "Ready".

Vyshnavi knew what a money feature does to a queue. A shopkeeper who cannot find ₹18,000 does not send an email; she rings, and rings again. Vasanth Egambaram, who ran support, had 40 agents trained on the existing product, a help centre with no page on the new feature, and no macros, which are saved reply templates an agent inserts and edits. His queue already took 2,100 contacts a day.

The only evidence on demand was Larkspur's March 2026 refresh of its QR codes, shown to 48,000 merchants, which produced 3,456 contacts in its first week: 7.2 per cent. If "Ready" was wrong, the cost would not stop at angry merchants. Every existing customer would wait behind them, and Larkspur's merchants had plenty of alternatives a phone call away. The readiness review was on Thursday 29 October.

2. The idea

Support and operational readiness is the condition in which the people who answer customers, and the materials and routes they depend on, can absorb the demand a release will create at the speed customers need it absorbed. It has five parts: knowledge (help articles and internal runbooks), tools (macros), skill (training), route (an escalation path, meaning a defined way to pass a case to someone with more authority) and capacity (agent-minutes).

It exists because teams tend to treat deployment as the finish line, and customers meet the product only after it. The discipline descends from ITIL, the service-management library first assembled by the British government in the late 1980s, from the operational readiness reviews of aerospace and nuclear work, and from the production readiness reviews that Google's 2016 book on site reliability engineering made familiar. Vyshnavi could say it in one sentence: "We are ready when the first thousand confused customers can get a correct answer faster than they can get angry."

3. How it actually works

The sequence is arithmetic first, craft second. Step one forecasts contacts, which means exposed customers multiplied by a contact rate, spread across days by an observed shape. Step two multiplies by handle time, the average minutes an agent spends on one contact, to give workload. Step three divides by the productive minutes one agent offers in a day.

Step four is where the four artefacts earn their keep, and the figure shows that each pulls a different number. Help articles reduce how many contacts arrive; macros and training reduce how long each takes; an escalation path stops hard cases occupying a first-line agent for twenty minutes; extra staff add minutes directly. Implicit steps follow: plan for the peak day, not the average, name one owner who may delay the ramp, and test with a rehearsal in which agents answer realistic cases cold. It also tests the documents themselves: an article that reads well to its author can send a stranger to the wrong screen.

One further point is easy to miss. Each step produces a number that someone must own. If the forecast belongs to product, the handle time to support and the staffing to finance, then nobody owns the comparison in step three, and that comparison is where the answer to the question lives. Vyshnavi's first act was therefore to put all three numbers on one page.

4. A worked example

Vasanth supplied three inputs. A trained agent is productive for 360 minutes of an eight-hour shift, since breaks, meetings and coaching take the rest. The 2,100 existing contacts a day take 6 minutes each, so baseline work is 12,600 minutes, against 40 × 360 = 14,400 available: 87.5 per cent occupancy. And a surge pool of 8 agents could be borrowed from the collections queue, giving 48. The week also contains Diwali on Sunday 8 November. The 2,100 baseline is deliberately pre-festive and flat, because it is the figure the October queue actually showed; festive volume will lift it, so the Thursday and Friday readings, which fall inside the build-up, decide the ramp.

Vyshnavi's forecast raised the March rate by a quarter for a money feature: 7.2 × 1.25 = 9.0 per cent. Week-one contacts at 60,000 exposed are 60,000 × 0.09 = 5,400. Figure 2 spreads them over the days using March's shape; the first day carries 22 per cent, or 1,188 contacts.

The first pass assumes the March experience: with no macros and no briefing, agents took 10 minutes per launch contact against 6 for an ordinary one, because they searched for the answer while the merchant waited. Launch work on day one is 1,188 × 10 = 11,880 minutes. Add the baseline 12,600 and the total is 24,480, which divided by 360 is 68 agents. Against 48, Larkspur is 20 short. Table 1 shows what happens when one input changes at a time.

ScenarioExposedDay-one launch contactsMinutes eachLaunch minutesPlus baselineAgents neededAgainst 48
A: 20%, no prep60,0001,1881011,88024,48068.020.0 short
B: 20%, macros60,0001,18867,12819,72854.86.8 short
C: 10%, no prep30,000594105,94018,54051.53.5 short
D: 10%, macros30,00059463,56416,16444.93.1 spare

Baseline work is 2,100 contacts × 6 minutes = 12,600 minutes. Agents needed = total minutes ÷ 360. Day-one contacts = exposed × 0.09 × 0.22.

Neither lever alone suffices. Macros and training (B) cut the gap from 20 to 6.8; halving exposure alone (C) cuts it to 3.5; only both (D) fit within 48. Even D runs at 16,164 ÷ 17,280 = 93.5 per cent occupancy, thinner than the 87.5 per cent of a normal day, so it passes on arithmetic but leaves little room for a forecast error. Queues lengthen sharply as occupancy approaches the ceiling, which is why Vasanth treated 93.5 per cent as a warning rather than a pass. A rate of 11 per cent instead of 9 would add 0.02 × 30,000 × 0.22 = 132 more day-one contacts at the 30,000 exposure, roughly 2.2 agents' worth at 6 minutes each, which would consume most of the 3.1 spare.

5. Six nuances

Readiness is an input to launch readiness, not a synonym

Launch readiness asks whether the whole release can go: engineering, legal, marketing, support. Support readiness is one gate within it. A product can be operationally ready and still unfit to ship, and a product that is fully built can be stopped at the support gate for want of one missing page. The distinction matters because the two reviews have different owners, different evidence and different power to say no.

Capacity is not capability

Forty-eight agents supply minutes, not answers. If agents cannot resolve a settlement query, the minutes are spent and the customer calls back, so the measure to watch beside occupancy is whether a contact was resolved the first time.

The contact rate is an analogy, not a measurement

The 7.2 per cent comes from one earlier launch and the 25 per cent uplift is judgement. Choose the closest analogue honestly, then state a range; a forecast that cannot be wrong cannot be tested either. Money features, which touch a customer's income, tend to draw more contacts than cosmetic ones, so the analogue should match on the stakes and not only on the size of the audience.

Deflection is not avoidance

A help article lowers contacts only if customers find and understand it. A contact caused by a confusing screen is a product defect, and writing a macro for it hides the defect rather than fixing it. The useful habit is to tag every launch contact by cause, so that the three commonest causes reach the product team within days.

An escalation path needs an owner and a clock

"Raise it with engineering" is a queue with no end. A usable path names who receives the case, how severe cases are classed, and how soon they must respond. Without that clock, the first-line agent holds the customer on the phone while waiting for an answer that has no due date.

Readiness cannot tell you the feature is right

It prepares you for the failures you imagined. It cannot find the ones you did not, which is why the plan needs a ramp and a trigger to pause it, and why training given a month early is partly forgotten by launch week.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early and large

In consumer products, volume dominates and deflection through articles and in-app guidance matters most; Larkspur's shopkeepers write in Hindi, Kannada and Tamil, so each macro needs a translation and each help article a local-language version. In B2B, accounts are few and large: readiness means admin training, a named customer-success manager and contractual response times, and one unanswered query can threaten a renewal. In a marketplace there are two customers with opposing interests, so support must handle disputes and trust questions as well as how-to queries.

Scale changes the mechanism. An early-stage company's readiness is often one founder, one document and a Slack channel, and that is adequate. A large one works through shifts, outsourced vendors and weeks of training lead time, so the capacity decision must be made earlier than any launch date feels natural.

7. Common mistakes

Counting heads, not minutes

From outside: "we had 40 agents last month" and a queue that explodes on day two. The belief is that headcount equals capacity. Diagnostic: multiply forecast contacts by handle time and divide by 360. In Larkspur's case the 40 agents looked sufficient until the minutes were counted, because 40 × 360 = 14,400 minutes already carried 12,600 of routine work.

Training once, early

From outside: agents escalate everything or contradict each other. The belief is that attending a session equals knowing. Diagnostic: give five agents three real cases cold and count correct resolutions. If fewer than four of five reach the right answer without help, the training was a presentation and not a preparation.

Planning for the average day

From outside: service levels breach on days one and two, then recover. Over the week the average is 5,400 ÷ 7 = 771 contacts a day, but day one carries 1,188, about 54 per cent more. Diagnostic: read the analogue's daily shape before sizing.

8. What good looks like

At a good review, the support owner presents a table like Table 1 with the analogue named, the range stated and the peak day sized. Articles exist in three languages, macros have been used by agents in a rehearsal, and escalation names a person on call with a response time. Two triggers are written down: one that widens the ramp and one that stops it. The review ends with a decision, not the word "Ready". Crucially, the numbers are small enough to be checked in the room: anyone present can multiply 594 by 6 and see 3,564, and can ask what happens if the rate is higher. A good review welcomes that question, because a plan that survives it is more trustworthy than one nobody could test.

9. What Vyshnavi decided

On 29 October she rejected scenario A and chose D: expose 30,000 merchants, publish articles in three languages, write and rehearse macros, borrow the 8 agents for the first week, and name Vasanth as owner with authority to delay the ramp. She would widen to 20 per cent on Monday 9 November only if observed occupancy on Thursday and Friday stayed under 90 per cent (forecast 87.9 and 86.0) and no escalation was older than a day. She allowed the first two days to run hotter, up to 95 per cent against forecasts of 93.5 and 91.7, because early days are the least predictable and a breach there should trigger extra help, not a halt. Her reasoning was that halving exposure cost a week of benefit to 30,000 merchants, while a failed launch would cost trust with all 3,00,000.

To go further, study launch tiers, which decide how widely a release goes at first, and launch readiness reviews, the forum where this evidence is judged. Two questions to sit with. If the March contact rate had been 4 per cent, would she have chosen differently, and what would that reveal about which input matters most? And who in your organisation could say "not yet" to a launch, and have it respected?
exp40v2-qo.support.readiness:
Support and operational readiness

Two companies, two days apart, ask the same question — is support ready for what we are about to ship? — and find the honest answer is an arithmetic problem with a contested denominator.

1Two desks, one question

On Wednesday 21 October 2026 in Chennai, Yashaswini Govindarajan put one slide on the wall of Maargam Travel Technologies’ operations room. Maargam sells intercity bus tickets through a consumer app and closed 12,40,000 bookings in September; on Monday 16 November it would add rail ticketing at full exposure. Yashaswini, the VP of customer operations, had been asked to sign the launch readiness form.

Her slide held a short chain. Planners forecast 38,000 rail bookings in week one. At the contact rate Maargam’s own bus module produced in its first week, that meant 2,356 support contacts, of which 424 would resolve against the help centre, leaving 1,932 to reach an agent. The launch-week roster carried 36 agent-shifts. “I can tell you whether that is enough once you tell me which of these intents has a macro,” she said.

Yathartha Gorantla, the director of product who owned rail, thought 6.2 contacts per 100 bookings pessimistic: rail would land on users who already knew the app. Yashaswini thought it optimistic, because the rules a rail passenger asks about — quota, concession, the refund schedule — belong to Indian Railways, and an agent who cannot change a rule can only explain it slowly.

Two days later Yashica Gollamudi was having the same argument in Hyderabad with different numbers. Muthirai Systems sells export-documentation software to 118 enterprise accounts filing shipping bills through ICEGATE. A new module had been live to 14 design-partner accounts for the six weeks to Sunday 18 October: 289 tickets, 41 of them priority one. Wave two, 37 accounts, was set for Monday 2 November; wave three, the remaining 67, for December. Wave one, Yashica told Yaminee Guduru, the VP of product, had taught them a great deal about the escalation path and almost nothing reliable about volume.

2The idea, and the four positions people hold

Support and operational readiness is the state in which every function that will absorb the consequences of a release can recognise, resolve or correctly route what the release produces, before it reaches the people who will produce it. Its components are documentation inside and out, macros, agent training, escalation paths with named on-call owners, and staffed capacity — plus one routinely forgotten: the return path by which what support learns becomes a product change.

Two ancestries pull in different directions. The older is procedural: aerospace programmes formalised the operational readiness review, a gate at which a party independent of the builders certifies the operating organisation can run the thing, and ITIL codified the instinct from 1989, its 2007 service-transition volume contributing two survivors — service acceptance criteria agreed in advance, and early life support, a deliberately over-staffed period. The younger is economic: the Corporate Executive Board’s 2013 work on customer effort pushed the field toward measuring support in contacts per unit of usage rather than in satisfaction. The production readiness review Google documented in 2016 fused the two — a checklist owned by whoever carries the pager, holding a real veto.

Four positions follow, differing on the propositions they will sign. The gate school signs “a release that cannot be supported should not ship, and support holds the veto”; not “readiness can be learned from the first fortnight.” The early-life school signs “staff two weeks heavily, stage the rollout, write the docs from real tickets”; not “a pre-launch macro library predicts the intents you will see.” The deflection school signs “the artefact that pays removes a contact rather than answering it faster”; not “every launch deserves a runbook.” The discovery school signs “the first fortnight’s queue is the best problem evidence a product gets, and suppressing it destroys information”; not “the goal at launch is minimising contacts per booking.”

3Mechanics: the arithmetic experts actually run

Expert practice is five steps, of which the first and last are usually left implicit. Forecast the intent distribution from a named analogue, saying why it transfers. Price each intent in handle minutes twice, with the artefact and without. Convert priced demand into capacity in agent-shifts, not headcount. Instrument every door into the escalation topology. Then set exit criteria for early-life support, so over-staffing ends on evidence, not a date.

Maargam's analogue was its own bus launch of Monday 5 August 2024, and its shape is the most useful object in this discipline.

The curve decays, but neither to nothing nor fast. The rate falls strictly every week, 6.2 to 2.5; eight weeks in, the module still ran 31.6 per cent above the 1.9 per 100 it produces today in its twenty-seventh month. Absolute contacts fall every week except the last, where the promotion lifted bookings to 39,000 and contacts rose from 910 to 975 even as the rate fell.

From the week-one rate Maargam built Exhibit 2: 2,356 forecast contacts less 424 expected to self-resolve, leaving 1,932 queued, priced at 5.8 minutes where a macro exists and 11.0 where the agent composes a reply and looks up a rule.

Macros existed for four intents covering 1,305 contacts, 67.5 per cent of the queue; the four without one account for 627. The 7.49 is pooled, 14,466 minutes over 1,932 contacts, not the mean of 5.8 and 11.0, which is 8.4.

A Maargam agent delivers 5.2 productive hours — 312 minutes — in a shift, after breaks, briefings and the occupancy loss of waiting between chats. The forecast therefore needs 14,466 ÷ 312 = 46.4, so 47 agent-shifts. The roster carried 36: six agents on a six-day rota. The gap is 3,234 minutes, 22.4 per cent of the requirement.

Then the second-order effect. Had the three missing high-volume macros and a long-tail template been written, every intent would price at 5.8 minutes: 1,932 × 5.8 = 11,205.6 minutes, or 35.9 shifts, so 36. The roster Maargam had was exactly right for a macro library it did not have, and the margin was 26 minutes across a seven-day week, 0.2 per cent of rostered capacity. Readiness is the capacity plan in another unit.

4When it applies, and when it misleads

First: pre-launch readiness pays in proportion to how predictable the intent distribution is from an available analogue. Maargam passes — eight weeks of its own bus data, and a rail module sharing the payment rail and the account. Muthirai half-passes: it has a base rate from an earlier general-account module, but the new module’s content is a filing window set by a regulator, and no prior module has one.

Second: readiness pays in proportion to the asymmetry of a wrong answer. Muthirai passes decisively: an agent who misstates a filing deadline causes no re-contact, the customer misses a vessel and pays demurrage, and the mistake surfaces as a claim rather than a ticket. Maargam mostly fails — a wrong refund answer costs a second contact, recoverable within the hour.

Third: readiness pays in proportion to how slow or partial your rollback is. Maargam fails this too, and most consequentially. A consumer app with a feature flag can take rail to 12 per cent of users and read the real intent distribution for a fraction of what pre-writing the four missing artefacts costs. Yathartha’s instinct is correct given a flag and reckless without one.

The idea misleads at both ends. A readiness programme becomes a tax when its artefacts cost more than the information launching small would have bought; teams then relabel launches as experiments to get under the gate. At the other end, readiness that succeeds completely destroys the evidence the product needed: a fortnight in which every contact is deflected is a fortnight in which nobody learns which rule confused anyone.

5Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Readiness breaks where ownership is ambiguous, not where the problem is hard. In multi-product companies the failure is the straddling ticket: a rail refund paid out of a bus wallet belongs to two queues and two runbooks, and the tell is an excellent first response time beside a terrible resolution time. Mature firms appoint one duty manager for the launch window with authority to assign such tickets by fiat.

Two-sided products are routinely ready on one side only — the demand side is instrumented and politically expensive to get wrong, while the supply side files through a channel nobody owns. In regulated products a macro is a compliance artefact: a canned response misstating a cancellation rule is a representation, and firms under RBI or IRDAI supervision version their macros with the ceremony they give disclosures.

Hardware plus software introduces an audience the documentation misses: the person performing the step is often neither customer nor employee — a third-party installer, say — and no in-app guidance reaches them. AI-native products fail differently: the characteristic defect is not an error but a confident wrong answer, producing a ticket the agent cannot reproduce and the engineer cannot find. Readiness there means a retrievable trace keyed to something the user can quote, an escalation path for a bad model answer that skips bug triage, and a macro that neither promises a fix nor denies the behaviour.

At the seams, practice differs from publication. The published mechanism is a checklist with sign-off fields. The operative mechanism is that a named support manager holds a veto which is socially expensive to use, uses it perhaps twice a year, and keeps its credibility precisely by using it that often. A veto never exercised is a Jira field.

6Nine nuances that separate the expert from the competent

A falling rate inside a rising queue. Maargam’s week 8: the rate improved from 2.6 to 2.5 while contacts rose from 910 to 975, because bookings grew faster than the rate fell. The tell is a deck whose headline metric improves while the queue lengthens.

The pooled rate is not the mean of the rates. Exhibit 1 gives 3.56 contacts per 100 pooled against 3.78 as the mean of its eight weekly rates, six per cent apart, entirely because the worst weeks were the smallest. The tell is a figure that moves when the window changes.

Coverage is measured in volume, not artefacts. Maargam had macros for four of Exhibit 2’s eight rows, which a tracker records as 50 per cent. By forecast volume it is 67.5 per cent; by handle minutes the four gaps consume 6,897 of 14,466, or 47.7 per cent. The tell is a tracker that counts rows.

A plan with no slack is not a plan. The roster that exactly meets full-coverage demand clears it by 26 minutes. One agent absent for the week removes six shifts, 1,872 minutes against those 26. The tell is a roster built on the forecast with no shrinkage assumption stated.

An escalation path is the path people take. Exhibit 3’s 171 bypassing tickets are 59.2 per cent of wave one; among the 41 priority-one tickets the bypass share was 73.2 per cent, because urgency finds the shortest route to a human. The tell is a first tier reporting idleness while engineers report interruption.

The support window must match the product’s clock, not the office’s. Muthirai promised a 30-minute first response on priority one, 24 hours a day, five days a week. Nine priority-one tickets breached it, all nine arriving outside the covered window, because vessels sail at weekends. Median first response on those nine was 11 hours 40 minutes. Inside the covered window the median was 23 minutes and the slowest 28, answered by whichever engineer saw the channel first.

Not every design-partner number is the wrong base. Scaling wave one’s 3.44 tickets per account-week across the remaining 104 accounts’ first six weeks each — 624 account-weeks — gives 2,147 tickets and 305 priority ones; Muthirai’s general-population rate of 1.9 per account-week, at a 9.6 per cent priority-one share, gives 1,186 and 114, so the naive priority-one count is 2.68 times the other. But the weekend share of priority-one tickets, 22.0 per cent, is a property of trade flows rather than cohort engagement, and transfers better than the ticket rate. Ask which mechanism generates each borrowed statistic.

Training is a half-life, not a date. Certification records when competence was demonstrated, not when it is needed, and a team certified for a launch that then slips three weeks is not a certified team. The tell is a readiness pack whose training line is green and whose last practice ticket is a month old.

The last box must be able to change something. For Maargam’s railway-rule intents — 161 cancellations and 118 quota queries, 14.4 per cent of the queue — the path terminates at a third party’s process. An agent can route, wait and explain, making the path real and resolution impossible. The tell is a severity definition promising resolution nobody inside the company can deliver.

7Where the differences are real, and where they are not

In consumer products the binding constraint is unit cost — contacts per transaction times handle minutes — so macros and self-serve dominate. In B2B and enterprise the constraint is contractual. Muthirai’s nine breaches each carried a service credit of two per cent of the monthly fee, ₹4,800 on an average account fee of ₹2.40 lakh, so ₹43,200 in wave one; the corrected forecast of 114 priority-one tickets at a 22.0 per cent weekend share gives, if the window is left alone, 25 breaches and ₹1.20 lakh at that same average. The money is trivial; the 25 renewal conversations are not.

Platforms and marketplaces repeat the asymmetry: two populations, two contact rates, one budget, and a political gradient that spends it on the visible side. Hardware differs furthest, because the installed base cannot be patched on Tuesday and whoever needs the documentation may never see a product screen. AI products differ in the defect’s shape, not the plan’s.

Stage matters less than is claimed. At seed stage the product manager is the support team, correctly: the loop is one person long. At growth stage the handoff is the whole problem, because contacts are answered by people with no standing to change the product. At enterprise stage readiness becomes contractual. What does not change is the arithmetic of section 3: demand in priced minutes over capacity in productive minutes is the same calculation for a three-person startup and for a bank.

8Three worked examples, one of them a failure

Maargam’s is the forecast case, Muthirai’s the measured one. The third is Mandali Devices, which sells connected cold-chain monitors to dairy and pharmaceutical distributors and did the readiness work properly for the wrong audience.

On Monday 11 May 2026 Mandali shipped firmware that changed the device pairing flow. Documentation was rewritten, the central team retrained, a runbook published. Nobody checked that pairing is performed almost entirely by third-party installers. Over the next 19 days 3,250 units were installed and first-paired; 371 failed, 11.4 per cent against a 2.1 per cent baseline that would have produced 68. The 303 excess failures each needed a site revisit at ₹1,850 — ₹5.61 lakh.

The recovery was not a documentation fix. On Saturday 30 May the team rolled the firmware back to the 1,950 installed units with live connectivity, 60.0 per cent of the 3,250, shipped new units on the rolled-back build, and issued a three-language installer card for the other 1,300. The ₹5.61 lakh was never the cost: one pharmaceutical distributor put a 1,400-unit order worth ₹131.6 lakh on hold, against which the revisits were 4.3 per cent.

9Failure modes and their early warnings

Every mode below has appeared on this page. Each has a cheap diagnostic available weeks before launch and an expensive one afterwards.

10Where experts genuinely disagree

The first disagreement is whether support holds a veto. The gate position rests on an asymmetry: the cost of an unsupportable launch is borne by a function that did not choose it, and without a veto the readiness conversation is advisory. Its evidence is every launch that shipped with a green checklist and a red queue. For it to be wrong, staged rollout and rollback would have to reliably make a readiness failure recoverable — which is what Maargam’s flag does and what Mandali’s firmware, reaching 60.0 per cent of the units it had to reach, does not.

The second is whether macros should be written before launch. The early-life position is that an intent distribution is cheap to measure and expensive to guess, and that a pre-written library encodes the team’s theory of confusion rather than the users’. Its strongest evidence is that Maargam’s forecast rests on a 2024 analogue and a rate two competent people dispute. For it to be wrong, the first fortnight’s contacts would have to be costly enough that answering them slowly beats answering some wrongly.

The third is the deepest and least discussed: whether deflection at launch is a gain or a loss. The discovery position holds that an article intercepting 424 contacts has also destroyed 424 observations of what confused a user, at the moment they are most valuable. Nobody has a clean measurement either way, because the counterfactual is unobserved by construction.

11What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this does three things differently. They convert readiness into minutes and shifts early rather than late, because every component resolves into either fewer contacts or shorter ones. They name the base of every borrowed rate out loud, and distinguish a statistic that transfers by mechanism from one that transfers by analogy. And they treat the escalation path as an empirical object: instrument the doors, read which one people use, and move the official path to meet the real one. The merely studied practitioner produces a complete checklist; the expert produces a number, a named denominator, and a roster that survives one person falling ill.

12What each of them decided

Yashaswini and Yathartha did not resolve their disagreement about the 6.2; they routed around it. Rail would go live on 16 November to 12 per cent of users, which if they book at the average rate means 4,560 bookings and about 283 contacts, 232 queued after the same 18.0 per cent deflection. That is enough to mark the top two off from the rest — the gap from second to third is 21.9 tickets, 2.5 standard errors on the difference — and not enough to order those two against each other, at 1.4, or to separate third from fourth, at 0.6. Nor is it enough to size the smallest: the quota-rules intent would show about 14 tickets, standard error roughly four. The three missing macros would be written from the first 400 real tickets, and full exposure would wait on an exit criterion, not a date.

Yashica did not try to enforce Muthirai’s front door. She made the shared channel the official priority-one path for every account in waves two and three, instrumented it, and extended the priority-one window to seven days for both waves. She declined to roster against either forecast, writing both into the wave-two plan with a trigger: if the first fortnight exceeded 1.9 tickets per account-week by more than half, wave three would move to January.

Discussion questions

1. Maargam’s own figures show that complete macro coverage would bring launch-week demand to 11,206 minutes against 11,232 rostered, a margin of 26 minutes. What would you have to believe about absence, attrition and handle-time variance to roster to that margin, and what is the cheapest way to find out whether you believe it?

2. The gap between Muthirai’s two forecasts — 1.81 times on tickets, 2.68 times on priority ones — turns entirely on which cohort is the right base. What measurement, obtainable before 2 November, would settle it — and if none exists, which forecast should the roster be built on?

3. If the discovery argument of section 10 holds, a consumer product should never enter a launch with complete macro coverage. Is that conclusion acceptable? If not, locate the step in the argument you reject.

13Going deeper

  1. Release management and launch readiness — the parent discipline; this is one of its gates, and the one most often waved through.
  2. Launch tiers and launch readiness — scaling readiness demand to a launch's size, so a tier-three feature does not buy a tier-one runbook.
  3. Launch readiness reviews — the meeting itself: who attends, who may say no, and what evidence it can demand.
  4. Testing and quality basics — the upstream determinant of the contact rate; every defect shipped becomes handle minutes.
  5. Bug triage and severity — how a ticket becomes a product change, and where section 6's last nuance bites.
  6. Staged rollouts and rollback — the substitute for readiness that section 4's third claim turns on, and what makes failure recoverable.
  7. Incident management and postmortems — what happens when readiness fails loudly rather than slowly.
  8. SLAs, SLOs and error budgets — the quantitative language for Muthirai's promises, including what a service credit actually prices.
  9. Beta and early-access programmes — where design-partner data comes from, and so where section 6's wrong-base nuance is manufactured.
exp40v2-qo.performance.budget:
Performance budgets

1. Two decisions, five days apart

On Thursday 8 October 2026, Deeptha Karanth, head of product at Saltgrid Systems in Pune, read a clause her largest customer had inserted into a renewal. Saltgrid sells loan-origination software to banks and non-bank lenders; its decisioning API answers about 42 lakh credit decisions a month. The clause committed Saltgrid to a 95th-percentile response time of 800 milliseconds from 1 December 2026, with service credits attached. September's measured figure was 1,240 ms; the median was 310.

Her platform lead, Devanand Kulal, wanted a gate: any build whose replayed trace pushed the 95th percentile above 800 ms would fail its checks. Dinesh Kartha, who runs enterprise delivery, objected that the slowest tenants have the largest rule-sets, so one global gate would stop features the fast tenants had paid for. They disagreed not about the engineering but about what a budget is for.

On Tuesday 13 October, Dhruti Kottary, chief product officer of Sparrowline Learning in Hyderabad, met the same question in another currency. Sparrowline's spoken-English tutor serves 23 lakh monthly active users on ₹8,000-to-₹12,000 Android handsets, who complete 38 lakh sessions a month at roughly ten turns each. A new model scored better on its conversation-quality rubric but raised time to first audio from 1,100 ms to 2,400 ms and cost per completed turn from ₹0.21 to ₹0.38 — over 3.8 crore turns a month, ₹79.8 lakh becoming ₹1.444 crore, or ₹64.6 lakh more a month and ₹7.75 crore a year.

Deeptha's budget came by contract, in one currency; Dhruti's had to be invented, in two. The hard part is never the number.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A performance budget is a numerical limit on a measurable property of a product — load time, payload size, latency, cost per request — fixed in advance, divided among competing claims, owned by someone named, and carrying a consequence when crossed. Those last three clauses are the practice: a limit with no allocation is a slogan, with no owner nobody's, with no consequence a wish.

The device is borrowed from aerospace mass budgets and chip power budgets, where the global constraint is physical. Software has none, which is the problem the practice was invented for: nobody decides to make a product slow, each addition is defensible alone, and the sum is a product no one chose.

The web community responded first: Steve Souders's work from 2007 established that front-end cost dominated perceived speed, and Tim Kadlec's writing from 2013 named the budget as a tool, set before design begins. Google's RAIL model (2015) and Core Web Vitals (2020) supplied shared thresholds — a "good" Largest Contentful Paint is 2.5 seconds at the 75th percentile of real visits — which ended the argument about whose number to use. Jeffrey Dean and Luiz André Barroso's 2013 paper on tail latency then showed why averages mislead, and site-reliability practice reframed the limit as an objective carrying an allowance for failure.

Five positions are held, separable by the proposition each will sign.

  • The gate school. Signs: a budget with no automatic consequence decays within two quarters. Will not sign: that elasticity must justify the number.
  • The objective school. Signs: the correct number of breaches is not zero; unspent allowance is waste. Will not sign: a blocking threshold on a lab measurement.
  • The field-data school. Signs: budget only what is measured on real users at a stated percentile. Will not sign: a synthetic test carrying a consequence.
  • The competitive school. Signs: the only defensible target is faster than the nearest alternative by a perceptible margin. Will not sign: thresholds imported from elsewhere.
  • The unit-cost school, new with generative products. Signs: the binding limit is cost per request, latency derived from it. Will not sign: that time is the primary currency.

Deeptha's customer is the competitive school with a contract; Devanand is the gate school, Dinesh the field-data school, Dhruti the objective and unit-cost positions at once.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Expert practice begins with decomposition, because an undivided limit cannot be enforced against anyone. Saltgrid's 800 ms splits across five stages, with September's measurements beside it.
