The measured columns carry no total, for two reasons. The bureau row covers bureau-touching decisions only, the other four all decisions, so the stage sums mix bases. More fundamentally they sum to 315 ms and 1,390 ms while the end-to-end figures are 310 ms and 1,240 ms. Both pairs are correct, because percentiles do not add: reaching the 95th percentile of all five stages at once is rare, so the parts exceed the percentile of the whole. A budget written as a sum of per-stage percentile targets is therefore stricter than the end-to-end target it serves.

The second piece concerns fan-out. A Saltgrid decision touches six internal services. If each independently exceeds its own 99th percentile on one call in a hundred, the chance a decision touches at least one slow service is not 1 per cent but 1 − 0.996 = 5.85 per cent — about 2.46 lakh of the month's 42 lakh decisions. So per-service tail targets must tighten as fan-out widens, or the end-to-end tail is set by arithmetic no service owner sees. Real tails correlate, pushing the figure below 5.85 per cent while making slow calls arrive in bursts.

The third piece is usually implicit: a latency budget is also a capacity budget. By Little's Law, requests in flight equal arrival rate times mean residence time. Saltgrid's month-end peak is 60 decisions a second at a mean of 0.42 s, so 60 × 0.42 = 25.2 are in flight against 32 workers, a utilisation of 78.8 per cent. In the simplest single-queue model response time scales as 1 ÷ (1 − ρ) and waiting as ρ ÷ (1 − ρ): at ρ = 0.7875 the first factor is 4.71 against 2.50 at the mid-month baseline of 0.60, reading as 1.88 times worse at month-end. Both halves are wrong for a pool. M/M/1 puts the mean wait at 0.7875 ÷ 0.2125 × 0.42 s = 1.56 s; Erlang-C over the same 32 servers, 0.42 s service and 60 arrivals a second gives about 8.5 ms at ρ = 0.7875 and 0.17 ms at 0.60. The single queue overstates the absolute wait by two orders of magnitude and understates the month-end worsening — about fifty times, not 1.88. Headroom near the knee is not linear.

4. When it applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions can be stated as tests. One: the quantity is measured on real users, continuously, at a stated percentile. Saltgrid passes — every decision is traced. Sparrowline only partly: traces arrive for 2.93 million of 3.8 million sessions, or 77.1 per cent, and the missing 870,000 sit on the cheapest handsets. The first act of budgeting there is to fix coverage, not pick a limit.

Two: the limit binds against something the team wants. Both pass, which is why both arguments hurt. Three: degradation is cumulative and hard to attribute. Saltgrid passes — its 95th percentile rose through four releases with no culprit. Sparrowline fails outright: one model swap moved 1,300 ms, and where a single decision dominates, a budget is bureaucracy around a choice that should just be made. Four: an owner exists who can both spend and refuse. Sparrowline passes it, Dhruti owning both currencies herself. Saltgrid fails it — the real content of Devanand and Dinesh's disagreement: nobody owns the bureau call.

The idea misleads in three situations. Where value is a step function — a regulated cut-off, a settlement window — a deadline is the instrument, since being 40 per cent under is worth nothing. Where the quantity is off the critical path, a budget buys engineering nobody feels. And in a re-platforming, a gate blocks the only route to meeting it.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

The sharpest case is the budgeted resource you do not own. Saltgrid allocates 300 of its 800 ms to the bureau, 37.5 per cent of a limit it buys rather than engineers, while the bureau's contract commits only to a 95th percentile of 900 ms. Thirty-eight per cent of decisions touch it; the other 62 per cent are repeat borrowers served from a 30-day cache. The whole population's 95th percentile falls inside the bureau group, but only if the cache-served 62 per cent contribute no breaches — which Exhibit 1 does not show, since the four non-bureau stages' p95s sum to 830 ms and the slowest tenants carry the largest rule-sets. On the most favourable reading, (95 − 62) ÷ 38 requires at least 86.8 per cent of bureau-touching decisions under 800 ms, and more for every cache-served decision that misses. Deeptha is committing to a percentile of the bureau-path end-to-end distribution that nobody has measured.

Multi-product organisations hit a shared-shell problem: Saltgrid's design system is 186 KB of the console's payload, used by all five squads, and no squad will fund its reduction. The answer is a separate, centrally owned allocation for shared code, which mature companies do and rarely publish. Two-sided products hit an attention asymmetry: operators budget the consumer app tightly and leave seller tooling unbudgeted until seller latency constrains supply. Regulated products carry mandatory work on the critical path — Saltgrid's audit write cannot be removed, so it is budgeted at 90 ms and defended, not optimised. Hardware is budgeted per stock-keeping unit, a fleet holding devices the budget-setters never held. AI-native products budget time and rupees at once.

6. Eight nuances that separate expert from competent

Percentiles of parts exceed percentiles of wholes. The tell-tale sign is a decomposition summing past the measured total, as Exhibit 1 does at 1,390 against 1,240. That reads as a miscount; in fact both are right, and the allocation needs a slack term.

A population percentile lives inside a subpopulation. When one branch is slow and carries more than the tail share, the headline percentile is governed by at least a much lower percentile of that branch — the 86.8th for Saltgrid, higher if the fast branch breaches at all. The tell-tale sign is a team optimising that branch's median while the overall 95th will not move: the work hit the wrong percentile.

A gate without a documented override gets an undocumented one. The tell-tale sign is a skip label in commit messages, or a check whose failure rate falls to zero a month after it is made blocking. That reads as compliance; in fact an exception path has formed. Write the override into policy, with an approver and a visible count.

Laboratory budgets measure a device nobody owns. The tell-tale sign is a laboratory figure and a field figure moving in opposite directions across one release. That reads as a broken rig; usually both are sound, and the rig's device, network and cache state are simply not the fleet's. Synthetic tests are worth having — the only measurement available before shipping — but on a separate, looser budget; only the field budget carries a consequence.

Telemetry coverage biases the budget in a known direction. Sparrowline's traces cover 77.1 per cent of sessions and miss the slowest handsets. The tell-tale sign is coverage and the metric improving together. That reads as a win on both; in fact the comparison runs between two populations.

A budget in one currency is met by spending another. The tell-tale sign is the budgeted metric improving while an unbudgeted one — offline failure rate, battery drain, cost per request — degrades in the same release. That is not cheating; it is what a constraint does. Budget the second before enforcing the first.

A fleet average that breaches conceals a device that breaches badly. The tell-tale sign is a weighted mean just over the limit. That reads as a small general problem; it is usually a large local one, and the diagnostic is to recompute per segment.

Zero breaches is evidence of a loose budget, not a tight team. The tell-tale sign is a quarter in which the gate blocked nothing while the field metric drifted. That reads as a disciplined team; more often the limit was set where nothing lives. A limit that never binds measures nothing, and one blocking a quarter of builds has become the design process.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

The real differences are these. Consumer products can price latency in conversion, the population being large enough to measure elasticity. Enterprise products often cannot, since the user does not choose the product, so the budget becomes a renewal question — hence Saltgrid's clause. Platforms must budget the slowest participant, not the average, and publish the allocation, because tenants build against it. Hardware budgets are per-SKU and effectively permanent. AI products are the genuine addition: rupees per request is a budgeted quantity in its own right, trading against latency through model size and context length, and streaming splits time-to-first-token from time-to-complete.

Stage matters less than is claimed. A seed-stage team with one surface needs one number and the habit of looking at it, not a table. What changes with scale is ownership: the table appears when more than one team can spend the same resource, a structural threshold rather than a headcount one. The claim that budgets are a late-stage discipline does not survive Sparrowline, whose cost budget is already urgent at 40 engineers.

8. Three worked cases

8.1 Saltgrid's byte allocation: a ceiling divided before the work began

By December 2025 the console's payload had reached 980 KB. Deeptha set a 420 KB ceiling and divided it before any work began.

Exhibit 2. Saltgrid console payload against allocation, by squad, in kilobytes; brackets are deficits.
SquadCurrent (KB)Allocation (KB)Deficit (KB)
Shell and design system (shared)186150(36)
Origination262110(152)
Collections21485(129)
Reporting19650(146)
Integrations12225(97)
Total980420(560)

Every one of the five squads is over its allocation, deliberately: headroom anywhere invites trading before any reduction happens. Reporting was cut from 196 KB to 50, its charting library having loaded on every page for a screen 4 per cent of sessions reached. Nine months later the payload was 468 KB — a miss against 420, and the first fall in three years.

8.2 Sparrowline's two currencies, and a symmetric comparison

First, what the three latency figures are. The 1,100 ms, 2,400 ms and 1,650 ms are component sums on Sparrowline's reference handset and network — a bench decomposition, not a field statistic. Exhibit 3 is the field distribution of per-session median time to first audio, and the two do not coincide: 760,000 of the 2,930,000 traced sessions, or 25.9 per cent, sit under 1.2 s and 38.2 per cent in the next bucket, so interpolation puts the median traced session near 1.70 s against the 1,100 ms bench figure. That 600 ms is nuance four's gap, on a population that already excludes the slowest handsets.

Dhruti compared adopting the new model now against holding it for a latency programme. The rubric predicted a 3.0-point gain in the share of sessions reaching turn eight, with probability 0.55 that the gain is real at that size, the experiment being incomplete. A prior within-user test put the cost of moving time to first audio from 1.1 s to 2.4 s at 4.0 points, with probability 0.80.

Exhibit 3. Sparrowline sessions with usable traces, by median time to first audio, September 2026.
Time to first audioSessionsReaching turn 8Share reaching turn 8
Under 1.2 s760,000486,40064.0%
1.2 to 2.0 s1,120,000660,80059.0%
2.0 to 3.0 s680,000346,80051.0%
Over 3.0 s370,000155,03041.9%
Total / pooled share2,930,0001,649,03056.3%

Footnote: the rows cover only the 2,930,000 sessions with usable traces, so the slowest handsets are under-represented. The total row holds the pooled ratio, 1,649,030 ÷ 2,930,000, not the mean of the four rows. The cross-sectional gap between fastest and slowest rows is 22.1 points, far larger than the 4.0-point within-user estimate used below, plausibly because slow sessions also carry cheaper handsets and worse networks; reading 22.1 as a causal coefficient is the central error available here.

The third option is not adopting the model at all, which scores 0 on this scale, and it is the one the arithmetic favours. Shipping now has an expected value of (3.0 × 0.55) − (4.0 × 0.80) = 1.65 − 3.20 = −1.55 points. Holding keeps the same weighted gain and changes the cost leg: the programme has probability 0.60 of bringing time to first audio to 1,650 ms, where the estimated cost is 1.5 points, and 0.40 of leaving it at 4.0. Expected cost is 0.60 × 1.5 + 0.40 × 4.0 = 2.50, weighted by the same 0.80 to give 2.00, so expected value is 1.65 − 2.00 = −0.35 points. The delay must be weighted too, and here Dhruti's first version went wrong: it divided a probability-weighted gain by a certain six weeks, when on the programme's own 0.60 success probability and a ten-week fallback the expected delay is 0.60 × 6 + 0.40 × 10 = 7.6 weeks. Weighting the gain while treating the delay as certain makes holding look cheaper than it is.

Taken alone the points say hold the model indefinitely, and the calculation omits the ₹64.6 lakh a month it adds, which argues the same way. What takes Dhruti past them sits outside the calculation: the figures price one release's effect on reaching turn eight, while the rubric gain is her only lever on retention beyond it, and the latency cost is removable by engineering, as the programme's 750 ms on first-token time shows. A decision resting on judgement the numbers do not contain should say so, and attach a budget to the leg they left out.

8.3 Stillwater Instruments: a budget that failed on the dimension it did not name

Stillwater, in Coimbatore, sells diagnostic laboratories a battery-powered point-of-care blood analyser with a companion app; 7,400 units sit across three SKUs. In March 2026 its product lead, Dakshitha Kedila, budgeted the 95th-percentile time from sample to displayed result, enforced it as a release gate, and met it on the median device within two months. In July the field-service queue tripled.

Exhibit 4. Stillwater: time from sample to result, 95th percentile, by SKU, July 2026.
SKUUnitsBudget (s)Measured (s)
S-100 (2023 flash controller)1,3309.011.8
S-200 (2024)3,4207.07.4
S-300 (2026)2,6506.05.6
Total / fleet-weighted average7,4007.007.55

Footnote: units are a sum; the time columns are averages weighted by units, 51,810 ÷ 7,400 and 55,842 ÷ 7,400. Applying "a SKU breaches when measured exceeds budget": S-100 by 2.8 s, S-200 by 0.4 s, S-300 not at all — two of three, covering 4,750 of the 7,400 units, or 64.2 per cent.

Two things had gone wrong, and only the second was interesting. The first was segmentation: the budget was verified on the S-200, which had itself since drifted 0.4 s past its limit, and a fleet-weighted 7.55 s against 7.00 looked like a 0.55-second general problem while concealing a 2.8-second one on 1,330 units. The second was substitution: the cheapest way to meet a device-side budget was to move analysis to the cloud, which cut on-device work by 340 ms a run and left the operator waiting 90 seconds for a timeout whenever the laboratory's connection dropped. Offline behaviour was not budgeted, so it was free, so it was spent. Recovery took eleven weeks: a per-SKU table, a second budget on time-to-usable-result with the network disconnected, and a gate converted into a weekly allowance report.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

  1. The decorative budget. Early sign: the number appears in quarterly reviews but in no check. Diagnostic: what shipped late because of it? Caught late, the next budget has no credibility.
  2. Substitution. Early sign: the budgeted metric improves while an unbudgeted quantity moves with it. Diagnostic: what did we spend here? Stillwater paid eleven weeks.
  3. The unowned allocation. Early sign: one row has no name against it. Diagnostic: who can refuse a claim on this allowance? Caught late, at renewal, with credits attached.
  4. The ratcheted gate. Early sign: the limit tightens after every good quarter. Diagnostic: what did the last 200 ms buy a user? Caught late, it spends a roadmap on nothing perceptible.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Gate or allowance. The gate position, steelmanned: decay is the only certain failure mode, attention the scarcest input, and automation the only mechanism surviving a reorganisation; the evidence is payloads growing wherever nothing blocks them. It is wrong if the exception path becomes routine. The allowance position: a limit never breached is set in the wrong place, and what matters is spending allowance deliberately. It is wrong if nobody is accountable for a budget merely reported.

Is latency causal, and at what size? The strong position rests on injected-delay experiments, randomised and hence causal: a widely cited Amazon result from 2006 put 100 ms at about 1 per cent of sales, and Jake Brutlag's 2009 Google experiment measured 0.59 per cent fewer searches per user from an injected 400 ms delay. The sceptical position holds that published elasticities come from a handful of unusual products, that observational estimates — like Exhibit 3's 22.1-point spread — are dominated by device and network confounding, and that the answer for any one product is unknown until it runs its own injected-delay test, which is cheap and almost never run.

What currency binds in AI-native products. One camp holds that cost per request is the real budget and latency downstream of it; the other that users notice time, not rupees, so a cost budget is finance dressed as a product constraint. Sparrowline's figures support both: ₹7.75 crore a year is company-scale, 1,300 ms user-scale.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this divides before measuring, because an undivided limit has no owner. They state population and percentile in the same breath as the number, and refuse a figure without them. They name the second currency before enforcing the first, a constraint redirecting cost rather than removing it. Asked whether a budget works, they say how often it bound.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Deeptha signed a modified clause. The 800 ms commitment covers the 62 per cent of decisions served without a bureau call; bureau-touching decisions carry a separate 1,400 ms commitment, the bureau's contribution reported monthly as a line item Saltgrid does not own. Devanand got his gate on the four stages Saltgrid controls, with an override requiring Deeptha's signature and a published count; Dinesh got per-tenant allocations for rule evaluation. One number over a mixed population had been the defect, not its strictness.

Dhruti held the model, to ship at 1,650 ms on the reference path after an expected 7.6 weeks, and set two budgets, each with its statistic and population named. On the field distribution of per-session medians, 3,000 ms at the 90th percentile — a ceiling Exhibit 3 already breaches, since only 87.4 per cent of traced sessions come in under 3.0 s. And ₹0.32 per completed turn, which the shipped model breaches on day one by ₹0.06, the gap owned by the model team rather than written off. She funded trace coverage first, since a budget set against 77.1 per cent of sessions is set against the wrong population.

  1. Saltgrid's split commitment makes the reported figure harder to interpret. When does a two-number commitment serve the customer better than one looser one?
  2. Sparrowline funded telemetry coverage before setting a limit. What would have to be true of the missing 870,000 sessions for that sequencing to be wrong?
  3. Stillwater replaced a blocking gate with a weekly report after it was satisfied by relocating work. Was the gate the problem, or the budgeted quantity — and what evidence would distinguish them?

13. Going deeper

  • Scalability and performance — supplies the models a budget allocates against; without them the table is arithmetic only.
  • Testing and quality basics — a budget is enforceable only as a test; the lab-versus-field split is one too.
  • Bug triage and severity — latency regressions arrive as low-severity reports and need a rule of their own.
  • Release management and launch readiness — where the consequence lives: gate, override and approver are release objects.
  • Staged rollouts and rollback — how allowance is spent safely, and why a breach need not be an incident.
  • Incident management and postmortems — turns a breach into a changed allocation, not a tightened number.
  • SLAs, SLOs and error budgets — the formal generalisation, and the vocabulary Deeptha's clause needed.
exp20v2-qo.performance.budget:
Performance budgets

1. A Monday in September

On Monday 14 September 2026, Chithra Janardhanan, head of product at Rivulet Bazaar, opened a one-page memo she had asked for the previous Thursday. Rivulet Bazaar is a Kochi-based grocery ordering app with about 1.4 million monthly active users, mostly on Android phones costing around ₹9,000. Her analyst, Cibin Jayasooryan, had taken 60,000 home-screen sessions from the week of 31 August to 6 September and sorted them by how long the first usable product grid took to appear.

The table was uncomfortable: the slowest sessions converted at half the rate of the fastest.

Exhibit 1. Home-screen sessions by time to first usable product grid, week of 31 August to 6 September 2026
Load-time bucketSessionsOrdersOrders per 100 sessions
Under 2.0 s18,0001,2607.0
2.0 to 3.0 s24,0001,4406.0
3.0 to 4.0 s11,0005505.0
Over 4.0 s7,0002453.5
Total / average (pooled)60,0003,4955.83

Interpolating inside the buckets, the median session loaded in 2.5 seconds, but the 75th-percentile session (the point below which three-quarters of sessions fall) took about 3.3. The festival campaign opening on 12 October carried ₹2.4 crore of acquisition spend aimed at 5,00,000 first sessions, mostly in smaller cities. At the current mix and the unrounded 5.825 orders per 100 sessions, that traffic yields at most about 29,100 orders; smaller-city sessions may sit nearer the 3.5 to 5.0 buckets. Each full point of conversion was worth 5,000 orders.

The decision on her desk was not whether to make the app faster. Charles Jayanarayanan, the Android engineering lead, proposed a hard rule: a build whose home screen missed a stated limit would fail its automated checks and could not ship. Marketing wanted three promotional features on that screen before 12 October, and the rule would delay some. Charles said the figure had crept up in each of the last four releases and would probably keep doing so without the rule.

2. The idea

A performance budget is a numerical limit on a measurable property of the product, such as load time, bytes transferred or response latency, that the team agrees in advance not to exceed, with a named owner and a defined consequence when the limit is crossed. Like a financial budget, it is a ceiling divided among competing claims.

The problem it was invented to solve is gradual decay. Nobody decides to make a product slow; each addition is defensible alone, and the sum is a product no one chose. The practice was articulated for the web in the early 2010s, with Tim Kadlec's 2013 writing on setting a performance budget among the best-known early statements, building on years of work by Steve Souders and others on front-end speed. Google's RAIL model (2015) and Core Web Vitals (2020) later supplied shared thresholds; a "good" Largest Contentful Paint, for instance, is 2.5 seconds or less at the 75th percentile of real visits.

Chithra's sentence for the meeting was this:

Every feature spends seconds and kilobytes from a budget we agreed in advance, and a feature that does not fit has to be paid for by removing something else.

3. How it actually works

A working budget has seven steps.

First, choose a metric that tracks what the user experiences, here "time to first usable product grid" rather than "server response time". Second, choose the percentile and the reference conditions. Rivulet chose the 75th percentile, a ₹9,000-class phone with 3 GB of memory, and the Lighthouse slow-4G profile of 1.6 Mbps and a 150 ms round trip. Third, set the number from evidence, whether outcome data or an accepted external threshold, not taste; Exhibit 1 shows what slowness costs Rivulet. Fourth, split the total into component budgets so that each team can tell what it is spending. Fifth, measure continuously, in the lab on every build and in the field on real users. Sixth, wire enforcement into the release process. Seventh, name an owner for the number and for the exception process.

The implicit steps: state the percentile, because a median hides the slowest quarter; give the gate a noise tolerance, since a single lab run can wander, perhaps by a tenth of a second, so Rivulet takes the median of five; and provide an exception route, or engineers will treat the gate as an obstacle.

4. A worked example

Cibin borrowed the 2,500-millisecond target at the 75th percentile from the Core Web Vitals threshold (Exhibit 1's decline is smooth and has no knee at 2.5 seconds), split it into five lines, and measured the app in the lab.

Exhibit 2. Time budget against current lab-measured spend for the home screen, in milliseconds; stage figures are lab p75 values added together, not the p75 of the total
StageBudgetCurrentOver (+) or under (−)
Network round trips and server700800+100
Downloading critical bytes6001,100+500
Decoding and drawing images500750+250
App start-up and layout400650+250
Reserve for variation3000−300
Total2,5003,300+800

The download line is where the plan lives or dies. At 1.6 Mbps, a payload of 120 kilobytes is 960 kilobits and takes 960 / 1,600 = 0.6 seconds, exactly the 600 ms line. The home screen currently moves 220 kilobytes before it is usable (1,760 kilobits, or 1.1 seconds). The network line follows the same logic: four round trips at 150 ms plus 100 ms on the server is 700 ms. The app therefore carries a byte budget of 120 KB: 30 KB of product data, eight thumbnails at 7 KB each (56 KB), 20 KB of fonts and a 14 KB banner. Those items sum to 120.

Second pass. Change one input: the reference connection falls from 1.6 to 1.2 Mbps, which is plausible for the smaller cities the campaign targets. The same 120 KB now takes 960 / 1,200 = 0.8 seconds, which is 200 ms over its line, and the whole budget is breached unless something is cut. To fit 600 ms at 1.2 Mbps the payload must be 600 ms × 1.2 Mbps = 720 kilobits, or 90 KB, so 30 KB must go. Shrinking the thumbnails to 5 KB each saves 16 KB (8 × 2), and deferring the banner until after first paint saves the other 14. The new total is 30 + 40 + 20 + 0 = 90 KB. The method was unchanged; the answer moved, and the choice of what absorbs the cut became explicit.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

A budget is not a target, an SLO or a measurement

A target is a hope and a measurement is an observation. A service-level objective (SLO) is a promise about a service, usually with an allowed failure rate. A budget is a spending limit, divided among teams and enforced when crossed. All four use the same numbers, but only the budget changes what an engineer may merge.

The percentile is a policy decision

In Exhibit 1 the median session meets 2.5 seconds while the 75th-percentile session misses by about 0.8. A budget stated on the median would have told Chithra the app was fine. The percentile decides whose experience counts. Exhibit 1b makes the interpolation visible: the median sits on the budget line, the 75th percentile sits to its right.

Lab and field answer different questions

Lab measurement (a fixed device and network, run on each build) is repeatable and catches regressions the day they appear. Field measurement, or real-user monitoring, shows what customers experience, including devices nobody tested. A lab gate without field checks drifts from reality; field data without a lab gate arrives too late to prevent anything.

Exhibit 1 shows association, not cause

Slow sessions are disproportionately on weak phones and weak networks, and those customers may order less for reasons unrelated to speed. The gradient from 7.0 to 3.5 orders per 100 sessions is a reason to take speed seriously, not a forecast that fixing it recovers the difference. A cheap check compares conversion within one device tier across buckets.

Components can pass while the total fails

Component budgets locate responsibility, but they interact: smaller images lower the download line and may raise the decoding line if re-compressed in a costlier format. The end-to-end total is the budget; the components are the accounting.

A budget cannot say whether a feature is worth its cost

A budget prices what a feature spends; it cannot say whether the promotional carousel earns more than the 40 milliseconds it costs. That judgement stays with product management. A thoughtful newcomer should ask who set the number, from what data, at which percentile, and what happens on the day it is breached.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products

The mechanics are constant; the metric, reference condition and the person who feels the pain change.

Exhibit 3. Illustrative budget shapes by product type
TypeTypical budgeted measureWhose conditions set the reference
ConsumerTime to first usable screen, p75; bytes before first useThe cheapest phone and slowest network in the growth segment
B2BReport or dashboard generation, p95; API latency, p95The largest customer's data volume, on an office desktop
MarketplaceSearch results, p95; seller listing upload sizeBoth sides: a buyer on a weak phone and a seller on shared Wi-Fi

In consumer products users leave within seconds, so budgets are tight and tied to conversion. In B2B the user is often captive, so pain surfaces later as support tickets and renewal friction, and the budget is often written into contracts as an API latency commitment. In marketplaces a team that budgets only for buyers will find sellers abandoning listing flows on the phones they own.

An early-stage company of fifteen engineers can keep one budget in one person's head and enforce it by conversation. A large company needs a ledger, an owner per surface and automated gates, because no individual knows what every team shipped.

7. Common mistakes

Budgeting the average

The symptom is a green dashboard beside store reviews saying "slow". The misunderstanding is that a mean describes a typical user. The diagnostic: plot the 50th and 75th percentiles side by side, split by device tier.

A budget without an owner or a consequence

The symptom is a number creeping up 30 or 40 kilobytes a release while everyone agrees it matters. The misunderstanding is that a published number enforces itself. The diagnostic: who may block a release for breaching it, and ever has?

A lab-only budget

The symptom is green builds and unhappy customers. The misunderstanding is that a reproducible number is a representative one; the lab device no longer resembles the field. The diagnostic: compare lab and field figures for the same build over a week.

A number copied from a competitor

The symptom is a budget everyone meets trivially or no one can meet. The misunderstanding is that a borrowed limit has been tested against your own customers. Rivulet borrowed its 2.5 seconds and used Exhibit 1 to check that slowness cost it orders. The diagnostic: which of your data supports the number?

8. What good looks like

Handled well, the Monday memo carries four things on one page. It has a metric a customer would recognise, a percentile and reference condition stated in a sentence, and a threshold backed by Rivulet's own sessions. It splits the total into the five lines of Exhibit 2, each with a named team. It sets an exception rule, for example that any feature adding bytes must remove at least as many, or its owner must publish the request with a date to repay it. And it names the two people who can say no: Chithra for the number, Charles for the gate. On a bad release day the argument is then about arithmetic, not opinion.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

Chithra adopted the budget on 14 September, with two adjustments. The gate would initially fail builds only above 2,600 ms, a 100 ms tolerance, and tighten to 2,500 ms after the campaign, so that the first weeks taught the team how noisy its own measurements were. And of the three marketing features, the banner and one carousel would ship only after the thumbnails and fonts had shrunk to the byte line. Her reasoning was that the 0.8-second gap in Exhibit 2 could not be closed by willpower, but it could be closed by a ledger on which every kilobyte had a name beside it.

To go further, study scalability and performance, the topic this one builds on, to learn how to measure latency and throughput properly, and then real-user monitoring, which turns a budget from a rule into a feedback loop. Post-launch operations, where budgets live, are the block most often missing from product programmes.

Two questions to sit with. Rivulet's budget protects its slowest quarter of sessions. Who, in your product, is invisible at the percentile you currently watch? And if a feature you believe in does not fit the budget, what are you prepared to remove to pay for it?
exp40v2-qo.testing:
Testing and quality basics

Unit, integration, end-to-end, exploratory — and the question underneath all four: what must be true before real users can reach this change?

1. Two release candidates, a day apart

On Monday 6 April 2026, in a converted textile shed off Bengaluru's Hosur Road, Bhuvanesh Iraiyappan had a release candidate and a festival. He is director of product at Porunai Daily, a grocery app with 4.2 million monthly active users and about 1.9 million sessions a day. Release 7.4 rewrote the checkout basket so one order could split across a UPI handle and the app's stored wallet: 214 commits on a branch cut the previous Thursday. Marketing had bought inventory against a demand peak beginning Wednesday. His engineering lead, Balamurugan Indupalli, wanted a week of exploratory work on the new payment states. Against that, Iraiyappan held a feature flag that switched the basket off for every user in about ninety seconds. The question was never whether 7.4 was correct, but how much uncertainty to buy down before release, given how cheaply he could buy it down after.

Some three hundred and sixty kilometres by road to the south-south-west, on Tuesday 7 April, Bijoya Immandi faced the same question with every sign reversed. She is vice-president of product at Pothigai Systems, a Coimbatore firm whose combined point-of-sale and weighing terminal sits on the counter of 38,000 kirana shops and pharmacies. Firmware 3.9 let the GST rate table refresh over the air and changed the tare-weight routine. The second touched the computation deciding the weight a customer pays for, which under the Legal Metrology Act 2009 makes the instrument's verification stale — so that half could not ship over the air at all. And Immandi had no flag. A terminal that stopped booting meant a technician in a van: ₹2,400 a visit, 23 days median to clear a state.

2. The idea, and the four schools that will not agree about it

Testing is the deliberate execution of a system to find out where it is wrong. Glenford Myers put it starkly in The Art of Software Testing (1979): testing is executing a program with the intent of finding errors, so a test that finds nothing has failed. Dijkstra supplied the boundary condition — testing shows the presence of defects, never their absence. Every argument here sits in that gap.

The four tiers are distinctions of scope, not of virtue. A unit test exercises one unit of behaviour with collaborators replaced by doubles: milliseconds to run, and it names the line when it fails. An integration test exercises a seam you own — your service against your schema, your consumer against a provider's contract. An end-to-end test drives the assembled system through a user's interface, and so fails for reasons unrelated to the change. Exploratory testing is a person with a charter, a time box and a question, designing tests while running them; Cem Kaner named it in the 1980s and Jonathan Bach's session-based test management (2000) made it accountable without a script.

The tiers were invented against one pathology: where testing happened only at the end, debugging was unbounded and nobody could say what remained. Boehm's cost-of-change curve (1981) gave that a number, Kent Beck's test-driven development (2002) a discipline, Cohn's pyramid (2009) a shape. Then the shape became doctrine and four schools formed.

The unit-centric school signs that defects are cheapest to find where the least code is in scope; it will not sign that a passing unit suite says anything about whether the product works. The integration-weighted school — Spotify's honeycomb, Kent C. Dodds' testing trophy (2018) — signs that products fail at their seams, not inside their functions; it will not sign that integration tests are affordable at unit granularity. The human-centred school of James Bach and Michael Bolton signs that only a thinking tester finds the defect nobody specified, and not that coverage measures anything. The production-first school — Charity Majors on observability, Google's SRE error-budget model (2016) — signs that at scale the honest test environment is production, and will not sign that this excuses shipping untested code.

3. Mechanics: containment arithmetic, worked

Experts reason about containment, not tiers. The formal treatment is phase containment effectiveness: for each stage, the defects it found divided by those still open when it began. Porunai reconstructed this for 7.4 six weeks on, taking all 48 defects attributed to the branch and asking where each was first found.

Figure 1. Where each of release 7.4's 48 defects was first seen. Containment before general availability: 46 of 48, or 95.8 per cent.

Read the containment column rather than the counts and the practice changes shape. Unit tests caught the most defects outright, 21. But no stage contained a higher share of what reached it than exploratory testing's 8 of the 13 still open, or 61.5 per cent — above unit's 43.8 per cent, above canary and beta's 60.0, above every automated stage. That follows from ordering rather than merit: each automated stage hands its successor a residue enriched in the defects it is blind to, and a human with a charter is blind to a different set. Indupalli's phrase: the suite filters out the defects you have imagined.

The second-order effect is that remediation cost is a property of when a defect is found, not of the defect. Porunai timed its fixes at a loaded ₹1,800 an hour.

Table 1 — Release 7.4: defects by stage of discovery and the hours they consumed.

Hours are first response plus fix plus verification; the escaped row also carries support, the hotfix train and customer communication, and has no containment share because nothing followed it. Weighted mean over all 48: 224.8 ÷ 48 = 4.68 hours, ₹4,04,640 in all.

Two defects — 2 of 48, 4.2 per cent of them — consumed 92 of the 224.8 hours, 40.9 per cent of the effort. That ratio, not Boehm's curve, is the number to carry. It also exposes the implicit step: nobody had written down why 140 end-to-end tests and five two-hour charters were the right investment. The charters produced 8 defects in 10 session-hours, 0.80 per session-hour; the suite produced 5. Neither figure says whether to buy more until you know what a miss costs — and that is set outside the test plan, by how fast you see a defect in production and how cheaply you undo it.

Figure 2. Both firms run the same four pre-release stages, then diverge: Porunai's lane ends in a flag flip, Pothigai's in a van. The recovery arrow prices every box above.

4. The conditions, stated so they can be tested

That detection may be moved after release is not a philosophy. It is three conditions, each checkable.

One: the post-release window must be large enough to see the incidence you care about. With per-session failure probability p and n exposed sessions, the chance of seeing a defect at least once is 1 − (1 − p)n, and the sessions needed for a 95 per cent chance are ln(0.05) ÷ ln(1 − p). Porunai's canary runs at 1.5 per cent of traffic for ninety minutes — 1,781 sessions on a flat 1.9 million-session day, but its 21:00 to 22:30 window runs at 1.7 times the daily mean, so exposure is 3,028.

Table 2 — What Porunai's ninety-minute canary at 1.5 per cent of traffic can see.
Incidencep per sessionExpected in 3,028Chance of seeing it onceSessions for 95%
1 session in 1000.0100030.28over 99.99%299
1 session in 4000.002507.5799.95%1,197
1 session in 2,0000.000501.5178.01%5,990

Rows assume independent sessions and an incidence that does not vary by hour; the last column is rounded up.

So the canary is a competent instrument for a one-in-four-hundred defect and close to useless for a one-in-twenty-thousand one. Reaching 95 per cent on the rare class needs 59,914 sessions, 19.8 times the present window — about fifty hours at 1.5 per cent of traffic at the day's mean rate, or the same ninety peak minutes at a shade under 30 per cent. Iraiyappan can buy that; Immandi cannot. Her first ring of 400 terminals has a 35.9 per cent chance of exposing a defect that bricks one terminal in 900; 95 per cent needs 2,695. The rings were sized for blast radius, and nobody had computed what they see.

Two: recovery must be cheap and fast relative to the harm done while you wait. Ninety seconds against ₹2,400 and 23 days is not a difference of degree. Three: the harm accruing during detection must be reversible. Here the idea turns actively misleading. Money moved is not reversible, nor a weight a customer paid for, nor a lapsed verification cured by rollback. On those surfaces the pyramid-versus-production argument is a category error, as is any appeal to the pyramid where risk lives in configuration and third-party contracts rather than your own logic.

5. Hard edges

In a multi-product company the hard problem is the shared library. Porunai's payments module serves the consumer app and a seller tool, and a provider change that satisfies the provider's own tests can still break a consumer. That is what consumer-driven contract tests exist for: the provider runs its consumers' expectations in its own pipeline, so the seam has an owner. Two-sided products add a trap, because a change can be right on every buyer screen and wrong in the buyer-seller pairing, which is nobody's page.

Regulated surfaces turn test evidence into an artefact. Pothigai's weighing path cannot be revised over the air without re-verification, so its test records are documentation a Legal Metrology inspector may ask for — which changes what a test must record, not merely whether it passes. Hardware adds the constraint with no software analogue: no rollback, only recall, so device-in-the-loop rigs and golden units carry the weight a web team puts on canaries.

AI-native features break the oracle. Porunai's substitution recommender has no correct answer, only a rubric, so its gate is an evaluation set: 1,200 historical orders, a required 92 per cent top-1 agreement with human raters. Build 7.4 scored 93.1 per cent. The standard error on that proportion over 1,200 items is 0.73 points, so the 95 per cent interval runs 91.7 to 94.5 — and the threshold sits inside it. The gate passed, but the data cannot distinguish this recommender from one sitting exactly on the threshold. At organisational seams the same holds for people: the two teams whose contract nobody owns are the two whose defects nobody predicted. Mature firms say no release ships without a full regression pass, and in fact run a reduced suite, a canary and a named on-call engineer, keeping the full suite nightly.

6. Eight things an expert sees differently

Coverage detects a necessary condition; it does not measure quality. Untested code is a risk; tested code is not thereby correct. The tell is coverage climbing while escapes sit flat — Porunai gained 22.8 points and nothing moved. The obvious reading is that they tested the wrong things; the truer one is that coverage counts lines executed, not states or inputs visited.

Flakiness compounds with suite size, and destroys a gate rather than degrading it. If each of N tests fails spuriously with probability f, a run is clean with probability (1 − f)N. Pothigai's 2,400 device-in-the-loop tests at f = 0.001 give 9.06 per cent: a clean run takes about 11.0 attempts, and runs average 2.4 spurious failures — 2.64 among the runs that actually fail. The tell is retry counts; the obvious reading, that a few bad tests need fixing, misses the exponent.

Figure 3. Pothigai's device-in-the-loop suite, 2,400 tests. A flake rate most engineers would call negligible leaves under a tenth of runs clean.

A test double is a frozen belief about somebody else's system. True when written, it decays silently. The tell is a mock whose last edit predates the provider's last schema change — a question a product manager can ask without reading code. Mocks are not bad practice; a mock is a claim, and claims need an expiry, which a contract test supplies.

Exploratory testing is not manual regression testing. Its output is not a pass or a fail but new test cases and questions: hypothesis generation, charter-driven and time-boxed. The tell is whether a session leaves written charters and a debrief. A team whose exploratory day is a re-walked checklist has bought the cost and none of the yield, then concludes the practice fails.

The denominator of a defect rate is sessions, not users, and tickets are not incidence. A one-in-four-hundred-sessions defect reaches 3.3 per cent of users inside a month — about 1.4 lakh at Porunai's scale — if every user averaged the 13.6 sessions that 1.9 million a day across 4.2 million monthly actives implies. Dispersed usage pulls the real reach below that, and the 13.6 assumes monthly actives are the base producing the sessions. Neither caveat shows in the session rate, which is the point. Tickets are a filtered, lagging proxy whose ratio to incidence nobody measures. The tell is quoting tickets as prevalence; ask what share of affected sessions produced one.

The cost-of-late-detection curve is right in direction and weakly sourced in magnitude. Laurent Bossavit's The Leprechauns of Software Engineering (2015) traced the famous ten- and hundred-times multipliers to thin, non-reproducible origins. An expert argues direction — here 0.4 hours against 46 — from data of their own. The tell is citing a hundredfold without naming the dataset.

The least-tested path with the largest blast radius is usually the recovery path. Rollbacks, flag flips, back-fills and firmware fallbacks are exercised rarely and under stress. The tell is a runbook never executed in anger. Porunai's flag flip is the whole justification for shipping early, so it is the one behaviour to rehearse every release rather than assume.

Some quality attributes are structurally invisible to assertions. A button that fits “Pay” and breaks on the Tamil string, a screen reader reading a price as a date, copy accurate and alarming — all pass and fail with users. The tell is a defect class arriving only through reviews or support. The answer is eyes, on a schedule, in the languages shipped.

7. How this differs by product type and by stage

Consumer products have cheap rollback and enormous samples, so detection can legitimately move right: Table 2's formula is universal, but its useful rows need sample size, and only traffic supplies it. Business and enterprise products invert both terms, because one tenant may be the whole sample. Pothigai's largest pharmacy customer holds 1,900 of the 38,000 terminals, 5 per cent of the fleet, and will not agree to be a canary; its acceptance window is a contractual artefact, not a test stage, and detection cannot move right because there is no anonymous crowd to move it into. Platforms and marketplaces live on versioned contracts and deprecation windows; hardware cannot roll back at all; AI products replace the boolean with a distribution, so the gate needs an interval and a sample size.

Stage matters less than people claim, and in a specific way. At seed stage exploratory testing plus a flag genuinely dominates, because the regression surface fits in one head. Automation starts paying when it stops fitting — a function of surface area and staff turnover, not headcount. At scale the work shifts again, from writing tests to managing their reliability, because Figure 3 arrives. What does not change is the first question: how fast would we see this, and what would it cost to undo?

8. Three worked examples

The first is small and went right. Porunai's refund service added an optional field and made an existing one nullable. The consumer-driven contract test in the payments module failed inside the provider's own pipeline: 1.6 engineer-hours from red to merged. Reaching all users it would have sat in the 46-hour column, a 28.8-fold difference — though those 46 hours carry support and hotfix work a contract-test fix never triggers, so the two are not like-for-like engineering time. The seam had an owner only because somebody wrote the consumer's expectations down.

The second is Immandi's rings. Ring 1 at 400 terminals gives a 35.9 per cent chance of exposing a one-in-900 bricking defect; ring 2 at 3,800 gives 98.5. Across the fleet the expected count is 38,000 ÷ 900 = 42.2 terminals, so at ₹2,400 a visit the direct remediation is about ₹1,01,333; stopped at ring 2 the expectation is 4.2 terminals, or ₹10,133. Immandi resized ring 1 to 2,700 terminals to reach the 95 per cent detection point.

The third failed, and is the useful one. Through the second half of 2025 Porunai ran a coverage programme: line coverage from 61.4 to 84.2 per cent across twenty releases.

Table 3 — Porunai, escaped defects by half-year. An escape is first reported after general availability.
WindowReleasesEscaped defectsEscapes per releaseLine coverage
Jan–Jun 202520402.0061.4%
Jul–Dec 2025 (coverage push)20412.0584.2%

The 1.65 is the pooled rate, 99 ÷ 60; with equal release counts it equals the mean of the three. Standard errors below treat escapes per window as Poisson.

Coverage rose 22.8 points and escapes went from 2.00 to 2.05 a release. The difference is 0.05 against a standard error of 0.45, which is 0.11 standard deviations: indistinguishable from nothing. The diagnosis, once Indupalli classified the 41 escapes, was that 26 lay in configuration, third-party responses and regional text rendering — places a unit test of Porunai's own logic would never have reached. The recovery added no unit tests at all. What it added was five exploratory charters a release, consumer-driven contracts on three provider seams, and the canary of Table 2. Escapes fell to 0.90 a release: a drop of 1.15 against a standard error of 0.38, or 3.0 standard deviations, and a 56.1 per cent reduction — while coverage slipped to 83.1 per cent. The windows are sequential and other things changed, so the confound is real. But the one thing that did not rise was coverage.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

The flaky suite. Early sign: merges that needed a retry. Diagnostic: what share of red builds last month were real? Caught late, the team has trained itself to ignore the gate, and the next real failure ships.

Happy-path-only coverage. Early sign: a ticket mix dominated by states no test visits — expired sessions, partial payments, denied permissions. Diagnostic: name the last test written for a failure state. Caught late, escapes cluster in recovery code.

Quality as a terminal phase. Early sign: lead time from branch cut to release lengthening as release frequency falls. Diagnostic: how many commits are in the candidate? Caught late, batch size has grown until no canary localises what broke.

No post-launch thinking. The most commonly missing block, in curricula and in practice: a release checklist with no monitoring, no adoption measure, nothing scheduled after day one. Early sign: the plan ends at launch. Diagnostic: who looks at this on day seven, and what would make them act? Caught late, the market does the testing.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Shape. The pyramid's defenders argue from latency and localisation: 9,100 unit tests running in four minutes give an engineer a hundred corrections a day, which no integration suite can. The honeycomb's defenders argue from where defects are — 26 of Porunai's 41 escapes sat outside its own logic. For the pyramid to be wrong, unit-level defects would have to be rare and cheap in a codebase; for the honeycomb to be wrong, integration tests would have to be as fast and diagnostic as unit tests. Both conditions are architecture-specific.

Where detection belongs. The production-first position rests on real evidence: no staging environment reproduces 1.9 million daily sessions, and canary and beta together caught three defects the four pre-release stages missed. The gate-first position rests on the three conditions of section four, all of which fail for Pothigai. For production-first to be wrong you need harm accruing faster than you can observe it, or recovery you cannot execute — Immandi's fleet exactly.

Coverage targets. One camp holds that a floor prevents the worst outcome, untested code shipped under deadline. The other holds that any number becomes a target and then a ritual, and points at 22.8 points for nothing. Settling it needs a controlled comparison nobody has run; what exists is one firm's three windows.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this asks which tests to write. Someone who has internalised it asks first how fast the defect would be visible and how expensive to undo, and only then allocates. They size a canary from an incidence they name out loud, so the gap between 3,028 sessions and 59,914 is a decision rather than a habit. They treat a flake rate as a product risk, not an engineering annoyance. They know which quality attributes no assertion can see. They rehearse the recovery path every release. And they can say what they decided not to test, and what that choice is worth.

12. What each of them did

Iraiyappan shipped 7.4 on Tuesday 7 April behind the flag, at 1.5 per cent of traffic and then into the store rollout's first 5 per cent step overnight — but he extended the first window from ninety minutes to roughly five hours: ninety peak minutes deliver 3,028 sessions and see a one-in-two-thousand defect 78.0 per cent of the time, and the 5,990 sessions Table 2 puts at the 95 per cent point take about five hours at the day's mean rate — under three if the peak rate held throughout, longer as traffic falls away overnight. He bought detection, not certainty. Immandi split firmware 3.9: the GST rate table shipped over the air through resized rings, and the tare-weight change went into a release requiring re-verification, scheduled with the Legal Metrology process rather than against it. She bought the only thing available to her, more testing before the van.

  1. Porunai's escapes fell 56.1 per cent while coverage slipped. What evidence would separate the charters, the contracts and the canary as causes, and what should Iraiyappan have instrumented in advance?
  2. Immandi moved ring 1 from 400 to 2,700 terminals. What has she given up, and under what incidence assumption would 400 have been the better choice?
  3. Both firms ran the same four pre-release stages. If each had to delete one permanently, which should each delete, and what does that imply about what the stages are for?

13. Going deeper

Deploying a web product
The prerequisite: testing becomes a real question once a deploy can reach users. It sets your recovery arrow.
Bug triage and severity
Containment says what you caught; triage decides what to do. The 46-hour column is its output.
Hardware quality: yield, reliability, field failure
Where Immandi's constraints come from; field failure is the hardware escape rate.
Release management and launch readiness
Turns section four's conditions into a checklist somebody signs.
Staged rollouts and rollback
Makes Table 2 operational: ring sizes, hold criteria, the rehearsed rollback.
Incident management and postmortems
What happens when escaped defects land, and how containment gets corrected.
SLAs, SLOs and error budgets
A principled answer to how much escape is acceptable.
Support and operational readiness
The detector you did not design. Section six took its denominator; this is its capacity.
Beta and early-access programmes
The sampling instrument for products too small for a statistical canary.
exp20v2-qo.testing:
Testing and Quality Basics

What must be tested before real users see this change?

1. A retry, a festival and a green dashboard

On Monday 26 October 2026, Akilan Haridoss, product manager for payments reliability at Nilavu Pay, a Chennai bill-payment app built on the UPI rails and the Bharat Bill Payment System (BBPS), had to decide whether a Thursday release would go out as planned. The change was a retry: when a customer's UPI debit succeeded but the biller's confirmation timed out, the app would ask the biller again instead of showing "payment failed". Of the app's 2,40,000 daily bill-payment attempts, 4.0 per cent, or 9,600, failed this way. The team expected the retry to cut that to 3.0 per cent, recovering 2,400 payments a day at about ₹14 of net revenue each. Diwali falls on Sunday 8 November, and festive-week volumes could only grow.

The automated pipeline was green. Aadhira Harishankar, head of engineering, saw no reason to wait. Abishek Hayagreevan, the QA lead, disagreed. The change touched 6,000 lines of code; the end-to-end suite had been skipped on the last two releases because it took 70 minutes and failed intermittently; and nobody had yet sat down and tried to break the feature by hand. A retry that fires twice charges a customer twice. Akilan had until Thursday to decide what "tested" would mean, and what saying so would cost.

2. The idea

Testing is the practice of running software on purpose, with a prediction of what should happen, to find where it does something else. Its sharpest early statement is Edsger Dijkstra's, around 1970: testing can show the presence of bugs, never their absence. The problem it addresses is older than the discipline: programmers inspecting their own work see what they intended, not what they wrote.

Practice divided into four layers. A unit test checks one small piece of code, such as a function that computes a retry delay, in isolation; Kent Beck's SUnit (1994) and its Java descendant JUnit made these cheap to write and fast to run. An integration test checks that separate components cooperate, such as the app server and a biller gateway. An end-to-end test drives the whole product as a user would, through screen, network and database. Exploratory testing, a term Cem Kaner introduced in the 1980s, is a skilled person designing and running tests simultaneously, letting each result decide the next. Mike Cohn's "test pyramid" (2009) argued for many fast tests at the base and few slow ones above.

Akilan's sentence for the meeting: "Each layer exists to catch what the cheaper layer below cannot, and we buy layers until the next one costs more than what it would catch."

3. How it actually works

Abishek's method has six steps, and the second and fourth are the ones teams leave implicit. First, list what changed and what that could break. For the retry he found five risks: the delay calculation, timeout detection, the second call to the biller, the receipt screen and the nightly reconciliation file. Second, assign each risk to the cheapest layer that can see it. The delay calculation is arithmetic, so a unit test; the second call needs the app server talking to a simulated biller, so integration; the receipt needs a real phone and network, so end-to-end. A risk that fits no layer, such as what happens if the customer switches apps mid-retry, goes to exploratory testing.

Third, run the cheap layers first and stop on red: a unit failure found in four minutes costs less than the same one found after seventy. Fourth, decide the oracle, the thing that tells a test what the right answer is. For the retry it is a ledger rule: one customer debit produces exactly one biller credit. Without an oracle a test can run and prove nothing. Fifth, fix exit criteria before results arrive, so no one argues them down afterwards. Sixth, record where each defect was found, because that log is the only honest source of the catch rates used below.

Figure 3 previews the arithmetic of the next section. Each layer removes a share of what reaches it, so the bars shrink fastest early and slowest late: the later layers see fewer defects, and the ones they see are by construction the ones cheaper layers missed.

4. A worked example

Abishek's history supplies the inputs. The last four releases averaged 8 defects per thousand changed lines, so 6,000 lines imply 6 × 8 = 48 latent defects. Catch rates are conditional, meaning the share of defects reaching a layer that the layer finds: 50 per cent for unit tests, 50 for integration, 25 for the flaky end-to-end suite and one in three for a day of exploratory testing. These are judgements from his log, not measurements.

Table 1. Expected defects through each layer
LayerDefects enteringCatch rateCaughtEscaping
Unit4850%2424
Integration2450%1212
End-to-end1225%39
Exploratory933.3%36

Plan A, shipping Thursday, stops after integration: 12 defects escape. Plan B runs all four and ships Monday 2 November: 6 escape. To price an escape, take a duplicate-debit defect live for two days: 0.5 per cent of 2,40,000 payments is 1,200 a day, so 2,400 customers, at ₹330 each (₹180 of support contact plus ₹150 of expected churn) is ₹7.92 lakh, plus ₹1.08 lakh of hotfix and reconciliation effort, ₹9.00 lakh in all. Abishek assumes one escape in six is money-affecting; each of the others costs ₹0.4 lakh.

Table 2. Expected cost of escapes (₹ lakh)

Plan B saves ₹11.00 lakh and has its own price. Four days' delay forgoes 2,400 recovered payments × ₹14 = ₹33,600 a day, ₹1.344 lakh; eight person-days at ₹5,200 is ₹0.416 lakh; together ₹1.76 lakh. The net is ₹9.24 lakh in Plan B's favour.

Second pass, one input changed. The integration tests use a biller simulator that never times out, so Abishek cuts integration's rate from 50 to 25 per cent. Plan A: 24 enter integration, 6 are caught, 18 escape, of which 3 are money-affecting (₹27.00 lakh) and 15 are not (₹6.00 lakh): ₹33.00 lakh. Plan B: the same 18 enter end-to-end, 4.5 are caught, 13.5 reach exploratory, 4.5 more are caught, and 9 escape: 1.5 × 9.00 + 7.5 × 0.4 = ₹16.50 lakh. The saving is ₹16.50 lakh and, after the same ₹1.76 lakh price, the net is ₹14.74 lakh. A weaker early layer raises the value of the later ones; it does not replace them.

At Nilavu's 8 per thousand, Plan B is far above break-even. At 2 per thousand (12 defects) the saving is ₹2.75 lakh, still ₹0.99 lakh ahead of its cost. The answer flips only for changes far cleaner than the 8 per thousand its last four releases averaged.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Verification is not validation

Testing checks a product against what it was meant to do. Whether that intention matches what customers need is validation, answered by users, not suites. A perfectly tested retry could still solve a problem customers do not care about.

Catch rates belong to defect types, not layers

Unit tests are strong on arithmetic and weak on timeouts. The 50 per cent figures are averages over a mix, and the simulator problem in the second pass shows how one environmental gap erases a layer's value for one whole class.

Coverage measures execution, not checking

Ninety per cent line coverage means ninety per cent of lines ran during tests. It does not say anything was asserted about the results. A test with no oracle raises coverage and catches nothing.

Layers are not independent

The arithmetic multiplies conditional rates, which is only fair if each layer's rate was measured on what survived the layer before. If one engineer misunderstands the biller contract, the code and its tests share the error, and every layer misses it together.

A flaky test is worse than none

A suite that fails for no reason teaches people to rerun until green. Nilavu's skipped suite had already been trained out of the process: red had stopped meaning anything.

A green run is weak evidence of absence

Dijkstra's point stands. Before relying on any result, ask what the oracle was, what this layer cannot see, and when its catch rate was last compared with the defects that actually reached users.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; small and large

Table 3. Where the emphasis moves
ProductDistinctive exposureEmphasis
ConsumerMillions of devices, no chance to ask users what happenedStaged rollout, device matrix, monitoring
B2BFew accounts, each with its own configuration and contractIntegration tests against customer setups
MarketplaceTwo sides whose states must agreeEnd-to-end scenarios across buyer and seller

Nilavu is consumer, with a marketplace edge: billers are the second side. An early-stage company often has no QA team, so a founder's exploratory afternoon on the money path is the highest-value test available. A large company has the opposite problem: thousands of automated tests, whose maintenance and flakiness need a deliberate budget.

7. Common mistakes

"The pipeline is green, so it is tested"

Symptom: a clean dashboard and a customer-reported defect on the same day. Misunderstanding: green means the existing tests passed, not that the right ones exist. Diagnostic: plant a known defect in a branch and see which layer, if any, turns red.

The inverted pyramid

Symptom: a pipeline that takes hours and fails at random, so releases wait. Misunderstanding: realism equals value, so everything goes through the screen. Diagnostic: count tests per layer and time to first failure signal.

Testing as a phase at the end

Symptom: a QA queue before every release. Misunderstanding: testing follows building. Diagnostic: ask how long the oldest change in the release has waited, unchecked, since it was merged.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Tuesday morning produces, from one person in half a day, the risk list and an oracle for each risk. Two engineers spend a day and a half shrinking the 70-minute suite to the three scenarios that touch money, which makes it trustworthy. Three people hold exploratory sessions from Wednesday afternoon with written charters: break the retry by killing the network, switching apps, and paying the same bill twice. The release goes to 5 per cent of users on Monday, with the ledger rule checked automatically. That last step is not in the cost model and lowers the price of any escape.

9. What Akilan decides

Akilan chose Plan B. The reasoning was not that testing is virtuous but that the expected escape cost fell from ₹22.00 lakh to ₹11.00 lakh against a ₹1.76 lakh price, and that the net stayed positive in every case he tried: ₹9.24 lakh on the base inputs, ₹14.74 lakh when integration lost half its catch rate, and ₹0.99 lakh even for a change a quarter as defect-dense. He told Aadhira the pipeline was green and uninformative on this change, because nothing in it had yet been asked about a timeout, and she agreed to the new date on that basis.

Next, learn bug triage and severity, because the "one in six is money-affecting" assumption is a severity judgement, and hardware quality, where escapes cannot be hotfixed. Two questions to sit with. Which of your own current releases would you be unable to defend with a list of what its tests cannot see? And if your most trusted layer quietly lost half its catch rate, how would you find out before your customers did?
exp40v2-qo.rollout:
Staged rollouts and rollback

A ramp is not a safety feature. It is a purchase of information about a change, and the price is exposure.

1Two decisions, five weeks apart

At 9.40 on the evening of Saturday 7 March 2026 the mandate-success guardrail on the Kolusu app tripped for the second four-hour window running. Kolusu Technologies, a Bengaluru savings-and-payments app with 36,00,000 users eligible for its new UPI autopay flow, had ramped it six days: 1 per cent on 2 and 3 March, 5 per cent on the 4th and 5th, 25 per cent from the 6th. Tharun Devulapalli, who owned release engineering, flipped the flag off at 9.42; reversion took ninety seconds. Failures had risen from a baseline of 8.6 per cent to 9.0 per cent: a real regression, and small.

Tarunya Dandapani, Kolusu's VP of product, spent Monday 9 March arguing with Tanika Dronamraju, who ran experimentation, about what the six days had bought. Dronamraju held that the first four were theatre: the 1 per cent stage could not have detected the defect, and its silence had been read as reassurance. Dandapani held that the ramp kept the damage to a few hundred failed mandates.

Two days earlier and 360 kilometres south, Tulasi Durairajan had met the mirror image. Kudirai Mobility, a Coimbatore maker of connected electric two-wheelers, had pushed firmware v4.3 to its 2,40,000-vehicle fleet from 2 February in stages of 0.5, 3, 15 and 100 per cent. On 5 March the first service tickets arrived: motors derating to 40 per cent power, on a fleet that already had the build. On Tuesday 14 April Durairajan had to approve the v4.4 ramp, and the question was whether percentages had ever suited a fleet that cannot be rolled back.

2The idea, and the four schools that disagree about it

A staged rollout is the deliberate exposure of a change to a growing, bounded share of a population under observation, with a pre-committed procedure for halting and reversing it. Three quantities define any ramp: the exposure it accumulates, the detection power at each stage — the smallest regression it would notice — and the reversion latency with which it can be withdrawn. They cannot be optimised together, and the one fixed last, reversion latency, determines the other two.

The ancestry predates software. Shewhart's 1920s control charts established a pre-set limit that forces an action, not a discussion; Wald's 1945 sequential analysis formalised deciding as data arrives. Canary releasing entered the vocabulary through Humble and Farley's Continuous Delivery (2010). In India it also sits inside NPCI change-management circulars and, for Kudirai, AIS-156 type approval and the recall machinery that followed the 2022 battery-fire investigations.

Four schools disagree about purpose. The blast-radius school holds that a ramp bounds harm — no change reaches more people than you can apologise to — and will not sign that the ramp exists to measure. The measurement school holds that every rollout is an experiment whether treated as one or not, so allocation follows power and a holdback outlasts 100 per cent; it will not sign 1 per cent for two days as a safety measure. The operational-readiness school holds that stage 1 tests the pager and the runbook rather than the patch, and will not sign a stopping rule: the decision must be a named human's. The continuous-deployment school holds that long ramps are a symptom of weak testing, and signs "a thirty-second rollback makes most of a ramp ceremony".

3Mechanics: what the ramp buys at each stage

Start with Kolusu's numbers. Across the eligible base of 36,00,000 users, 1,80,000 mandate-creation attempts arrive daily, and the guardrail is the mandate failure rate, baseline 8.6 per cent. Against the holdback, the smallest regression detectable at 80 per cent power and two-sided 5 per cent is

MDE = (zα/2 + zβ) √[ p(1−p) (1/nt + 1/nc) ], with p(1−p) = 0.086 × 0.914 = 0.078604 and zα/2 + zβ = 2.80.

Exhibit 1. Kolusu's ramp: what each stage could detect, at 1,80,000 attempts a day.

Corrected column: Bonferroni across 60 tests (6 guardrails × 10 daily checks), α′ = 0.05/60 = 0.000833, z = 3.34, inflating each MDE by 4.18/2.80 = 1.49×. MDE columns are stated to three decimals, which is what Figure 2's bar widths encode. Two conventions hold throughout: each stage is analysed on its own data, not pooled across stages, and stages are counted in whole days — including the day two on which the flag came off at 9.42 p.m. The total row sums attempts only.

Three second-order effects follow. First, the 1 per cent stage sees nothing smaller than 1.315 points; Kolusu's defect was 0.42, with power of 14 per cent at stage 1 and 50 per cent at stage 2 — a coin flip. It was caught on day two of the 25 per cent stage, at an MDE of 0.302. Four days of silence measured the instrument, not the change. Second, power stops improving where teams keep ramping: 25 to 50 per cent over equal days holds the sample at 5,40,000 attempts and only rebalances it, so the MDE falls from 0.247 to 0.214 — down 13.4 per cent for twice the exposure. Third, multiplicity goes unpriced: six guardrails checked daily for ten days is 60 tests, so uncorrected the expected spurious trips are 3.0 and the chance of at least one is 1 − 0.9560 = 95.4 per cent. Correcting inflates every MDE by 49 per cent, pushing stage-3 day-2 from 0.302 to 0.451 — above the real defect.

The step most often left implicit: reverting code does not revert state. Over six days the treated arm handled 1,11,600 attempts at a 9.02 per cent failure rate, writing 1,11,600 × 0.9098 = 1,01,534 mandate records in the new schema. The flag flip took ninety seconds; making those records readable by the old path took three days. Honest reversion latency was ninety seconds for traffic and three days for state, and only the first was in the runbook.

An over-the-air push is an offer, not an install: of 36,000 vehicles offered v4.3 at the 15 per cent stage, 22,320 completed the flash within 48 hours — 62 per cent — while 89 more interrupted mid-write and needed a service-centre reflash. Where a downgrade exists at all, reversion needs a charging session with connectivity and charge above 40 per cent, which 56 per cent of the fleet fails on a given day, so on an independent daily draw the share still on it decays as 0.56t: across that 22,320-vehicle cohort, 12,499 vehicles after 24 hours, 3,920 after 72, 385 after a week, a half-life of ln(0.5)/ln(0.56) = 1.20 days, or 28.7 hours.

4When the instrument applies, and when it misleads

Five conditions, as testable claims. One: reversion latency is short relative to time to detect. Kolusu, ninety seconds of traffic reversion against days — satisfied once the state path is made reversible. Kudirai, a 28.7-hour half-life against a defect needing weeks — violated. Two: the guardrail moves within the stage's horizon. Mandate failures move in minutes; Kudirai's derate needed 11 charge cycles at a median 2.4-day interval — 26.4 days, invisible to a 72-hour stage. Three: exposure is randomised independently of outcome. Kolusu hashes user identifiers; Kudirai drew its first cohort from an opt-in list. Four: harm scales with exposure. For a step function it does not: a wrongly debited mandate is reportable whether it hits one customer or a lakh, and one derated Kudirai vehicle triggers the same recall assessment as a thousand. Five: outcomes are independent across units. Kudirai's vehicles are; Kolusu's merchants are not, because a treated payer changes an untreated merchant's settlement file.

It actively misleads in three situations. Load defects do not appear below a traffic threshold, so a ramp ending at 50 per cent has tested nothing about 100 per cent: the last step is the dangerous one. Cold-start effects make p99 latency worse in almost any canary, for reasons unrelated to the change. And for effects that accumulate per user — habit, retention, trust — two days at 1 per cent measures novelty, not the change.

5Hard edges: seams, strata and two-sided contamination

Kudirai's fleet is not one population: a proportional 0.5 per cent draw of 1,200 vehicles would give revision C 240 units, and the self-selected cohort gave it 38. A percentage of a heterogeneous fleet is a lottery over which subpopulation is tested.

Exhibit 2. Kudirai's fleet by motor-controller revision, with the stage-1 cohort of 2 February 2026.
