Drawn from the early-update opt-in list, which over-represents metro riders on the best-connected units. Revision C, the only one the v4.3 defect touched, was under-sampled by 240/38 = 6.3×.

The seams compound. Ramping the payer side of a two-sided flow changes merchant settlement files, so Kolusu must cluster by merchant; with an intraclass correlation of 0.04 and a mean 38 payments per merchant the design effect is 1 + 37 × 0.04 = 2.48, so the effective sample is 40 per cent of the nominal one and Exhibit 1's MDEs would all rise by √2.48 = 1.57× for a settlement-side guardrail. Exhibit 3 and the mandate example read a user-level guardrail and are shown unclustered. Across a multi-product suite ramps interact: with nine concurrent ramps each at 25 per cent, 1 − 0.759 = 92.5 per cent of users sit in at least one treatment, so no arm is clean. Regulated contexts add a change window and a reporting clock. For hardware the seam is the service network: Kudirai's 142 service points absorb 89 interrupted flashes and not 3,000. For AI products the guardrail is a distribution, and a ramped model contaminates its own control by generating what becomes training data. Nor are the organisational seams as described: Kolusu's registry held 1,284 flags, 417 pinned at 100 per cent beyond ninety days, 23 parked mid-ramp and unowned.

6Eight distinctions that separate the expert

The first stage is a sensitivity setting, not a safety setting. The tell is a team that cannot state the minimum detectable effect of its own 1 per cent stage; Kolusu's was 1.315 points. The obvious reading — small exposure, small risk — confuses the size of the harm with the chance of noticing it, and a stage that notices nothing buys delay.

The holdback must outlive the launch. The tell is a dashboard whose "versus control" column disappears the day the flag reaches 100 per cent. Experts hold 2 to 5 per cent back for sixty days, because retention and support contact rate resolve on a horizon longer than any ramp.

Novelty and primacy pull in opposite directions and both decay. The tell is a stage-3 lift smaller than stage-1's with no code change between, which teams read as a regression. It is usually novelty wearing off in the earliest cohort while the newest is still inside its own: compare each stage to its own control, never another stage.

Reversion latency, not perceived risk, sets the ramp's shape. The tell is a team with ninety-second flags running a ten-day ramp — or one with a 28.7-hour reversion half-life running the same ramp. Risk feels like the input, but it is unobservable beforehand; reversion latency is measurable today, and bounds what a mistake accumulates.

Exposure must be integrated across the ramp, not read off the current stage. The tell is a post-mortem beginning "only 25 per cent were exposed". Kolusu's stages accumulated 4,26,600 attempts against the 18,00,000 of ten days at full exposure, 23.7 per cent — 2.37 full-exposure days, not the final stage's 50 per cent.

A guardrail needs a pre-registered threshold and a pre-registered action. The tell is thresholds in a document and the decision in a meeting. Kolusu's threshold tripped at 9.40 on a Saturday and the flag was off at 9.42 because the action was written down; where only the threshold is, trip-to-decision takes hours of argument.

Rolling back code is not rolling back state. The tell is a runbook with no step that touches data. Kolusu's ninety-second flag flip left 1,01,534 records in a schema the old path could not read. Experts make the forward path write what the previous version still reads for as long as the ramp and holdback run.

Sticky assignment stops being random the moment anyone can leave. The tell is treatment-arm retention improving every week of a ramp with no further changes. If users can opt out, uninstall or be excluded by an agent, the surviving cohort is selected on the outcome being measured, and the gap widens like a win.

7Where the practice genuinely differs, and where it does not

In consumer products traffic is abundant, so power is cheap and exposure binds: Kolusu reaches a 0.214-point MDE in the three days of its 50 per cent stage. In B2B software the constraint inverts. Kattalai Systems, a Pune billing platform, has 340 enterprise accounts, so a 5 per cent ramp is 17 accounts and no statistical guardrail exists at that n. Thrisha Desikachari's team ramps by tenant and substitutes reconciliation — every invoice must match the legacy engine to the paisa — possible only because the answer is known exactly. In self-hosted deployments percentage ramps do not exist: customers approve release calendars, so versions stage across customers. Marketplaces cluster-randomise; hardware ramps by stratum with a cohort floor; AI products hold a slice out permanently.

By company stage the difference is mostly whether measurement exists. At 400 daily actives making one attempt each, a 50/50 split gives 200 attempts an arm and an MDE of 7.85 points on the same 8.6 per cent base: it catches catastrophes and nothing else, so a seed-stage ramp is a blast-radius and rehearsal device. At growth stage stale flags become the dominant risk; at scale the ramp becomes infrastructure with its own SLOs. What does not change is the trade in Figure 1; only the numbers entering it.

8Three worked examples

Kolusu, March 2026: the ramp worked and its first half did not. The 0.42-point regression was caught on day two of the 25 per cent stage, after 3,600 + 18,000 + 90,000 = 1,11,600 treated attempts, implying 1,11,600 × 0.0042 = 469 extra failed mandates. Traffic reverted in ninety seconds; state took three days and 1,01,534 migrated records. The first four days bought 21,600 attempts and no information.

Kattalai, January 2026: a ramp with no statistics in it. The billing-engine replacement went to 6 accounts, then 34, then 340. At the 34-account stage reconciliation found three mis-billed by ₹640, ₹18,400 and ₹1,12,750 — ₹1,31,790 in total — all sharing one tax configuration present in 38 of the 340 accounts, 11.2 per cent of the base. Scaling the mean miss of ₹43,930 across 38 accounts gives ₹16.69 lakh; but across three observations spanning ₹640 to ₹1,12,750 the standard error of that mean is ₹34,790, so the figure is ₹16.69 lakh give or take ₹13.22 lakh. The decision was sound; the number was no forecast.

Kudirai, February to April 2026: the failure. Three conditions defeated it. The cohort was self-selected, giving revision C 38 vehicles instead of 240; stages ran 72 hours against a defect needing 26.4 days; and the change rewrote the battery-management calibration table, so reverting to v4.2 was impossible — Figure 3 is v4.4's designed downgrade path, not February's. First tickets arrived 5 March, day 31 — twenty-two days after the fleet reached 100 per cent on 11 February, day 9 of three 72-hour stages. Of 48,000 revision-C vehicles, 93 per cent had installed within thirty days, giving 44,640, and the derate presented in 6.8 per cent of those, or 3,036 vehicles. Root cause landed 14 March, v4.3.1 on 20 March, and 93 per cent of revision C was on the fix by 3 April, day 60. Direct cost: 1,174 service visits at ₹1,850 and 47 cell-pack replacements at ₹24,500 — ₹21.72 lakh plus ₹11.52 lakh, or ₹33.23 lakh. Recovery ran forward rather than backward.

9Failure modes and their early warnings

An underpowered first stage read as a safety gate. Warning sign: the ramp has never once been halted at stage 1. Diagnostic: what is the smallest regression this stage catches, at what false-alarm rate? Caught late, Kolusu's defect costs 1,80,000 × 0.0042 = 756 extra failures a day.

A guardrail horizon shorter than the defect's clock. Warning sign: every stage runs the same length whatever changed. Diagnostic: how many duty cycles does this failure need? Cost of late: ₹33.23 lakh at Kudirai.

A self-selected canary. Warning sign: stage 1 is an opt-in list or an employee cohort. Diagnostic: name one covariate on which it differs from the population. Cost of late: 38 revision-C vehicles where a random draw gave 240.

A rollback never rehearsed, and state written forward. Warning sign: the runbook has no data step and the last drill was at a previous employer. Diagnostic: if we flip the flag now, what does the old code read? Cost of late: three days of migration on top of a ninety-second fix.

Ramps abandoned part-way. Warning sign: flags parked at intermediate percentages. Diagnostic: who owns each flag not at 0 or 100, and what decision awaits? Kolusu found 23, none tested and none retired.

10Where experts genuinely disagree

The sharpest disagreement is between the slow ramp and the fast holdback, and arithmetic settles it only once a prior over defect sizes is fixed.

Exhibit 3. Two designs against two defects, on Kolusu's numbers, evaluated daily.
Design0.42 pp defect: days to detect0.42 pp: treated attempts exposed5.32 pp defect: days to detect5.32 pp: extra failures
1/5/25/50 ramp61,11,600196
50/50 holdback from day 1190,00014,788

The 5.32-point defect is a 38-point failure increase in a device cohort that is 14 per cent of the base: 0.14 × 38 = 5.32 points in aggregate, above both designs' day-1 MDE of 1.860 and 0.370 points. Day-1 extra failures: 1,800 × 0.14 × 0.38 = 96 at 1 per cent and 90,000 × 0.14 × 0.38 = 4,788 at 50 per cent. Both rows use uncorrected daily tests; for the 0.42-point defect the same correction needs two days of holdback or seven of ramp, while day 1 stands for the 5.32-point defect.

The measurement steelman is the first three columns: a 50/50 holdback finds the small defect in one day having exposed 90,000 attempts, where the ramp takes six days and exposes 1,11,600. The ramp is slower and harms more, because exposure accumulates while the instrument is too blunt to use it; Dronamraju's version is that the only defects a slow ramp catches early are ones a holdback catches early too. The blast-radius steelman is the last column: for the concentrated defect the ramp's first day costs 96 extra failures and the holdback's 4,788. Dandapani's is that for that defect the organisation survives the ramp's 96 in a day and not the holdback's 4,788. Both are right about their own defect class; what would settle it is the distribution of defect magnitudes a team ships, which neither camp measures.

Two further disagreements are live. Whether the proceed decision is a statistical rule or a named human's judgement: automated analysis halts earlier and more often, and by the arithmetic above spuriously about three times over a ten-day ramp, so the position turns on an unmeasured cost of false halts. Whether a holdback should persist past 100 per cent: the measurement school says long-run effects can reverse sign, the reliability school says a permanent holdback is a permanently untested code path; both would move given a measurement of how often reversal happens.

11What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this asks about reversion latency before percentages, and for its state and traffic components separately. They state the MDE of the stage they are about to run, unprompted, and skip a stage that sees nothing. They set stage duration from the defect's clock, not the release calendar, and write the data step into the runbook. They read a clean ramp as information about its own sensitivity, not the change. They close flags. They go straight to a large holdback when reversion is cheap, and refuse to ramp when it is not.

12The two decisions

Dandapani chose a two-stage re-ramp: 1 per cent for one day as an operational smoke test with no statistical claim, then 50 per cent against a 50 per cent holdback with corrected thresholds, a written halt action, and 5 per cent held back sixty days. She accepted the 90,000 attempts exposed on the first measured day, reasoning that ninety-second reversion makes exposure recoverable and that the now backward-compatible migration no longer binds.

Durairajan did the opposite. Kudirai's v4.4 plan replaces percentages with four stratified cohorts of at least 400 vehicles per controller revision, sets a 28-day stage for anything touching the battery-management system, and gates stage 1 on a validated downgrade path. Without a downgrade there is no ramp.

Discussion questions. (1) Kolusu's re-ramp exposes more attempts on its first measured day than its old ramp did in four. Under what conditions is that the more conservative choice? (2) Kudirai's 400-vehicle floor fixes cohort size but not selection. What would a defensible random draw from a connected fleet cost in installs forgone? (3) Both firms now hold a cohort back after launch. Who is accountable for those users, and on what date does the holdback itself become the defect?

13Going deeper

  • Feature flags and progressive delivery — the mechanism under every ramp.
  • Release management and launch readiness — whether a ramp can halt at all.
  • Beta and early-access programmes — self-selected cohorts, in pure form.
  • Firmware and OTA updates — where the downgrade path is the design.
  • Geographic and staged market rollout — ramping by place, strata visible.
  • Testing and quality basics — the same defects, caught cheaper.
  • Bug triage and severity — what turns a guardrail trip into a halt.
  • Incident management and postmortems — where the exposure integral belongs.
  • SLAs, SLOs and error budgets — spendable exposure, quantified.
  • Support and operational readiness — support meets your ramp via tickets.
  • Change management for users — two populations, two products.
exp20v2-qo.rollout:
Staged rollouts and rollback

How to ramp by percentage, watch guardrails and reverse a change without drama.

1. A midnight switch

At ten past four on Monday 12 October 2026, Sunitha Chockalingam, chief product officer of Jayam Pay, a Bengaluru payments app with 2 crore daily active users, had a one-line plan on her screen: move every user to the new payment-routing engine at midnight. The engine decides which partner bank's pathway on UPI (the Unified Payments Interface, the instant-payment rail run by NPCI) carries each payment. Engineers expected it to lift the payment success rate, then 97.2 per cent, by a few tenths of a point.

The downside was easier to count. Users make about 1.5 payments a day, so Jayam Pay carries 3 crore payments daily, and each percentage point of success lost is 3 lakh failed payments a day. Diwali falls on Sunday 8 November; the code freeze, after which nothing ships, begins on Thursday 29 October.

Sivakami Chavali, head of reliability, put a different question: not whether to ship, but how many customers should be allowed to discover the team was wrong. Sridhar Chintala, the data scientist, added that the daily dashboard could not tell a 0.3-point drop from an ordinary Tuesday. The meeting turned on his remark. Nobody doubted the code had passed testing; the question was what testing could never show.

2. The idea

A staged rollout, also called a phased or canary release, exposes a change to a growing slice of users in steps, and before each widening compares that slice with the users who have not received it. (The name comes from the caged canaries that miners carried because the birds fell ill before the miners did.) Rollback is the pre-agreed, rehearsed route back to the old behaviour for whoever has been exposed.

It exists because testing before release cannot reproduce real users, real partner banks and real load. Large web companies, Facebook and Google among them, built tooling in the late 2000s to send new code to a small share of traffic first; around 2018 the analyst James Governor popularised the label "progressive delivery", and feature flags (switches in code that turn a behaviour on for chosen users) became the usual instrument.

Two terms carry the weight. A guardrail is a metric that must not worsen however good the change looks otherwise, such as payment success. A rollback trigger is a threshold on a guardrail, written down in advance, that obliges a reversal. Sunitha's sentence for the room was: "We are not deciding whether to ship; we are deciding how much of the customer base is allowed to find out we were wrong."

3. How it works

The first step is choosing the unit. Jayam Pay buckets by user, not by payment: a hash of the user ID plus a per-release salt (a random string that reshuffles who is selected each time) yields a number from 0 to 9,999, and users below 100 form the 1 per cent stage. The hash is deterministic, so nobody flips between old and new engines, and widening to 5 per cent (numbers below 500) keeps everyone already exposed.

The second step, the one practitioners leave implicit, is writing the gate before the ramp starts: which guardrails, compared against which group, over how many hours, and at what gap a rollback becomes mandatory. Jayam Pay's gate compares success in the exposed slice with unexposed users over the same hours; the trigger is a gap of 0.20 points or more. Staff and test accounts are excluded from both groups.

The third step is the hold. Each stage runs a minimum time even if early numbers look fine, because payment behaviour has a daily rhythm and some outcomes, refunds for instance, arrive hours later. The fourth is the read, which ends in one of three verdicts: promote, hold longer, or roll back. The fifth is the rollback itself, calm only if rehearsed. Sivakami's team switches the flag off during the 1 per cent stage on purpose and times it, and the runbook names who may do so at 2 a.m. without asking permission.

4. A worked example

Success is a yes-or-no outcome with p = 0.972, so the variance of one payment is 0.972 × 0.028 = 0.027216. If an exposed slice is share s of users and makes n payments, the control group makes n(1−s)/s, and the standard error of the gap in success rates is the square root of 0.027216 / (n(1−s)). At the 1 per cent stage n is 3,00,000 a day, so n(1−s) = 2,97,000 and the standard error is 0.0303 points. A drop is caught with 80 per cent probability, at a 5 per cent one-sided false-alarm rate, when it is at least (1.645 + 0.842) = 2.487 standard errors: 2.487 × 0.0303 = 0.075 points. Table 1 repeats this at each rung.

50%13,46,6842.2

The 24-hour hold at 1 per cent now cannot certify safety against the smaller harm; the early rungs guard against large faults, and fine ones become visible only from the 5 per cent rung up.

5. What a learner must notice

A rollout is not an experiment

Guardrails look for harm; they do not show the engine is better. A claim of lift needs a test designed for it, with fixed group sizes and duration, whereas a ramp changes both every day.

Percent of what

Users, payments, merchants and banks are different denominators. If one issuer bank accounts for 4 per cent of payments, the 1 per cent slice sends it only 12,000 payments a day, so a fault confined to that bank is far harder to see than the overall figures suggest.

The clock matters as much as the percentage

A stage that spans no weekend misses weekend behaviour, and metrics such as chargebacks mature over days. A 24-hour hold cannot see a harm that takes three days to appear, whatever the share.

Some failures only appear at scale

A partner bank's rate limit or a database ceiling may bite at 40 per cent and never at 1. Watch capacity metrics (latency, queue depth) at every rung, and treat each widening as a new experiment rather than a continuation.

Not everything can be rolled back

Switching a flag off restores the code path, not a data migration already applied, an app version already installed, or a notification already sent. For such one-way changes the honest plan is roll forward: a fix, not a reversal.

Many guardrails, many false alarms

With 20 independent guardrails each carrying a 5 per cent false-alarm rate, the chance that at least one trips by luck in a stage is 1 − 0.9520 = 64.2 per cent. Separate the few guardrails that can force a rollback from those that merely prompt a look, and ask before relying on any ramp: who is the control group, and what cannot be undone?

What a clean ramp cannot tell you

A ramp that passes says the change did no measurable harm to the metrics watched, among the people exposed, over the hours observed. It cannot say that unwatched metrics are healthy, that users will still like the change in a month, or that the last half of the base will behave like the first.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace

Table 4. Where the unit of ramp changes
SettingUnit of rampCharacteristic difficulty
ConsumerUserPlentiful data; novelty effects
B2BAccountA 1% slice may be three customers
MarketplaceCity or regionOne side affects the other

In consumer products, like Jayam Pay, volume makes the statistics generous. In B2B software, with perhaps 300 accounts, 1 per cent is three customers, so the ramp is by account, often opt-in and agreed with the customer in advance. In marketplaces a change for 1 per cent of drivers alters prices and matching for the other 99 per cent, so slices are cities. Early-stage companies lack the traffic to power a gate and lean on manual watching of a handful of users; large companies automate the gate so that a human is paged only on exceptions, and run many ramps at once, which is its own source of confusion when two changes overlap in the same slice.

7. Common mistakes

Ramping by calendar

Symptom: percentages rise on schedule whether or not anyone looked. Misunderstanding: time is treated as evidence. Diagnostic: ask "what number would have stopped this stage?"; no answer, no gate.

Choosing guardrails after seeing the data

Symptom: a dip appears and the meeting argues over whether that metric counts. Misunderstanding: thresholds are treated as discussion points. Diagnostic: check that the trigger was written in the ticket before the first user was exposed.

A rollback nobody has run

Symptom: the reversal takes hours and someone proposes a quick forward fix. Misunderstanding: the flag is assumed to work. Diagnostic: time a deliberate rollback during the smallest stage.

8. What good looks like

Sunitha's accepted plan resembles the schedule below: 1 per cent on Tuesday 13 October, 5 per cent on Wednesday, 20 per cent on Thursday, 50 per cent from Friday through the weekend, everyone on Monday 19. Triggers are in the ticket, the rollback has been timed, and Sivakami may use it alone. What marks the plan as good is that no meeting is needed to interpret a bad read: the trigger is arithmetic fixed beforehand, not an opinion formed under pressure.

On Tuesday the plan is tested. At the first four-hour read the 1 per cent slice shows a gap of 0.30 points, 4.05 standard errors, past the 0.20 trigger. Sivakami switches the flag off, and the cost is about 150 extra failed payments. The team fixes a timeout on one issuer bank's pathway and re-runs the ladder.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

Sunitha rejected the midnight switch. She approved the ladder, the 0.20-point trigger and Sivakami's authority to reverse alone, accepting that 100 per cent would arrive six days later than the midnight plan. Her reasoning: the engine's upside was a few tenths of a point, the downside was 3 lakh failed payments per point per day in the weeks that decide Diwali, and the ladder bought a measurement the midnight switch could not.

Read next the preceding topics, feature flags and progressive delivery, and release management and launch readiness. Then the topics this one unlocks: beta and early-access programmes, firmware and over-the-air updates (where rollback may be impossible), and geographic and staged market rollout.

Two questions to sit with. First, which one change in your own product could you not reverse, and what would a ramp for it have to look like? Second, if your guardrail moved by 0.1 point at 5 per cent exposure, who decides, and by what rule written before the moment arrived?
exp40v2-qo.incidents:
Incident management and postmortems

When something breaks, what is a product manager’s job — and what happens afterwards? Two companies, one argument, and the arithmetic that decides both.

1. Two companies, two live decisions

At 19:12 on Wednesday 16 September 2026 the payment-confirmation service at Ilakkai Pay began returning errors. Ilakkai Pay is a Bengaluru consumer app on the UPI rails: 43.2 crore payment attempts in a thirty-day window, an objective of 99.9 per cent of attempts succeeding. Evening is its peak; at 19:12 it was taking 20,000 attempts a minute, exactly twice its thirty-day average minute rate. Thirty per cent began failing. The first alert fired at 19:19, a commander was appointed at 19:24, the first public post went up at 19:31, and failures returned to baseline at 20:04 after a configuration rollback.

Nobody argues the engineering response was slow. What Rajeshwari Bhamidipati, the VP Product, must decide on 6 October is narrower. The runbook’s comms clock starts when an incident is declared, and on that clock the team posted in seven minutes against a ten-minute commitment; on the clock customers experienced, in nineteen. Her counterpart Rithvik Bapatla says an onset clock punishes the team for detection latency it is already fixing. Rathika Burra, who runs support, has a different number: 9,480 contacts in the 112 minutes from 19:12, against a four-Wednesday mean of 1,185 for the same slot — eight times normal. The 8,295 excess is 2.7 per hundred of the 3,12,000 attempts that failed — different spans: contacts over 112 minutes, failures over 52.

About 350 kilometres south-east, Inthuja Systems in Chennai makes connected temperature loggers for pharmaceutical cold chains: 9,600 units in the field, reporting temperature excursions. On Tuesday 11 August it pushed firmware v4.7.2 to the whole fleet at once. By Monday 17 August, 1,316 had gone silent. Ravindra Bollapragada, Director of Product, must decide on 20 August what the postmortem’s single committed action item is — his two candidates cost a week and a quarter.

2. The idea, and the four schools that disagree about it

Definition. An incident is an unplanned degradation needing coordinated response outside normal work. A severity level is not a measure of badness; it is a contract binding a named response: who is paged, how fast, who talks to customers, what stops. A postmortem is an account written afterwards to change the system, not record the event.

The command structure came from wildfire. The Incident Command System, built by Californian fire agencies in the 1970s, gave the field its durable idea: during an event, authority is separated from expertise, so one person commands and does not debug. ITIL (1989) formalised the ticketing half and bequeathed root-cause analysis from Toyota’s five whys.

The postmortem’s lineage runs instead through safety research. NASA’s Aviation Safety Reporting System (1976) established that honest near-miss reports require immunity from sanction. Perrow’s Normal Accidents (1984) made failure structural in tightly coupled systems; Reason’s Human Error (1990) supplied the layered-defences picture, and Managing the Risks of Organizational Accidents (1997) the substitution test. Cook’s How Complex Systems Fail (1998) and Dekker’s The Field Guide to Human Error Investigations (2002) went further: operator actions are locally rational on the information available, so “human error” names the end of an investigation, not a finding. Hollnagel’s Safety-I and Safety-II (2014) asked instead how work usually succeeds. Allspaw’s 2012 account of blameless postmortems at Etsy carried this into software; Google’s site-reliability practice (2016) added the error budget.

Four positions contend, and a practitioner should know which.

  • The root-cause school. Signs: every incident has a findable underlying cause, and finding it closes a class. Will not sign: that root causes do not exist.
  • Resilience engineering. Signs: the operator acted reasonably on what they could see, and the incident emerged from normal work. Will not sign: that the cause was human error.
  • The error-budget school. Signs: reliability above the objective is waste, and a quarter with no incidents means too little shipped. Will not sign: that every incident needs a postmortem.
  • Just culture, after David Marx (2001). Signs: blameless means blame-free, not accountability-free. Will not sign: that nobody is moved off a rotation.

3. Mechanics, worked through

The first mechanism is the currency. An objective of 99.9 per cent over 43.2 crore attempts permits 4,32,000 failures: the error budget, denominated in failed requests, not minutes. The burn rate is observed failure share divided by permitted share — on 16 September, 30 per cent against 0.1, a burn rate of 300.

Now the step usually left implicit. The familiar alerting table — 14.4× for one hour consumes 2 per cent of a thirty-day budget — multiplies rate by elapsed fraction of the window, assuming requests arrive uniformly in time. The incident ran 52 minutes of 43,200, so that gives 300 × 52 / 43,200 = 36.1 per cent. The true figure is double, because the window sat at twice the average request rate: 3,12,000 failed attempts against a 4,32,000 budget is 72.2 per cent consumed in 52 minutes. Net of the 624 that would have failed anyway, 3,11,376 are attributable, or 72.1 per cent. Time-weighted figures understate peak consumption by exactly the traffic multiplier, and that is what most dashboards report.

The second-order effect matters more. Baseline noise over the rest of the window — 0.06 per cent of the other 43.096 crore attempts — is 2,58,576 failures, which is 59.9 per cent of the budget on its own. The incident takes the window to 132.1 per cent and the achieved rate to 99.868 per cent against a 99.900 objective. An incident this size is survivable only where the ordinary-day failure rate is low; Ilakkai Pay’s was not, which is a release-process finding.

Severity scales are the second mechanism, written as conditions one on-call engineer can evaluate alone at 02:00.

Table 1 — Ilakkai Pay severity contract, December 2025. Condition and burn rate are one test twice over: burn rate is failure share ÷ 0.1 per cent.
LevelConditionBurnResponseComms
Sev1Core flow at or above 5% failing; any funds/integrity error≥50×Commander in 5 minPost in 10 min, then 30-minutely
Sev2Named flow at 1% to under 5%, or Sev1 with workaround10 to <50×On-call in 15 minPost in 60 min
Sev3Non-core, below 1%<10×Next business hourIn-app only
Sev4No customer-visible effect—BacklogNone

The 16 September event failed 30 per cent of attempts: Sev1 on the first condition, declared twelve minutes after onset.

The third mechanism is the postmortem. Its omitted step: separate the timeline, contestable only on facts, from the analysis, contestable on judgement, and circulate the timeline first. Merge them and the review argues interpretation while facts are still wrong.

4. When the apparatus applies, and when it misleads

Four testable conditions decide whether the machinery fits. Apply each to both.

One: the population at risk is observable in near-real time. Ilakkai Pay passes; it knows its per-minute success rate. Inthuja fails, and that is the heart of its incident: a logger that stops reporting looks identical to one at a depot with no coverage, so heartbeat loss was never alarmed. The severity scale then has no input at all.

Two: mitigation is separable from diagnosis. Ilakkai Pay passes: the rollback at 20:04 restored service while the cause was unconfirmed. Inthuja fails hardest here, because firmware rollback arrives on the next check-in and the affected units are those that no longer check in. All 1,316 needed a visit: at about ₹900 each, ₹11.84 lakh; rebuilding the records by hand, 2.5 hours a unit at ₹1,100 fully loaded, added ₹36.19 lakh. Total ₹48.03 lakh.

Three: the error budget is the right currency. Ilakkai Pay passes; a failed payment attempt is retryable and a small fungible loss. Inthuja fails: the obligation attaches per consignment and is binary, so either the temperature history is complete or the stock is quarantined. Budget language actively misleads here: a team adopting it will under-respond to one failed unit under a vaccine store.

Four: blamelessness is affordable. Both pass, asymmetrically. At Inthuja the postmortem becomes a deviation record in a quality-management system, and a regulated document is discoverable. Write it anyway, knowing that separating fact from speculation does legal work.

Two situations defeat the apparatus. A security breach inverts the comms sequence: containment and evidence preservation precede disclosure, on a regulatory clock: CERT-In’s six-hour requirement starts when an organisation notices, earlier than when it declares. And a degradation that never crosses a threshold is never an incident, which is how products die of unalarmed milliseconds.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Inthuja’s staged-rollout policy existed on paper and required 5, 20 and 100 per cent cohorts; its firmware channel had no cohorting at all, because cohorting was built for the mobile app by another team, and no one held both facts. On v4.7.2 a unit went silent when its daily sync landed in a thirty-minute window — one chance in forty-eight per cycle — and sync times drifted daily, so the healthy pool depleted multiplicatively.

A 5 per cent cohort held 72 hours would have shown 30 silent units of 480 — 6.25 per cent, a signal a promotion gate would have caught, had anyone watched heartbeat loss. That is a rollout lesson masquerading as an incident.

Other seams repeat in predictable shapes. On a two-sided marketplace a scale keyed to consumer-visible failure rates scores a total outage of seller order webhooks as Sev3, because buyers see nothing; each condition must name a side. In multi-product companies the mature answer is that the platform owns severity while each product owns comms. In regulated settings the declaration timestamp acquires legal weight, quietly rewarding late declaration; the counter-measure is cheap, reversible declaration. In AI-native products the failure often has no error rate: one model update at a document-processing vendor moved refusal rates from 2.1 to 6.8 per cent of requests, a 3.2-fold rise with no exception and no alert, found nine days later in ticket volume. Mature companies make evaluation regressions alertable, so an incident can be declared on a metric nobody has complained about.

6. Eight nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

One: severity is a response contract, not a measure of badness. The tell is a team debating Sev1-versus-Sev2 while the error graph still climbs. They look careful; they are converting response time into deliberation time. Experts make low severity cheap and trivial to upgrade.

Two: diagnosis, not repair, is where the time goes. The 52-minute impact was 7 minutes to detect, 5 to declare, 24 to localise and 16 to mitigate: engagement 23 per cent of the impact, diagnosis 46, repair 31. The tell is a team that has bought faster rollbacks — the 31 per cent — and nothing that says which component moved.

Three: mean time to resolve is the wrong statistic. Durations are heavily right-skewed, so the mean describes no incident the team has had. The Verica open incident database reports argued this from 2021.

Table 2 — Impact duration, nine Ilakkai Pay Sev1/Sev2 incidents, January to September 2026, minutes.
Minutes1114182329415296418

Sum 702; mean 78.0; median 29; mean ÷ median 2.69. The 418-minute incident alone is 59.5 per cent of all impact minutes; the other eight average 35.5.

Four: communication is a product surface with a price. The tell is a support queue spiking harder than the incident warrants. Rathika Burra argues the nineteen silent minutes put Ilakkai Pay’s eight-fold contact spike there — an argument, not a measurement: most arrived after the first post, sixty of them follow recovery, and nobody has priced a contact.

Five: “blameless” describes the account, not the consequences. The tell is a postmortem in which no person appears, only passive systems. That is over-correction: the new view says an operator acted rationally on available information, not that people are absent. Naming who saw what, when, makes the information environment visible.

Six: action items are a liability, not an asset. The tell is a team reporting how many items a postmortem generated. Experts report open items, their age, and how many incidents repeated a class already listed. Fourteen items usually means nothing was decided.

Seven: the second incident of a class is the signal; the first is noise. The tell is a repeat rate, not a count. Counts move with traffic, releases and monitoring coverage; repeat rate moves with whether the last postmortem worked.

Eight: who finds the incident matters more than how fast it is fixed. Of 97 incidents at Ilakkai Pay in 2025, 23 were reported by customers before any monitor fired — 23.7 per cent. Above roughly a quarter the binding constraint is observability, and incident process is the wrong spend.

7. How this differs across product types and stages

Table 3 — Where the difference is real.
TypeWhat a Sev1 isWhat the postmortem must add
ConsumerA core-flow failure rate, per minuteNothing special; designed here
B2B SaaSOne named account wholly blocked, any volumePer-account impact, for the renewal conversation
EnterpriseA contractual service level breached, credits dueA customer-facing version for procurement
Platform / marketplaceAny one side wholly blockedEach side separately; aggregates hide one-sided outages
HardwareAnything needing physical accessField-service cost, and whether a remote fix exists
AI productsAn evaluation regression, with no error rateWhich evaluation would have caught it, and why it was not gating

Stage changes less than people expect and one thing more. Before product-market fit the apparatus is two sentences: who gets called, and who tells customers. A four-level scale in an eight-person team adds classification work, not capacity. What changes sharply is when on-call becomes a rota rather than a person: below roughly a dozen engineers the founder-engineer is the rota, and the first real investment is the second trained commander. That regulated industries need heavier process is mostly false — they need the same process plus a records obligation. What differs is reversibility: a consumer app rolls back, a hardware fleet does not.

8. Three worked examples

Ilakkai Pay, 16 September. The response worked; the accounting did not. The incident consumed 72.2 per cent of a budget that ordinary noise already claims 59.9 per cent of, taking the window to 132.1 per cent and the achieved rate to 99.868. The most useful finding: a 0.06 per cent ordinary-day failure rate leaves no room for one bad evening.

Inthuja Systems, 11 to 17 August. 1,316 of 9,600 units silent — 13.7 per cent of the fleet, ₹48.03 lakh to recover, a blast radius 43.9 times a real canary’s. Two of the seven calendar days were the weekend of 15 and 16 August, but the weekend explains nothing: heartbeat loss was never alarmed, so four working days passed with 776 units — 8 per cent of the fleet — silent by Friday the 14th, and a distributor’s call raised it, not a monitor.

The example where the approach failed. In the second half of 2024 Ilakkai Pay set a 90 per cent completion target on every action item. Completion rose from 54.2 to 85.6 per cent in two quarters, and changed what people wrote: a later read of those 118 items found 63 — 53.4 per cent — were add-a-log-line or update-the-runbook items. The share of incidents repeating a known class rose from 19.6 to 31.4 per cent, but that is 1.35 standard errors on these samples and not a finding; what persuaded the team was reading the items, not counting them. The target was withdrawn in 2025; from January 2026 the recovery was one must-ship item per postmortem, with an owner and a date.

Table 4 — Postmortem action items, Ilakkai Pay. “Repeat” counts incidents whose class appeared in an earlier postmortem.

Of the 214 items opened in 2025, 58 were completed by their stated date, 95 late and 61 never. On-time completion moved from 27.1 per cent (58 of 214) to 88.6 (39 of 44), 61.5 points on a standard error of 5.67 — nearly eleven, though H1 2026 items had less time to fall due, flattering the later figure. The repeat column is not significant: its three moves are 1.35, 0.58 and 1.17 standard errors.

The honest reading is uncomfortable. Items opened per quarter fell from 53.5 in 2025 to 22 in H1 2026 and items ever completed from 38.25 to 21 — a 45.1 per cent fall in repair volume — while on-time completions per two quarters rose from 29 to 39. Which matters is a judgement the data does not make.

9. Failure modes and their early warning signs

Table 5 — Six failure modes and the question that catches each early.
Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Severity inflationMost incidents are Sev1What share of last quarter’s Sev1s stopped other work?Paging fatigue
Severity deflationDeclaration follows customer contactWho may declare, and what does it cost them?Comms missed; a reporting breach
Postmortem theatreDocuments on time; items unownedName a class a postmortem closed this yearYears of repeats, a credible archive
Item accumulationItems over two quarters old outnumber newHow many are open, and how old?Nobody consults it
Blame leakageFewer near-misses reported each quarterWhen did someone last write up an incident they caused?The cheapest data source closes
Commander as debuggerThe commander is typing in the terminalWho decided to mitigate, and when?Mitigation waits on diagnosis

Two deserve emphasis: no dashboard shows them. Blame leakage presents as an improving metric — fewer reported near-misses — which is why it survives; the 1976 reporting-system designers knew it, and the industry keeps rediscovering it. And commander-as-debugger recurs wherever the vocabulary was adopted without the discipline: a commander who is also best able to fix the problem will start fixing it, and then nobody is running the incident.

10. Where competent experts genuinely disagree

Whether root cause is a coherent object. The root-cause position at its strongest is not naive: an investigation without a stopping rule produces no decisions, so picking an intervention point and calling it the cause is a necessary engineering act. Its evidence is a repair record: classes of failure that visibly stopped recurring. The new view answers that the stopping rule is set by what the organisation finds convenient to fix, so it selects cheap causes; its evidence is cases where the same root cause was fixed repeatedly and incidents continued. For the root-cause position to be wrong, repeat rates would have to be invariant to closed action items; no clean test has been published.

Whether the PM belongs inside the incident. One camp holds that the PM is the comms lead: what customers are told is a product decision with retention consequences. The other holds that product presence pushes toward optimistic disclosure and premature mitigation, so an engineer owns comms and the PM follow-through. The second camp cites posts softer than the facts; the first, disclosures nobody reads.

Whether MTTR should be measured. The sceptical position is that durations are lognormal, aggregate means therefore uninterpretable, and reporting one invites optimising the wrong tail; Table 2 shows the shape, mean 78.0 against a median of 29. The defence is that any metric can be gamed, and a team with no duration measure cannot see its response degrading. What would settle it: whether teams tracking MTTR have shorter tails.

Whether blameless is sustainable at scale. Just culture holds that a policy of no consequences is not credible where consequences exist for everything else, so it will be quietly violated — worse than a stated boundary. Pure blamelessness holds that a stated boundary reads as a threat and suppresses reporting in the cases that matter most. Both read the aviation record.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently within one incident. They declare early and at low severity, having made that cheap. During the event they ask two questions only: what reduces impact fastest, and who is telling customers. They do not ask what caused it; that competes with mitigation for the same people. They treat the first public post as a product artefact with a deadline from onset. Afterwards they circulate a timeline before an analysis, insist on one committed repair rather than fourteen, and track repeat rate, not incident count. And they read their durations as a distribution, which is how they know whether they have a response problem or a detection problem.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Rajeshwari Bhamidipati does not re-point the severity scale. She moves the comms trigger off severity and onto burn rate: a public post is required when the burn rate holds above 14.4× for ten minutes, measured from onset. That is 1.44 per cent of attempts failing, inside the Sev2 band, so the trigger fires on incidents the team now handles quietly. Tightening the sustain window from the conventional hour to ten minutes cuts what the alarm lets run before firing from 4 per cent of the budget to 0.67: at the evening rate of 20,000 attempts a minute, 17,280 failures against 2,880, and it fires fifty minutes earlier. Both are double the time-weighted figures, for the reason section 3 gives.

Ravindra Bollapragada does not make firmware cohorting the committed item, though it is the real fix, and funds it as a quarterly programme. The must-ship item is a heartbeat-loss alarm on the first cohort of any release: a week against a quarter, and the thing that turns 1,316 silent units into 30.

Questions for discussion. (1) Rajeshwari’s trigger will post during incidents customers would not otherwise notice. What evidence would tell her within a quarter whether that trade was worth making? (2) Inthuja cannot compute severity from telemetry, because silence and no-coverage are indistinguishable. What would a severity scale look like for a fleet whose failures are unobservable? (3) On-time completion rose while repair volume fell 45.1 per cent. Which should the head of engineering be held to?

13. Going deeper

  • Logging, monitoring and observability — incidents are what it detects; 23.7 per cent customer-first is the verdict.
  • Being on call as a PM — where severity contracts stop being paperwork.
  • Leading through a crisis — the same command separation, organisation as the failing system.
  • Security incidents and breach response — containment first, on a regulatory clock.
  • Supervised learning in production — where silent regressions dominate.
  • Blameless postmortems that change things — how one committed repair ships.
  • AI incident response — no error rate, evaluations as the only detector.
  • Testing and quality basics — incident reduction is mostly upstream.
  • Bug triage and severity — the same scale in slow time, haggling affordable.
  • Release management and launch readiness — where the cohorting gap belonged.
  • Staged rollouts and rollback — the 43.9-fold blast radius.
  • SLAs, SLOs and error budgets — the currency this page uses.
  • Support and operational readiness — the eight-fold contact spike is staffing before comms.
exp20v2-qo.incidents:
Incident Management and Postmortems

1. Seventy-one minutes after the release

At 9:10 on Wednesday 7 October 2026, Prathyusha Anantharaman, senior product manager for merchant payments at Hamsa Pay, opened a draft she disliked. Hamsa, a Hyderabad company, sells soundbox devices that announce each UPI payment aloud at 2,40,000 shops. On Tuesday evening a release had broken those announcements: customers' money moved, but the box stayed silent for 12 per cent of payments. At the evening peak of roughly 4,200 confirmations a minute, that is 504 silent confirmations every minute.

The draft postmortem, a written review of what happened and why, gave the cause as "engineer error: wrong flag value". Pandurangan Annavarapu, the engineering director, wanted the engineer named. A pharmacy chain with 310 outlets had asked for a call. The review was fixed for Friday 9 October. If she let the draft stand, engineers would learn to hide the next mistake. If she softened it, the chain would hear excuses.

Figure 1 divides the 67 minutes into three phases that recur in almost every incident. Eighteen minutes passed before anyone was paged, thirteen more before anyone declared an incident, and thirty-six before the damage stopped. Prathyusha's draft spent four paragraphs on the flag, the single configuration value that began the failure, and two lines on the rest of the 67 minutes. Her question was which of the two stories deserved the page. The flag explained why the incident started. The 67 minutes explained why it was large, and only the second story could be changed by anyone in the room on Friday. She also knew that 2,40,000 shopkeepers had no view of any of this: they had a silent box and a customer standing at the counter, and what Hamsa said next would decide whether they kept trusting the device.

2. The idea

An incident is an unplanned event that degrades a service customers depend on and demands a coordinated, time-boxed response. Incident management is the discipline of detecting it, classifying its seriousness, communicating, and ending it. A postmortem is the written review that follows, whose purpose is to change the system so the same failure is harder next time.

The method was invented for a problem that predates software. After the 1970 California wildfires, fire agencies developed what became the Incident Command System: fixed roles filled by whoever is qualified, not whoever is senior, so that fifty arriving experts did not produce fifty commanders. Software teams borrowed it, and Google's Site Reliability Engineering book (2016) popularised it. The postmortem half borrowed from aviation and from Sidney Dekker's "just culture"; John Allspaw's 2012 essay on blameless postmortems at Etsy brought it into technology. Without roles, a crowd argues while customers wait. Without blamelessness, people hide what they know, and the organisation learns only from the mistakes that were too large to conceal. Both ideas answer one question: how does an organisation behave well when its people are frightened, rushed and short of information?

The sentence Prathyusha could repeat in a meeting: "We run incidents by role rather than rank, stop the customer's pain before we understand it, and then study the system rather than the person."

3. How it works, step by step

First comes detection: an alert, a customer complaint or a staff member's hunch reaches a person who is obliged to act. Second is classification: assigning a severity, a number that says how seriously to respond (the bands appear in section 4). Third, declaration, which practitioners often leave implicit: someone says aloud, in a shared channel, "this is an incident, severity 2, Parameswari is commander." Until that sentence is spoken, nobody has authority to interrupt anyone else.

Fourth, roles are assigned, each held by a named person, so that nobody has to wonder who is deciding. Fifth, communication starts on a fixed cadence, say every fifteen minutes, because silence is read as indifference. Sixth, the team mitigates: stops the harm by any reversible means such as a rollback or a switch, without waiting to understand the cause. Seventh, someone with authority declares it resolved only after the customer-facing measure has recovered. Eighth, a scribe's running timeline becomes the postmortem's spine, and an owner is named for the review.

RoleHamsa, 6 OctoberOwns
Incident commanderParameswari Appaswamy, engineering managerDecisions, pace, assignments
ApproverPandurangan Annavarapu, engineering directorSign-off for Sev 2 rollbacks
Support leadPattabhi AlagarsamyTicket counts as an impact signal
Impact and comms ownerPrathyusha Anantharaman, productMeasuring impact, writing updates

The PM's seat is the last row, and it is easy to misread. She does not debug and should not command. She owns the answer to "how bad is this for customers?" and to "what do we tell them?" Her first merchant notice went out at 19:28, 23 minutes after the 19:05 declaration and 54 minutes after failures began, the number she most regretted.

4. A worked example

Hamsa's policy defines severity by customer-visible impact on a core flow.

At 19:05 the on-call engineer queried one of four equal-volume shards and saw 6 per cent of confirmations failing: Sev 2. The other three shards were failing at 14 per cent each. The pooled rate is (6 + 14 + 14 + 14) / 4 = 12 per cent, which is Sev 1. The director, in transit, had not approved a rollback by 19:20, when Pattabhi's ticket counts lifted the severity to Sev 1 and the commander could act herself; the rollback then took 21 minutes. With 4,200 confirmations a minute held constant (the real peak rose, so this understates), 12 per cent gives 504 a minute.

Pass 2 changes one input: the 19:05 query covers all four shards, so the reading is 12 per cent, the declaration is Sev 1, and the commander orders the rollback at once. Mitigation falls to the 21-minute execution time. The saving is 15 minutes, or 7,560 silent confirmations. At Hamsa's historical one support contact per 24 silent confirmations and ₹95 a contact, the actual run cost 1,407 contacts and ₹1,33,665; pass 2 would have cost 1,092 and ₹1,03,740, a difference of ₹29,925.

The rupees are small, and that is itself a lesson: the direct cost of an incident rarely justifies attention, while the damage to trust does. The 7,560 confirmations are shopkeepers who could not tell whether they had been paid, and that is what the pharmacy chain was calling about.

5. Seven nuances

Severity measures the customer, not the machine

Payment success read 99.1 per cent throughout, so a threshold on it never tripped. Define severity on what the customer experiences, then ask which instrument shows that. If no instrument does, building one is the first action item, ahead of any fix to the code.

Incident, outage and problem are different things

An outage is a total failure; this incident was partial. In the vocabulary of ITIL, a widely used service-management framework, a problem is the underlying cause, investigated later. Mixing them makes people debug during the response, when the only question that matters is how to stop the harm.

Mitigate before you diagnose

A rollback was possible from the moment the page fired at 18:52. Understanding why the flag misbehaved took until early Wednesday. Every minute spent diagnosing during harm is billed to customers at 504 confirmations.

Blameless does not mean accountless

Nobody is punished for a decision that made sense with what they knew at the time; the review asks what the engineer could see, not what hindsight shows. Actions still receive owners and dates. A review with no owners is a ritual.

"Root cause" is usually several causes

Here the flag, the missing check on it, the single-shard query and the severity rule each had to fail. Fixing only the flag leaves three open doors, and a review that lists one cause has usually stopped asking questions early.

A communication cadence is a promise

If you say fifteen minutes, send an update at fifteen even when it reads "no change". Skipped updates cost more trust than bad news.

A postmortem cannot prove the counterfactual

Pass 2's 7,560 is an estimate resting on assumed constant volume and a 21-minute rollback. It shows where time went, not what would certainly have happened. Ask what was not measured before relying on it.

6. How it differs by product and by stage

SettingImpact unitCommunication
ConsumerUsers affected, app-store and social reactionPublic status page, in-app banner
B2BNamed accounts, contractual uptimeDirect to account owners; credits
MarketplaceBoth sides; one side's failure starves the otherSeparate messages to buyers and sellers
Early stageOne person holds every roleOne-page review within 48 hours
Large companyRota, dedicated commandersLegal and regulator review added

Hamsa is a hybrid, and the table's rows are tendencies rather than rules: merchants are the business customers, shoppers are the payers. Regulated payments firms also owe regulators reports on certain incidents, which lengthens their communication chain. Early-stage teams should keep the roles and drop the ceremony: a founder who is commander, communicator and engineer at once should at least say aloud which hat is on, so that a decision made as commander is not later argued as an opinion. Large companies face the opposite risk, that process outlives its purpose and a Sev 3 receives the paperwork of a Sev 1.

7. Common mistakes

Symptom from outsideMisunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
Customers hear nothing for the first hourCommunication waits until the cause is knownRead the timeline: minutes from declaration to first notice
Postmortems conclude "human error"A person is the cause, so a person is the fixAsk: what would have stopped any engineer making this change?
The same incident recursWriting the review was the end of the workCount last quarter's actions closed with owner and date

A fourth, subtler mistake is calling severity from the first number seen, as at 19:05, because the first number feels like evidence and the team is under pressure to classify. The diagnostic is to ask what share of the system that number covers before anyone writes a severity in the channel.

8. What good looks like

In the handled-well version an alert on confirmation delivery pages someone within 6 minutes. The commander declares Sev 1 five minutes later from a four-shard reading, rolls back in 21, and the first merchant notice goes out inside ten minutes of declaration. Duration is 32 minutes and 16,128 silent confirmations, against 33,768, and the postmortem names a changed alert, a flag check and a severity rule, each with an owner and a date. Prathyusha's role is the same in both versions, but in this one she spends the first half hour measuring impact and writing the first notice, not discovering that she has no way to measure it.

9. What Prathyusha decided

She rewrote the cause as four contributing factors, removed the engineer's name, and kept the engineer's role in the timeline without the name. She told Pandurangan the name would buy one satisfied meeting and cost every future disclosure. She called the pharmacy chain on Wednesday afternoon with the timeline, the 7,560-confirmation estimate labelled as an estimate, and the dates below. Her reasoning was that a customer who is shown the real gap and a dated plan can judge the company, whereas a customer handed a culprit learns only that the company looks for one.

Next, read the pages on being on call as a PM and on blameless postmortems that change things: the first teaches the seat you will actually sit in, the second what keeps a review from becoming a ritual.

Two questions to sit with. Which dashboard at your company would still look healthy while customers are hurting? If a postmortem of your last incident named a person, what would your team stop telling you?
exp20v2-qo.beta:
Beta and Early-Access Programmes

How to run a beta that graduates features instead of stranding them.

1. Four weeks, 148 accounts, one decision

On Tuesday 10 March 2026, Inba Pasupathy, head of product at Arasu Books, a Coimbatore company that sells accounting and GST-invoicing software to small businesses, sat down with two colleagues and a spreadsheet. Ishvar Panneerselvam led engineering. Ilam Purushothaman led customer support. The subject was bank-feed auto-match, a feature that reads a customer's bank statement and pairs each line with the invoice or bill it settles.

Arasu Books had 3,200 accounts with a connected bank feed, the only accounts that could use the feature. The company's annual customer conference fell on Tuesday 24 March, and the sales team had promised a general launch there. A wrong match is not cosmetic: it can mark an unpaid invoice as paid, and the error then flows into a customer's GST filing. If Inba launched on schedule and the matching was weak, support would absorb it in public, in front of customers. If she delayed without a reason she could defend, the four-week beta would have taught the company nothing it could act on.

The beta had started on Monday 9 February. Of 400 accounts invited, 148 accepted and 61 were still using the feature in week four. The numbers were not disastrous and not clean. What Inba needed was a way to read them, and that is what this page supplies.

She had seen the other outcome. A previous feature, a payment-reminder tool, had entered an invited preview in 2025 with no review date. Nobody owned the question of whether it was finished, so it sat in the settings menu behind a beta badge, used by a few dozen accounts and maintained by no one. Inba did not want to repeat that, and she did not want the feature to ship by calendar momentum either.

2. The idea

A beta programme is a time-boxed release of an unfinished feature to a deliberately chosen group of real users, run so that their behaviour answers questions the team cannot answer internally. Early access is the looser cousin: a longer-lived, often opt-in channel in which users accept rough edges in exchange for early use. A graduation is the decision to move a feature from that channel to general availability, restrict its scope, or stop it.

The vocabulary comes from hardware. IBM is usually credited with calling internal tests "alpha" and customer-site tests "beta" in the 1950s. Software adopted the pair in the 1980s and 1990s. Google's Gmail, launched in April 2004, kept the label until July 2009, and Tim O'Reilly named the habit "perpetual beta" in 2005, a reminder that a label can persist after it has stopped meaning anything.

Two properties separate a beta from ordinary release. The group is chosen rather than self-selected by chance, which lets the team reason about whom the results describe. And the exit is decided in advance: at the end the feature goes to everyone, goes to some, or stops, and the evidence for each outcome is named before it exists.

The problem a beta solves is that internal testing reproduces what the team imagined, while real users reproduce what is true. The sentence Inba could repeat in a meeting: a beta is not a smaller launch; it is an experiment with a pre-written verdict.

3. How it works

A beta moves through five steps. Most teams do the second and the fifth, and the others are where programmes fail, because they are the steps that feel like paperwork while the product is exciting.

Write the gates first. A gate is a threshold set before data arrives. Inba's team wrote four on 2 February: auto-match acceptance at least 92 per cent; at least 60 per cent of activated accounts still active in week four; no open severity-1 defect; no more than 15 support tickets per 100 active accounts. Recruit a cohort that resembles the eventual market, not the most enthusiastic customers. Instrument every step from invitation to repeated use, and open one feedback channel. Review on a fixed date, and graduate, narrow or stop.

Three details stay implicit in most descriptions. First, every gate needs a stated denominator, because 61 active accounts means different things over 96 activated and over 148 accepted. Second, the cohort should be sized from the question: to judge a segment separately, the beta must contain enough of that segment to measure it. Third, narrowing is a legitimate result. A feature can pass for one slice of its users and fail for another, and a programme that only knows “ship” or “kill” will make the wrong call in one of the two slices.

In Arasu’s case, the instrumentation was an event for each suggested match, each acceptance, each edit and each rejection, tagged with account and statement type, plus a single feedback form linked from the reconciliation screen. Events carried the statement-type tag from the first day, but support tickets did not, a gap that mattered when the review arrived and one a careful team would have closed before inviting anyone.

4. A worked example, line by line

Arasu Books invited 400 of its 3,200 eligible accounts (12.5 per cent). Define each stage precisely: accepted means the owner agreed and connected a feed; activated means at least one auto-matched reconciliation within seven days; week-four active means at least one in 2–8 March.

The funnel gives the retention gate: 61 / 96 = 63.5 per cent, above the 60 per cent bar. Measured on accepted accounts instead it would be 41.2 per cent (61 / 148), so the base must be named. The accuracy gate needs item-level data, which is why instrumentation sits at step three and not after the review.

Second pass: change the mix. The beta cohort produced 70.7 per cent type-A items (13,000 / 18,400). Ilam's team estimated that 60 per cent of items across the full base would be type A. Holding each type's acceptance rate fixed, the production blend is 0.60 × 93.0 + 0.40 × 79.37 = 87.5 per cent. The beta flattered the feature by 1.5 points. For the blend to reach 92 per cent, type A would need to be 92.7 per cent of items. A single input moved, and the verdict hardened: the accuracy gate failed on both mixes, and the failure was larger on the one that resembles the market.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Beta, pilot, staged rollout and dogfooding are different things

Dogfooding is employees using the product. A pilot tests whether a whole offering works inside a few customers. A staged rollout sends the finished release to a rising share of users to catch faults. A beta tests an unfinished feature against a verdict. Mixing them up produces betas with no gates.

Acceptance is not accuracy

Customers accept matches they do not check. Ilam's team audited 500 matches accepted without edit and found 7 wrong (1.4 per cent). If that held across the beta, correct matches were about 16,147 of 18,400, or 87.8 per cent, below the 89.0 per cent headline.

The cohort decides what you can learn

Volunteers are more tolerant and more engaged than the market. Of 400 invitations only 37.0 per cent were accepted, and the 252 who did not accept are unmeasured. Their reasons are the least-visited part of the evidence.

Size is a statistical question

13,000 type-A items give a naive 95 per cent interval of about plus or minus 0.4 points, but items within one account are not independent, so the true interval is wider. Many items from few accounts is not many accounts.

Gates must be set before the data, not after

A threshold chosen after seeing 89.0 per cent will drift toward 89.0 per cent. Pre-writing is what makes the review a test.

Silence is not satisfaction

Of 148 accepted accounts, 87 were not active in week four. A feedback channel hears the loud fraction; only the event log shows who left quietly.

Beta cannot size demand

A free, invited beta cannot reveal willingness to pay, or behaviour once the novelty and personal attention end.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; small and large

Consumer betas recruit through app-store channels, such as Apple's TestFlight, which allows up to 10,000 external testers, or Google Play's closed testing. Volume is cheap, individual feedback is thin, and behaviour data matters most. B2B betas, like Arasu's, recruit by name, and one account is many users, so account-level counts are small and every account matters. Marketplaces must recruit both sides: a seller-side feature with no buyers in the cohort measures nothing, so cohorts are chosen by city or category. Supply-side and demand-side acceptance have to be read separately, because a seller who loves a tool says nothing about whether buyers can find that seller.

An early-stage company can phone every beta customer and graduate on judgement; its risk is having no gates at all. A large company has dedicated programmes, legal sign-off and a thousand testers; its risk is a programme that runs for years because no one owns the stop decision.

7. Common mistakes

The beta that never ends. Symptom: the same feature carries a beta badge for a year. Misunderstanding: the label is treated as a place to park work. Cheapest diagnostic: ask who can name the exit date and the person authorised to kill the feature.

Feedback treated as data. Symptom: roadmap changes follow the three loudest emails. Misunderstanding: sentiment mistaken for behaviour. Diagnostic: compare the share of accounts that commented with the share who stayed active.

A friendly cohort. Symptom: perfect beta numbers, then a weak launch. Misunderstanding: the cohort is a sample of the market. Diagnostic: compare the beta's mix of segments with the production base, as in the second pass above.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, the same beta would have started with a recruitment plan stratified by statement type, so type B had enough accounts to measure on its own. Tickets would have been tagged by type from day one. The four gates would have been signed by Inba, Ishvar and Ilam on 2 February, with a review date and a named person for each possible outcome. The cohort would have been closed at 150 accounts, so support could read each one's activity weekly rather than skim a dashboard. And the 24 March promise made to sales would have read "type A launch, type B on its evidence", not "the feature".

9. Closing

Inba did not launch the feature to everyone and did not postpone it. She graduated type A: acceptance was 93.0 per cent against a 92 per cent gate, and Ilam's estimate put type A at 60 per cent of production items. The retention (63.5 per cent) and zero severity-1 results were cohort-wide, not type-A figures, and tickets had not been tagged by type. The gate was written on acceptance, not audited correctness; applying the cohort audit's 1.4 per cent error rate to type A gives 91.7 per cent, just under the line. She therefore graduated type A on the gate as written, with a two-week watch that included a fresh audit of type-A items and retention and tickets cut by type. Type B stayed in early access with a stated exit date and a fix owned by Ishvar. Her reasoning was that a gate exists to say where the evidence holds, and it held for one statement type. She told sales to describe the launch as covering standard-format statements.

The natural next topics are staged rollouts and rollback, which govern how type A reaches the rest of the 3,200 eligible accounts safely, and pilots, which test whole offerings rather than single features.

Two questions to sit with. If Inba's four gates had been written after the data arrived, which would you expect to have moved, and by how much? What would you want to know about the 252 who did not accept the invitation before trusting any beta number?
exp40v2-qo.beta:
Beta and early-access programmes

Delivery & Technology › Quality, Release & Operations — how to run a beta that graduates features instead of stranding them.

1. Two decisions, one day apart

On Monday 19 October 2026, Jothika Ravuri had ninety minutes to decide how Baandhav Health Systems would put its next module in front of customers. Baandhav, in Pune, sells pharmacy and claims software to 1,180 hospital accounts — ₹88 crore of annual recurring revenue, an average of ₹7.46 lakh an account. Its previous beta, a claims-reconciliation module, had been declared ready in May and had then damaged nineteen customers in the four weeks after general availability on 22 June. The programme had looked generous: 180 accounts invited on 9 March, a four-week window from Monday 6 April to Sunday 3 May, 212 written reports. Over the weekend her release-engineering lead, Jnanada Rachamalla, had computed what it could actually have detected. The answer sat on one line: thirty-two per cent.

The next morning, Jeevesh Rajamanickam had the opposite problem at Bhaskarya Labs in Chennai. Bhaskarya's doubt-solving tutor, an AI-native app aimed at CBSE and state-board students, had been running an open testing track on Google Play since 6 April; 18,400 students had enrolled by 7 September. Their day-7 retention was 54.0 per cent against 39.0 per cent for the general population, and the growth team had built the 2 November launch review around that fifteen-point lift. Then, on Friday 16 October, his data scientist Jarul Ramasundaram delivered a randomised cell — two per cent of new users given the feature without being asked whether they wanted it. Those users retained at 41.5 per cent.

Jothika's beta had produced signal and almost no coverage. Jeevesh's had produced enormous coverage and a number that was mostly an artefact of who volunteered. The two failures look unrelated; they are one. A beta is two instruments welded into one chassis, and the two have opposite sample requirements.

2. The idea, and the four schools that disagree about it

A beta programme is the controlled exposure of unfinished software to real users outside the building, under an explicit agreement that it is unfinished, for a bounded period, with a decision at the end. Early access reverses the framing: the customer pays to be early. Three elements make it a beta rather than a soft launch — the users know, the window closes, there is a named gate at the close.

The vocabulary is usually traced to IBM's hardware test cycle of the 1950s and 1960s, where an A test was engineering verification and a B test field use by people who had not built the thing. The problem it solves is irreducible: behaviour is a function of environment, and no lab holds a representative sample of environments. Four schools disagree about what it is for.

The field-coverage school, from hardware and site-reliability practice, holds that a feature is not ready until it has survived a stated volume of exposure. It signs that exposure-weeks are the binding constraint on readiness. It will not sign that participants' enthusiasm should decide whether the feature ships.

The lead-user school, after Eric von Hippel's 1986 work on users ahead of the market, holds that the point is privileged information, not coverage: twelve engaged accounts beat twelve hundred shallow ones, because what you hunt is the workflow nobody anticipated. It signs that one observation can be decisive, and refuses that beta usage predicts mainstream usage.

The controlled-experiment school holds that any quantity a beta estimates is better estimated by a randomised ramp, because self-selection contaminates every comparison. It signs that opt-in cohorts cannot estimate effects, but not that they are worthless: it concedes defect discovery and surprise.

The commercial early-access school holds that willingness to pay, or to sign as a design partner, is the strongest pre-launch demand signal. It signs that money beats a survey, but not that the paying cohort's adoption curve generalises — it is the most selected cohort of all.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Start with the funnel, because the denominator is where beta reasoning goes wrong. Figure 1 traces Baandhav's 180 invitations down to the 24 accounts that cleared the exit bar written in advance — three or more distinct users running the module at least eight times inside a fourteen-day window.

Now convert the funnel into exposure. The 63 provisioned accounts spanned 252 account-weeks on paper. Instrumentation found genuine exposure in 96 — the 24 bar-clearing accounts, each active in all four weeks; the other 21 with any activity contributed sessions too scattered to count. So 38.1 per cent of the nominal 252 was real, and the 720 account-weeks implied by the invitations never existed.

Defect discovery has a closed form. If a defect bites with probability p per account-week, the chance that N independent account-weeks see it at least once is 1 − (1 − p)N. The defect that escaped hit 19 accounts in the 4,720 account-weeks of the four weeks after general availability — an implied rate of 19/4,720, or 0.403 per cent per account-week; every figure below uses that exact ratio, not a rounded 0.40 per cent. At 96 account-weeks the beta's chance of seeing it was 32.1 per cent; at the 720 the slide deck implied, 94.5 per cent. Nobody was unlucky; the programme was built to miss.

Inverting gives the planning number experts use: N = ln(0.05) / ln(1 − p) account-weeks for 0.95 detection — 149 at two per cent, 743 at 0.403 per cent. At Baandhav's 24 effective accounts that is 6.2 and 31 weeks. Six whole weeks gives 94.5 per cent, seven gives 96.6, so the honest version of Jothika's window was never "four weeks is enough" but "enough for defects above two per cent".
