A second-order effect follows, usually left implicit: the beta cohort reports far more and escalates far less. Baandhav's 212 reports over 96 real-use account-weeks is 2.21 a week, against 1,480 over 4,720 post-launch account-weeks, or 0.314 — a ratio of 7.0 whose denominators are not like for like: the 4,720 is nominal exposure, assuming every account used the module weekly, and the 212 includes reports from the 21 active accounts whose weeks are excluded from the 96. Both corrections shrink it, so 7.0 is an upper bound. Yet severity-1 reports were 9 of 212 in beta, 4.2 per cent, against 182 of 1,480 after launch, 12.3 per cent. The 8.1-point difference carries an unpooled standard error of 1.63 points, so 4.9 standard errors; the pooled two-proportion test, on 191 severity-1 reports in 1,692, gives 2.32 points and 3.5. It is not noise on either basis. Volunteers work around what paying strangers escalate.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions can be stated as testable claims. One: the feature's binding risk is environmental rather than behavioural. True at Baandhav — the defect was a tenant-configuration interaction no lab reproduces. Partly false at Bhaskarya, whose binding risk was whether ordinary students would use the feature at all, which is a question about behaviour and therefore about selection.

Two: the exposure you can buy covers the defect rates you care about. Table 1 answers this before the programme starts. Baandhav could buy 96 account-weeks; the rates it cared about needed 743. Bhaskarya's fortnight to 20 September held 11,400 active user-weeks from 7,300 weekly-active students, not the 36,800 two weeks of cumulative enrolment would imply — and 6,904 user-weeks already buy 99.9 per cent detection of a one-in-a-thousand per-user-week defect. Three: the learning loop fits inside the window. A feature used monthly cannot be judged in four weeks, whatever the cohort size. Four: a written, resourced path for non-graduation exists. Baandhav had none, which is why "do not ship" was never live in May.

The idea is actively misleading in three situations. When the decision is a demand estimate, an opt-in beta does not add noise but bias, of known sign and unknown size. When the feature's value depends on network density — a marketplace, a messaging surface — a thin cohort measures a product that does not exist yet. And when the real purpose is political cover, the programme will be designed to produce approval, and will.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

In a multi-product company the cohort is never drawn fresh: it is the standing list of accounts that said yes last time, so the eighth beta runs on a cohort selected eight times over. Mature companies rotate the pool and hold a measured share of first-timers; what they say they do is recruit afresh each round.

In two-sided settings the unit of exposure is the match, not the user. A beta on the supply side alone can pass every gate and break at launch, because demand-side behaviour was never sampled. The workable pattern is a geographic ring — one city, both sides — a staged rollout in a beta's clothes.

In regulated settings the label itself carries obligations. Bhaskarya's tutor is used by minors, so its open track sits under the DPDP Act's verifiable-guardian-consent requirement; a track that silently enrols thirteen-year-olds is not a beta but an exposure. Baandhav's customers hold service levels that do not pause for a beta addendum unless it says so in terms.

Hardware plus software inverts the economics: units are capital, so cohorts are small and windows long, and the job shifts from finding defects to pricing their rate into a warranty reserve. AI-native products add a second clock, because the model changes under the programme; a nine-week beta on a model replaced in week five has measured two products and reported one.

The seam that usually costs most is between product and support. Beta tickets in the general queue vanish into aggregate volumes, and one of the most informative signals — the account that quietly stopped using it in week two — is visible only to whoever was watching.

6. Eight things that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

One: a beta has two jobs with opposite sample requirements. Defect discovery wants exposure-weeks and does not care who supplies them; effect estimation wants randomisation and is destroyed by choice. The tell is a single exit criterion. An expert asks which of the two questions that gate answers, and finds it answers neither.

Two: self-selection is free on one side and fatal on the other. The obvious reading is that volunteers are keener, so you discount the number. The tell is a slide comparing beta retention with population retention. The bias has a known sign but no knowable magnitude without a randomised arm, so it cannot be discounted — only measured or dropped.

Three: the denominator is exposure-weeks, not invitations. Experts hear "we invited 180 accounts" as logistics and ask for account-weeks in which the feature was used. The tell is a status update headlining the biggest number in the funnel. At Baandhav the two differed by a factor of 7.5 — 720 against 96.

Four: the beta severity mix is not your severity mix. A programme reporting no severity-1 issues is usually reporting a forgiving cohort. Baandhav's beta put 4.2 per cent of reports at severity 1 against 12.3 per cent after launch. The tell is a review treating a clean severity profile as evidence rather than a composition artefact to be adjusted.

Five: the exit criterion and the withdrawal plan are one document, written before the invitation. Drafted afterwards, the criterion encodes whatever happened, and a feature that cannot be withdrawn is not in beta but shipped to a subset. The tell is that nobody can say what would have stopped the launch, or what happens to the 24 accounts if the answer is no. Baandhav's bar was written in advance — the only readiness row in Figure 1 — but it measured engagement, not risk, and no refusal was funded.

Six: instrumentation precedes recruitment. The event you forgot to log cannot be recovered, and the first week holds the richest first-use behaviour. The tell is a first week of data discarded as dirty. Experts gate the start on the instrumentation spec, ahead of the feature being complete.

Seven: the window is set by the slowest learning loop, not the engineering calendar. A month-end reconciliation feature observed for four weeks has been observed once. The tell is a window matching a sprint cadence. Experts count cycles of the behaviour and require two, which at Baandhav meant eight weeks.

Eight: a beta label is a contract, not a disclaimer. Experts read what the addendum actually suspends — service levels, support response, retention commitments, consent basis — and find it suspends less than assumed. The tell is a team offering "it's beta" against an escalation the agreement does not cover.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

Consumer products can buy exposure almost free: Bhaskarya's track generated 11,400 active user-weeks in the fortnight to 20 September, which detects a one-in-a-thousand per-user-week defect with near-certainty. That is weeks of use by the 7,300 students who opened the app, not the 18,400 cumulative enrolments since 6 April — the distinction nuance three insists on. What they cannot buy is an unselected cohort, so the consumer beta is an excellent defect instrument and a poor estimator. B2B and enterprise products are the mirror: cohorts are tiny, so coverage is hopeless, but each account can be instrumented and interviewed — which is why the lead-user school was founded on enterprise evidence.

Platforms and marketplaces face the density problem — a cohort of developers or sellers tests the API, not the economy. Hardware betas are capital-constrained and long, and deliver a failure rate for the warranty reserve rather than a yes-or-no gate. AI products add drift and a long tail of inputs, so the useful deliverable is a stratified sample of prompts and failures rather than a count.

By stage the differences are smaller than claimed. A seed-stage "beta" is usually a design-partner relationship, and the label imports gates the company cannot run. At growth stage the binding constraint becomes support capacity, not willingness to participate. At enterprise scale it becomes procurement: Baandhav's 40.0 per cent signature rate is a legal number, not an interest number. What does not change by stage is Table 1.

8. Three worked examples

A beta that worked by refusing. In 2025 Baandhav ran a narcotics-register module through a small programme: 14 accounts, nine weeks, 126 account-weeks, every account visited. Two accounts showed a stock-reconciliation mismatch in week six that no automated check caught. The gate — "zero unexplained reconciliation differences across two month-ends" — failed, and the module shipped eleven weeks late. That programme bought 126 account-weeks against the claims module's 96, from 14 accounts rather than 63.

A beta that failed, and the recovery. Bhaskarya's open track measured 54.0 per cent day-7 retention against a 39.0 per cent population — a fifteen-point lift that drove the launch forecast. Jarul Ramasundaram's randomised two per cent cell retained at 41.5 per cent, so the defensible treatment effect is 41.5 − 39.0 = 2.5 points, and 54.0 − 41.5 = 12.5 points, or 83.3 per cent of the naive gap, is selection. On a monthly cohort of 6,40,000 new users that is 16,000 extra day-7 retained students rather than 96,000 — a factor of six. The recovery was structural, not analytical: the open track was reclassified as a defect instrument with no estimation duty, and a standing one per cent holdout was built so the next feature needs no bespoke study.

A hardware early-access programme used correctly. Beltara Energy, in Coimbatore, placed 400 pre-production home-battery units with installers for nine weeks from 22 June to 23 August 2026 — 3,600 device-weeks — and recorded 11 field failures, 0.306 per cent per device-week. It plans to ship 42,000 units over the nine weeks from 9 November 2026. Shipping uniformly across that window leaves the average unit in the field 4.5 weeks, not nine, so the exposure is 42,000 × 4.5 = 1,89,000 device-weeks, not the 3,78,000 that 42,000 × 9 would imply. At 0.306 per cent that projects 577.5 failures, call it 578, or ₹19.65 lakh at ₹3,400 a return. Eleven events is thin: the Poisson interval runs roughly 5.5 to 19.7, and at a scale factor of 52.5 that spans about 290 to 1,035 units, a factor of 3.6 wide. Beltara is reserving at the upper bound.

9. Failure modes and their early warning signs

The stranded beta. A feature sits with a cohort because nobody owns the gate. Early sign: the window has been extended twice without a new exit criterion. Diagnostic: what date does this end, and who signs? Late cost: a permanent support surface with no roadmap owner.

The approval machine. The cohort is recruited from accounts that already want the feature, and the gate is satisfaction. Early sign: the recruitment note and the success metric name the same enthusiasm. Diagnostic: what result would have made us stop? Cost: a forecast wrong by a factor of six, as at Bhaskarya.

Coverage theatre. A large invitation list stands in for exposure. Early sign: the headline is accounts invited. Diagnostic: how many account-weeks of real use, and what rate does that detect? Cost at Baandhav was ₹45.6 lakh in credits across 19 accounts plus ₹31 lakh of churn at renewal, ₹76.6 lakh in all. Three more weeks of beta would have cost ₹6.5 lakh and lifted detection only from 32.1 to 49.2 per cent, so the expected loss avoided is 0.171 × ₹76.6 lakh, or ₹13.1 lakh — twice the price, not the twelvefold return the raw totals suggest.

The unfunded exit. Non-graduation is unaffordable by the time it is considered. Early sign: no migration plan. Diagnostic: price the withdrawal today. The abandoned cohort. Participants are never told what happened, and the next programme's acceptance rate falls: Baandhav's 40.0 per cent signature rate had been 58 per cent two programmes earlier. Diagnostic: what did we send the people who said yes last time?

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The field-coverage position, steelmanned: escaped defects are the only beta outcome with a measurable price, and Baandhav's ₹13.1 lakh of avoidable expected loss against ₹6.5 lakh of extra beta settles the cost-benefit in a single case. It rests on incident-cost data, unusually well measured, and would be wrong if most escaped defects were cheap and the rare expensive ones undetectable at any feasible exposure — in which case the money belongs in rollback speed.

The lead-user position, steelmanned: the findings that change products are single observations, not rates. Two accounts of fourteen found Baandhav's register mismatch, and no volume of exposure produces that without someone in the room. It rests on high-value findings being qualitative and non-recurring, and would be wrong if instrumentation could surface those workflows without the visits — an empirical question nobody has settled.

The controlled-experiment position, steelmanned: Bhaskarya's arithmetic generalises, so any beta number used in a forecast is a liability, and the right design is a permanent randomised ramp with a holdout. It rests on the decomposition in Figure 4 and a large experimentation literature, and would be wrong where randomisation is impossible — enterprise tenants, hardware units, regulated cohorts — which is where betas remain load-bearing.

The commercial position disagrees with all three: a paid early-access programme tells you something no randomised cell can, because nobody randomises a purchase order. It rests on revealed preference, and would be wrong if willingness to pay early is itself the selected trait — which the Bhaskarya decomposition makes plausible but does not prove for money.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this runs a well-organised programme. Someone who has internalised it does four things differently. They compute the detectable defect rate before recruiting, and say what the programme cannot find. They separate the two instruments by design, so no self-selected number reaches a forecast. They write the exit criterion and the withdrawal plan in one document, before the first invitation. And they report in exposure-weeks, so the number everyone remembers is the one constraining the conclusion. The signature is a readiness review where the product manager volunteers the programme's blind spot unasked.

12. What each of them decided

Jothika Ravuri split the programme. The ABDM-linked prescription module goes to twelve high-touch accounts for eight weeks — two month-end cycles, 96 account-weeks of instrumented use — for learning only, with a written non-graduation plan. The readiness gate moves to a staged ramp with a holdout, because Table 1 says only the ramp reaches the rates that cost ₹76.6 lakh. Jeevesh Rajamanickam took 2.5 points to the 2 November review rather than 15.0, sized the commitment to 16,000 students a month, built a standing one per cent holdout, and restricted the open track to users aged eighteen and over, with a separately consented guardian cohort for the rest.

Q1. Baandhav's beta had a 32.1 per cent chance of catching the defect that escaped. At what detection probability should a graduation gate be set, and who owns that number — product, engineering, or the customers carrying the residual risk?

Q2. The randomised cell cost five weeks and cut the forecast sixfold. Absent it, what evidence inside the open beta could have revealed the selection, and would it have survived the review?

Q3. Both firms ran one programme to answer two questions. What would separating them cost, and when is the combined programme still right?

13. Going deeper

Staged rollouts and rollback
Buys the exposure a beta cannot; unlocks gates that catch rare defects.
Pilots and beta programmes
The commercial sibling; unlocks design-partner economics.
Testing and quality basics
All a beta should not hunt; unlocks a defensible exit criterion.
Bug triage and severity
Makes the severity-mix correction computable; unlocks beta-to-production comparison.
Release management and launch readiness
Where the gate is enforced; unlocks evidence-to-ship-date.
Incident management and postmortems
Prices escaped defects, which justifies beta length; unlocks section 10.
SLAs, SLOs and error budgets
Says what an addendum can suspend; unlocks nuance eight.
Support and operational readiness
The seam where cohorts are won or lost; unlocks capacity planning.
exp20v2-qo.hw.quality:
Hardware Quality: Yield, Reliability and Field Failure

1. Two sets of numbers

On Wednesday 4 March 2026, Vinayan Edappally, head of hardware quality at Laterite Devices in Kochi, opened a spreadsheet that his reliability engineer, Vasuda Edakkara, had sent the night before. Laterite sells a Wi-Fi controller that starts and stops domestic water pumps, priced at ₹3,200. Lot 7, 12,000 units activated between 8 and 21 September 2025, had now spent twenty-four weeks in customers' homes. Lot 6, an earlier lot of 10,000, had drawn 1.1 per cent returns by the same age. Lot 7 had drawn 420 returns, or 3.5 per cent.

Vishnupriya Eralil, the chief operating officer, wanted a decision by evening. Lot 8, another 8,000 units, sat finished in the Sriperumbudur warehouse of Laterite's contract manufacturer, and the retail chains closed summer orders on Friday 20 March. Ship Lot 8 and Laterite might repeat Lot 7 in 8,000 more homes; hold it and the pump season might pass without stock.

The factory's own report was cheerful: first-pass yield on Lot 7 had risen from 96.0 to 97.0 per cent. Edappally needed to know which set of numbers described the product.

2. The idea

Yield is the share of units that pass the factory's tests. First-pass yield counts only units that pass at the first attempt, with no rework. Reliability is the probability that a unit keeps working for a stated time under stated conditions. A field failure is a unit that stops working in a customer's hands, and the field failure rate is failures per unit of operating time.

The discipline grew out of military electronics in the 1950s, when equipment that passed acceptance tests still failed in service. Its methods were codified in handbooks such as MIL-HDBK-217, which predicted failure rates by adding up component rates. From the late 1980s Gregg Hobbs developed HALT, highly accelerated life testing: stress a design far beyond its specification until it breaks, to see where it is weakest.

The sentence Edappally could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib was this: yield is what the factory caught, field failure is what it missed, and the gap between them is where the design and the process live.

3. How it works

Hardware has four places to find a defect, each costlier than the last. A design stress test (HALT) finds weak points before the design is frozen. The factory's end-of-line test finds units that are wrong now. A screen finds units that are right now but fragile: burn-in runs every unit powered and hot for hours so that weak ones fail in the oven rather than in a kitchen, and HASS, highly accelerated stress screening, does the same with stress levels derived from HALT. Whatever passes is shipped, and the customer becomes the fourth test.

Reading field data then runs in steps. First, fix the cohort: one lot, one serial range, one activation fortnight. Second, count the units at risk and their age. Third, tear down every return and classify it as a confirmed failure or no fault found (NFF), a unit that passes every bench test. Fourth, total the operating time, which is units multiplied by hours. Fifth, divide. Practitioners usually leave three things implicit: returned units stop accumulating hours, young units have not yet had time to fail, and none of this helps unless the serial number links the return to its factory record.

Table 1. Lots 6 and 7 at twenty-four weeks in service
LotBoards startedPassed first timeFirst-pass yieldShippedFinal yieldBurn-inReturnsReturn rate
Lot 610,3009,88896.0%10,00097.1%8 h1101.1%
Lot 712,20011,83497.0%12,00098.4%8 h on first 2,000; 2 h on 10,0004203.5%

First-pass yield = passed first time ÷ boards started. Final yield = shipped ÷ boards started, after rework and scrap. Return rate = returns ÷ shipped.

Table 1 contains the puzzle. Lot 7 beat Lot 6 on both yields and lost to it in the field, though the final-yield gain may partly reflect the shorter burn-in. The explanation pointed to a change note the factory had raised in July: burn-in cut from eight hours to two, to protect the shipping schedule. Burn-in does not alter first-pass yield, because it happens after the test that measures it; it can move final yield, since units failing in the oven are scrapped or reworked.

4. A worked example

Lot 7 was activated within a fortnight, so Edappally treated all 12,000 units as starting on 15 September. The cut-off was Monday 2 March, 168 days or 4,032 hours later. Operating time was 12,000 × 4,032 = 48,384,000 unit-hours. Returned units stop accumulating hours, but at about 70 per cent of the window lost each (returns cluster early), the 420 come to about 2.4 per cent of the total, so he ignored it and said so.

Teardown classified 96 of the 420 returns as NFF, which is 22.9 per cent, leaving 324 confirmed failures. The failure rate is 324 ÷ 48,384,000 = 6.7 per million hours. MTBF, mean time between failures, is the reciprocal: 48,384,000 ÷ 324 = 149,333 hours, which is 17.0 years of continuous running. Yet 2.7 per cent of the lot (324 of 12,000) had failed within 24 weeks. The two statements are compatible even under a constant rate, since 1 − e−4,032/149,333 = 2.7 per cent; the point of the next table is that the rate is not constant.

Table 2. Lot 7 by age, in four-week blocks

At risk = 12,000 less all earlier returns. Per million hours = confirmed ÷ at-risk ÷ 672 hours per block × 1,000,000. The average in the last row is pooled (324 ÷ 48,384,000), not a mean of the six rates.

Figure 2 shows a hazard that falls by a factor of seven between the first block and the last (14.9 against 2.1 per million hours). The single MTBF of 149,333 hours averages over a curve nowhere near flat. This shape, infant mortality, is the first leg of the so-called bathtub curve, in which failure rate falls early, flattens, and rises again at wear-out. Burn-in exists to remove it.

Second pass. Count every return, NFF included, as a failure. The rate becomes 420 ÷ 48,384,000 = 8.7 per million hours and MTBF falls to 115,200 hours, a drop of 23 per cent from a decision about classification alone. Under a constant rate, the chance of failing in the first 8,760 hours is 5.7 per cent with confirmed failures only, and 7.3 per cent with all returns.

5. Nuances

A return is not a failure

Some returns are customers who installed the unit badly or distrust it; here 22.9 per cent were NFF.

Compare lots at the same age

A young lot always looks better than an old one, because its units have had less time to fail. Edappally compared Lot 7 with Lot 6 at twenty-four weeks each.

MTBF is not a lifetime

It is a rate, valid for lifetime statements only if the rate is constant.

Yield and reliability answer different questions

Yield measures defects the test sees now; reliability concerns those it cannot yet see. A factory can raise yield and lower reliability in the same month, as Table 1 shows.

Acceleration is a model, not a measurement

Burn-in works because heat speeds chemistry. The Arrhenius model, from nineteenth-century physical chemistry, gives an acceleration factor of exp[(Ea ÷ k) × (1/Tuse − 1/Ttest)]. With an assumed activation energy Ea of 0.7 electron-volts, Boltzmann's constant k of 8.617 × 10−5 eV per kelvin, and 25°C against 55°C, the factor is about 12. Two hours in the oven then resembles 24 hours of normal use, and eight hours resembles 97. The 0.7 is an assumption; other failure mechanisms carry other values.

Extrapolation needs a shape

If the hazard continues falling by about a third each block, the next seven blocks (to week 52) add roughly 0.25 percentage points, giving about 3 per cent in year one against the 5.7 per cent that a constant rate implies. But wear-out can reverse the curve.

Association is not cause

Serial numbers allowed a split. The first 2,000 units, built under eight-hour burn-in, drew 36 returns (1.8 per cent); the other 10,000 drew 384 (3.84 per cent). Standard errors are 0.30 and 0.19 points, so the gap is real. But the 2,000 were also built before a new capacitor reel arrived, so burn-in is not the only difference, and 1.8 per cent still exceeds Lot 6's 1.1.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; small and large

In consumer products, volume is high, returns arrive through retailers, and NFF is large because customers return what they do not understand. In B2B, units are few, service engineers record failures, and contracts state reliability as uptime, so the record is cleaner but each failure matters more. In a marketplace, the platform often owns the return reason codes, so the seller sees a customer's label rather than a teardown and must build its own failure analysis. A start-up with 300 units cannot estimate a rate and should put five through HALT; a large company can fit Weibull curves.

7. Common mistakes

Quoting MTBF as life. The symptom is a data sheet promising seventeen years beside several per cent of annual claims. The misunderstanding is that MTBF is a lifetime. Convert it to a one-year failure probability and compare.

Comparing lots at different ages. The symptom is a newer lot that always looks better. The misunderstanding is that a return rate has no time dimension. Compare at equal age.

Celebrating yield. The symptom is a rising yield chart beside rising returns. The misunderstanding is that a test catches everything. Join factory and field records by serial number for one lot.

Treating NFF as noise. The symptom is a quarter of returns closing with no action. The misunderstanding is that a bench pass means the unit was fine. Re-test thirty NFF units under the customer's humidity and voltage sags.

8. What good looks like

A well-run Laterite would not face this meeting as a surprise. The change note cutting burn-in would need a quality sign-off with an estimate of its effect on early failure. The first lot after the change would be watched weekly by age block, so the 160 returns in the first four weeks would prompt a question in October rather than March.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

Edappally recommended that Lot 8 be re-burned to eight hours at about ₹22 a unit, or ₹1.76 lakh for 8,000 units. Shipped as it stood, Lot 8 would be expected to draw 3.84 per cent returns, or 307 units; at ₹1,400 per return (replacement plus freight) that is ₹4.30 lakh. Re-burned, it would draw 1.8 per cent, or 144 returns costing ₹2.02 lakh, plus the ₹1.76 lakh: ₹3.78 lakh. But the 1.8 per cent comes from units built with the old capacitor reel, and Lot 8 was built with the new one. The ₹0.52 lakh margin therefore holds only if burn-in accounts for the whole gap; if the reel explains it, the re-burn saves nothing and costs ₹1.76 lakh. Timing settled it: the oven handled 1,000 units a day, so eight working days on a six-day week from Thursday 5 March finished on Friday 13 March, a week before the retail cut-off, and the delay cost nothing. He asked Eralil to approve the re-burn, to quarantine the remaining new-reel stock, and to demand serial-linked build records, so that Lot 8's own returns would separate the two causes.

Next, study returns and reverse logistics, which turns returns into data, and reliability engineering, which fits Weibull curves in place of the constant-rate assumption.

Two questions to sit with. If the 2,000 early units had shown the same 3.84 per cent, what would you conclude about burn-in, and what would you investigate instead? What would you need to see in the second month of Lot 8 to believe the fix had worked, given that you cannot wait for twenty-four weeks?

Hardware quality: yield, reliability and field failure

What the field failure rate tells you about the product and the factory — and the ways it tells you nothing.

1. Two decisions, three weeks apart

On Monday 5 October 2026 Yashowardhan Guptan sat above the assembly line at Mithram Appliances in Coimbatore with a single sheet of paper. Mithram makes connected reverse-osmosis water purifiers; its seven-litre model had shipped since April, and the Diwali build would put 48,000 units through the line in the three weeks from 12 October. Yield at final functional test was up and warranty cost per unit flat, yet the sheet showed purifiers built in July and August coming back in their first month of service nearly half again as often as the April to June builds. The plant manager wanted a decision by Friday on ₹1.86 crore of chambers to stress-screen every unit for 38 minutes before despatch.

Three weeks later, on Monday 26 October, Yogitha Gowda chaired the service review at Maruvam Instruments in Bengaluru, which builds patient monitors for Indian hospitals. Her problem was the opposite shape: Maruvam's datasheet claimed a mean time between failures of 45,000 hours and the field, over the year to March 2026, had delivered 147,431. Nobody was pleased. The fleet average concealed a 2019-20 install cohort failing at 13.41 per cent a year, hospitals invoking uptime penalties on single monitors, and a question Yamuni Gurikar of service operations had put in writing: if a six-year-old monitor's power supply dies quietly at 3 a.m., is that a service event or a reportable safety issue?

Both are questions about yield, reliability and field failure rate, and the two need opposite things: Guptan needs the field rate to tell him about his factory, Gowda about her design. Expertise is knowing which a number can answer.

2. The idea, and the three schools that disagree about it

Three definitions, because most arguments here are definitional. Yield is the share of units presented to a step that pass it; first-pass yield counts only those passing without rework, and rolled throughput yield is the product of every step's. Reliability is the probability a unit performs its function for a stated duration under stated conditions; miss any of the three and it is not a figure. Field failure rate is the hazard rate of units in customers' hands: failures per unit of exposure, and exposure is time in service, not units shipped.

The history is one over-reach and its reactions. Weibull's 1951 paper gave a shape parameter β separating falling, constant and rising hazard — infant mortality below one, random failure at one, wear-out above. The 1957 Advisory Group on Reliability of Electronic Equipment report built on the constant-hazard case, whose sufficient statistic is its reciprocal, MTBF; MIL-HDBK-217 made that a parts-count prediction method in 1965, and by its 1995 final notice the US Army discouraged its use. Gregg Hobbs's highly accelerated life testing was the revolt: stress a design in steps until it breaks, record its limits, fix the weakest link, repeat.

Three schools survive, separable by what they sign. Physics-of-failure signs that margin is found only by stressing to failure, and not that a predicted MTBF is evidence of anything. Statistical demonstration signs that a quantified rate, even a biased one, is a usable input for spares and contracts, and not that margin discovery replaces a number. The field empiricists sign that the only test run on the real distribution of users is the field, and not that laboratory limits predict a field rate.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Mithram's line has four gated stations and Guptan's "yield is up" refers to the third; their product gives the rolled figure, so 48,000 starts at those rates imply about 43,074 units crossing untouched.

Exhibit 1. Mithram seven-litre line, first-pass yield by station, August 2026.
StationFirst-pass yield
Board test (AOI and ICT)97.4%
Pump and valve leak test98.6%
Final functional test94.1%
Cosmetic and pack-out99.3%
Rolled throughput (product of the four rates)89.7%

The second matters more and is usually left implicit: outgoing defect rate equals incoming latent defect rate times one minus test coverage, for that mechanism. Coverage is mechanism-specific, never a single number. Mithram's final functional test energises the harness and verifies flow; a crimp whose retention force has fallen from 78 newtons to 31 passes all of it. Coverage there is zero, so outgoing equals incoming whatever the headline yield does.

Third is acceleration, where laboratory hours become field years. For a thermally activated mechanism AF = exp[(Ea/k)(1/Tuse − 1/Tstress)], temperatures in kelvin, k = 8.617 × 10−5 eV/K. At 0.7 eV, 40 °C use (313 K) and 85 °C stress (358 K), the bracket is 8,123 × 0.000402 = 3.26 and the factor 26.1: a thousand stress hours stand for 26,110 use hours, or 2.98 years. Thermal cycling uses Coffin-Manson and humidity Peck. But — the point most often missed — a HALT yields no acceleration factor at all: it says where a design breaks, not when.

Fourth, proof is dear: a zero-failure demonstration at confidence C needs MTBF × ln(1/(1−C)) unit-hours, so Maruvam's 45,000-hour claim at 90 per cent confidence needs 103,616 and its observed 147,431 would need 339,472 — forty monitors for nearly twelve months.

Fifth is the screen. A HASS is a production stress screen run inside the operating limits HALT found, precipitating latent defects in hours rather than weeks. Two conditions make it legitimate: a safety-of-screen study showing repeated exposure does not consume useful life, and a measured catch probability against the defect classes you have. Mithram had the second: Yashitha Gatti's team built 60 deliberately weak crimps and 42 of 60 failed the profile, a catch probability of 70 per cent.

4. When the field rate tells you about the factory, and when it does not

Four conditions, stated so they can be tested rather than believed.

One: the field rate is informative about the factory only if build vintage is recoverable from the returned unit. Mithram passes — every harness carries a date code. Maruvam half-fails: install lags build by up to seven months, so its cohorts are keyed on install date.

Two: MTBF is a valid summary only where the fitted β is close to one. Mithram has fitted no β and should quote no MTBF until it has. Maruvam fails outright at β = 2.01, where a fleet MTBF averages populations no customer owns.

Three: a screen pays only where catch probability times cost avoided exceeds its cost plus the life it consumes plus the damage it does. Section 8 computes this for both.

Four: HALT margin is actionable only where field stress is characterised. Mithram passes, having measured a Coimbatore–Guwahati road lane at 6.2 Grms against an 18 Grms vibration weakness. For Maruvam it fails instructively: monitors live in air-conditioned wards, so the margin is enormous and the binding mechanism is time at a benign temperature. Where environment is mild and service life long the frame actively misleads — it certifies a design in no danger of overstress and considerable danger of wearing out on schedule.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product firms share components, so one escape arrives as several unrelated-looking signals; the tell is two products' return rates moving together in the same build weeks, and the fix is keying returns on component date code, which most warranty systems cannot do without an unbudgeted schema change. The same fragmentation shows at the seams: yield belongs to manufacturing, reliability to engineering, returns to service, warranty cost to finance — four functions, four denominators. What mature companies do, rather than say, is appoint one owner of the cohort table.

Regulated hardware turns the question from economic to legal. Maruvam's monitors fall under India's Medical Device Rules, and a failure mode that is silent rather than alarmed can convert a service statistic into a reportable field safety corrective action — a judgement about harm, not rate. Mature firms map each known mode to a harm class before a cluster appears, because that argument cannot be had calmly afterwards.

Hardware-plus-software products have a hazard curve firmware can move mid-life. A power-management change lifting a converter junction eight degrees shortens electrolytic life materially, and a cohort keyed only on build month then mixes pre- and post-change exposure in one row: connected products must be keyed on build month and firmware version. AI-native devices sharpen this: a model update changes average power draw with no hardware change, so the machine-learning team resets the Arrhenius clock.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

A HALT gives limits, not life. The expert asks for destruct limits in units and compares them with measured field stress. The tell is a deck quoting hours from a HALT — wrong because HALT uses stresses with no acceleration model, so converting it to time needs the assumption it avoids.

A HALT qualifies a design as built by one process. Mithram's February run used the original crimp tooling, so it could not have found the July weakness. The tell is a qualification report predating the current bill-of-materials revision: what was tested was a design-process pair, and only half was frozen.

MTBF is sufficient only under a constant hazard. The tell is one MTBF for a fleet with a wide age spread; plot hazard against age and read β first.

Returns are not failures. Of 1,043 service events on Maruvam's 10,300 full-year monitors, 431 closed with no fault found or a configuration change — 41.3 per cent — and only 612 replaced a part. The tell is a return rate moving with a promotion rather than a build vintage; treating returns as failures inflates the reliability problem and hides the usability one.

Rising first-pass yield beside rising field returns is a signature, not a coincidence. Usually limits were loosened, a station bypassed, or rework became efficient enough to mask an upstream shift. Track yield at first presentation and rework pass rate separately: flat defect volume with falling rework means something stopped being detected.

The denominator is the defect. Returns this month over installed base is a diluted hazard: a bad vintage of 109,000 units inside a base of 218,000 lifts that ratio about 13 per cent from its June low, while the vintage is half again worse. The tell is a dashboard that is suspiciously smooth.

Burn-in is a tax unless an infant-mortality population exists and the screen catches it. The first tell is no safety-of-screen study; the second is fallout reported as a benefit when it is a cost. The strongest evidence a screen works is screened vintages beating unscreened ones.

An "equivalent" part is equivalent in form, fit and function, never in reliability. Second-source approval tests electrical and mechanical parity — what equivalence means contractually — and says nothing about a different vendor's failure distribution. The tell is a change note with a parametric comparison and no life data.

7. How the practice differs by product type and company stage

In consumer hardware the return rate is substantially a commercial variable — channel policy, exchange windows, ratings — and the dominant cost is reverse logistics, not repair. In B2B and enterprise the base is known by serial and site, which makes cohort analysis easy and makes mean time to repair, not MTBF, the contractual number: Maruvam promises 98.5 per cent uptime per monitor per quarter, 32.4 permitted downtime hours out of 2,160, against non-metro repair averaging 71 hours. One failure in a quarter breaches that however reliable the fleet is.

For platforms and marketplaces the concept transfers weakly, and saying so is more honest than stretching it: an intermediary owning no hardware owns only complaint data.

Stage matters mostly through sample size. A startup with two failures in 400 units has a 95 per cent interval of roughly 0.06 to 1.8 per cent, so its rational spend is teardown of every return rather than statistics. At Mithram's volume statistics become decisive. At Maruvam's age the constraint is neither: a fleet installed six years ago must be repaired from components no longer made.

8. Three worked examples

Mithram: the vintage the dashboard hid

Yashvanth Gudde, who leads reliability engineering, rebuilt the data as build-month cohorts, counting returns by months in service rather than by calendar month.

Exhibit 2. Mithram returns by build cohort and months in service, at 30 September 2026.

April to June despatched 109,000 units and returned 600 in month one, a pooled 0.5505 per cent; July and August despatched 109,000 and returned 870, a pooled 0.7982 per cent — 45 per cent worse on the same denominator. The standard error of that difference of proportions, at a pooled 0.6743 per cent, is 0.000351 against a difference of 0.002477: a z of 7.07. Not noise.

Pull-testing returned harnesses found a second crimp tool introduced at Mallige Precision for the July build: retention force down from a specified 78 newtons to a measured 31 on a fifth of samples. The excess runs 0.248 percentage points in month one and 0.157 in month two, so 441 excess returns on the two vintages so far; at a blended ₹2,928 per return — ₹1,850 for the visit plus 22 per cent escalating to a ₹4,900 replacement — that is ₹12.9 lakh incurred to date. Where it settles the page cannot say: a cumulative-Weibull fit to those two points gives 2.34 points of lifetime excess and a geometric decay of the monthly excess gives 0.67, so what follows uses month-one returns only and is a floor.

Now the screen, with catch and collateral damage both weighted. A full HASS costs ₹1.86 crore of chambers over three years plus ₹18 a unit on 620,000 units a year — ₹1.74 crore annually — and its own fallout damages an estimated 0.15 per cent of good units, 930 at ₹4,900, a further ₹45.6 lakh: ₹2.19 crore in all. It earns its keep only on latent escapes, which across three previous models ran 3,690 returns out of 1.42 million units, 0.26 per cent, or 1,612 a year. The 0.70 catch probability was measured on crimps and does not transfer; Gudde used 0.55 for escapes generally and could not defend it. Even then the expected catch is 887 units a year at a net ₹2,588 each — ₹2,928 of field cost less ₹340 of rework — so ₹22.9 lakh of annual benefit against ₹2.19 crore of annual cost. The counterfactual matches periods rather than totals: the crimp's month-one excess was 102 returns on the July vintage and 168 on the August, so 135 a build month, of which 0.70 is 94.5 expected catches worth ₹2.45 lakh — against ₹14.5 lakh of screen cost for that month. It loses money even in its best month.

Maruvam: an MTBF that was never a number

Gowda's team used only the 10,300 monitors in service for the whole year to March 2026, excluding 1,100 installed during it, because partial exposure in the denominator was the error they were escaping. That gives 90,228,000 unit-hours and, on 612 confirmed hardware failures, an MTBF of 147,431 hours and a 5.94 per cent annual failure rate — but by install cohort it is not one population.

Mandrem Energy Systems: the screen that made things worse

Mandrem, a Pune maker of lithium packs for inverters, introduced a 72-hour burn-in at 55 °C on its 2025 vintage after a bad year. Fallout ran at 1.9 per cent of 96,000 packs built, so 1,824 were pulled and 94,176 shipped. Field returns at six months in service then rose to 2.51 per cent, 2,364 packs, against 2.14 per cent on the unscreened 2024 vintage of 84,000 packs, which is 1,798: the screen removed 1,824 packs and still shipped more failures.

Two causes were argued, neither isolated. The soak consumed cycle life — a belated safety-of-screen study put mean capacity fade at 2.9 per cent after ten exposures to the old screen against 0.31 per cent after ten of the replacement — and it needed two extra connector mate cycles per pack, damage it could not detect. Nor was the screen the only thing that changed: shortening the soak to eight hours at 40 °C and confining it to one suspect cell lot moved two variables at once, so the 1.86 per cent returned by the first 102,000 packs of the 2026 vintage, or 1,897, cannot be credited to either alone.

9. Failure modes, their early warnings and the cost of late detection

Vintage blindness. Sign: a field series moving a tenth when a cohort has moved by half. Diagnostic: what is the denominator, and when was it measured? Mithram caught it in the July vintage's second month; six further build months uncorrected, at 135 first-month excess returns a month and ₹2,928 each, is 810 returns and about ₹24 lakh.

Screening as a substitute for process capability. Sign: fallout stable rather than falling, so the process is not improving and the screen is now cost of goods. Diagnostic: what would it take to remove it? Caught late, it is politically unremovable.

MTBF in a contract. Sign: procurement specifying hours with no environment or duty cycle. Diagnostic: what β does our field data support? Caught late, six years of spares rest on a figure wrong threefold and silent about the cohort that fails.

No-fault-found treated as a service problem. Sign: the no-fault-found share rises while confirmed failures stay flat. Diagnostic: what are customers doing just before they call? Caught late it reads as unreliability, triggers hardware spending and leaves the cause untouched.

The qualification that ages out. Sign: end-of-life notices arriving faster than qualification cycles. Diagnostic: how many changes since the last HALT, and which touched a load or thermal path? Caught late, the shipping product shares only a part number with the qualified one.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether a quantified failure rate is worth producing. Physics-of-failure, at its strongest: every parts-count method validated against field data has been wrong by factors, Maruvam being an instance, and the standards bodies have retreated from prediction. Demonstration, equally strong: a biased number is still a planning input, and service contracts cannot be written against "good margin". The first is wrong if prediction bias is stable enough to calibrate out; the second if firms that abandon prediction actually instrument the field rather than budget by intuition.

Whether to screen everything, forever. The insurance position: unknown escape classes dominate known ones over a product's life, you cannot price what you have not seen, and a standing screen is the only defence needing no foresight. The Deming position: screening institutionalises an incapable process, its own handling damages units, and every inspection step is evidence something upstream went unsolved. Settling it needs a measured catch probability and a clean safety-of-screen study, and almost nobody produces either.

What the field return rate measures. One camp holds it the only reliability measurement made on the real distribution of users; the other that at a 41.3 per cent no-fault-found share it is a customer-experience measure, and treating it as reliability data corrupts engineering priorities.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this asks for the denominator before the rate, and when it was measured. They refuse to compare rates that do not share exposure — the distance between 0.517 and 0.840 per cent in Figure 3. They treat a yield improvement as a hypothesis about detection, quote no MTBF without a β, and accept no screen without a measured catch probability. They probability-weight both sides of a comparison, never one. And they hold both readings of the field return rate at once, factory and customer.

12. The decisions

Guptan declined the chambers. He reverted the Mallige tooling, funded a ₹9.4 lakh in-line fixture testing every harness two newtons above the field-failure threshold, and made date-coded cohort reporting at one month in service the plant's primary quality metric, displacing the installed-base ratio. A screen costing ₹2.19 crore a year to avoid an expected ₹22.9 lakh is insurance at nine and a half times its expected loss.

Gowda approved a staged module replacement, fan and power-supply capacitor assembly, across the 2019-20 and 2021-22 cohorts: 4,490 monitors at ₹4,100 each, ₹1.84 crore. The three-year benefit was ₹2.62 crore — ₹54.6 lakh of avoided service events, 289 a year at ₹6,300 each on the two mechanisms behind 169 of 248 and 120 of 196 cohort failures, held flat as a deliberate floor because β = 2.01 means the true figure rises; ₹156.1 lakh of avoided uptime penalties, on the stated assumption that each of those 289 failures breaches the uptime term once at ₹18,000, a 71-hour non-metro repair exceeding the 32.4 hours a quarter allows; and ₹51.1 lakh from the regulatory term, the fall in the probability of a reportable silent-failure cluster from 0.12 to 0.04 against a field action on 11,400 units at ₹5,600 each, or ₹6.38 crore — weighted on both sides, not only the side favouring action.

1. Mithram's screen fails its business case even in its best month. Under what measurable conditions would that reverse, and which could Mithram observe before committing the capital?

2. Maruvam's datasheet figure was wrong threefold and used for six years. Who should own that number, and what would make a published reliability figure falsifiable by a customer?

3. Gudde's 0.70 was measured and his 0.55 was not. What is the cheapest experiment that would replace the second, and what would it cost?

13. Going deeper

  1. Testing and quality basics — the sampling and coverage machinery assumed here.
  2. Returns, RMA and reverse logistics — where the ₹2,928 per return goes.
  3. Reliability engineering and field failure — Weibull fitting and censored data.
  4. Product recalls and field corrective actions — what Gurikar's memo was really asking.
  5. Bug triage and severity — reconciling severity with recovery counts.
  6. Release management and launch readiness — the gate that revalidates a qualification.
  7. Staged rollouts and rollback — the software analogue of a vintage.
  8. Incident management and postmortems — turning a cluster into a cause.
  9. SLAs, SLOs and error budgets — why 98.5 per cent uptime is a repair-time promise.
  10. Support and operational readiness — where the no-fault-found share is made.
exp40v2-qo.bug.triage:
Bug triage and severity

Which bugs matter, and how a team decides without drowning: severity as a measurement, priority as a plan, and the arithmetic that separates them.

1. Two boards, nine days apart

On the morning of Wednesday 14 October 2026, Lohitha Tatineni sat down in front of a list of five defects. She is director of product at Daftar Cloud, a Hyderabad company whose software files GST returns for 11,400 paying firms: 1,850 tax practices at ₹1,10,000 a year and 9,550 small businesses at ₹13,200, together ₹32.96 crore of recurring revenue. Her quality lane held four engineers, up from two in March; over the five working days to the GSTR-3B deadline on Tuesday 20 October, that plus a borrowed day made twenty-one engineer-days — exactly what the five defects needed, though not all would be spent by the 20th. Two were S1. One of those two, a rejection of e-invoice reference numbers on inter-state credit notes, had no workaround at all: the affected practice simply could not file. It was also, by the only measure her team could compute, the least valuable thing on the list.

Nine days earlier, on Monday 5 October, Leela Tanguturi had widened a firmware rollout. She is vice-president of product at Dhaara Mobility, a Coimbatore manufacturer with 68,400 electric scooters on Indian roads. Release 4.6 had gone to 2 per cent of the fleet on 28 September and 10 per cent on 1 October; on the 5th it reached 40 per cent, or 27,360 vehicles. By Tuesday 13 October her field team had logged thirty-one reports of regenerative braking dropping out at low state of charge in cold weather, against two in the previous ring. Loknath Tatachari, Dhaara's field-safety officer, wanted it rolled back that afternoon — which would also withdraw a charging-handshake fix that 4.6 carried.

Neither woman had a labelling problem. Both had correctly severitised defects and a queue that would not clear. That gap — between knowing how bad a defect is and knowing what to do on Wednesday — is where almost every disagreement in this field sits.

2. Severity, priority, and the quarrel they came from

Severity is a property of the defect: the size of the harm it does on each occurrence, to the user or to the business, independent of who is looking at it. Priority is a property of the queue: when capacity will be spent on this defect given its severity, how often it fires, how many it reaches, whether a workaround exists, what the fix costs, and what else is competing. Severity is a measurement. Priority is a plan. A measurement that changes because the plan changed is not a measurement.

The separation was not invented by software. Its direct ancestor is system safety engineering, where MIL-STD-882 crossed four hazard severity categories — catastrophic, critical, marginal, negligible — with probability bands to produce a risk matrix. The point of that matrix was that severity alone never authorised a decision; it had to be multiplied by likelihood first. Software inherited the vocabulary and mislaid the multiplication. IEEE Std 1044 made severity and priority separate attributes of an anomaly; IBM's orthogonal defect classification added defect type, aimed at the development process rather than the schedule; Bugzilla shipped both as editable fields and made the distinction a generation's default habit. Google's error-budget practice later argued that for availability failures the apparatus reduces to one number.

Four schools disagree substantively, not terminologically. Each signs a proposition the others will not.

SchoolSignsRefuses
Orthogonal classificationA crash on one unsupported phone is still S1Severity should count affected users
Single ordered queueAnything outside the top twenty is a bug you declinedKeeping a standing S2 backlog
Service levelsAn intact error budget compels no stopA label outranking the budget
Zero-bug policyA queue older than one sprint is a fictionDeferral as a legitimate outcome

Exhibit 1. Each position reduced to one proposition it signs and one it refuses.

3. The mechanics, worked

Expert practice computes a weekly exposure for each defect — modelled cost per occurrence times occurrences per week — then divides it by the engineering days the fix costs. The second step is the one usually skipped. Exhibit 2 is Daftar's five defects for the week of 5 to 11 October 2026.

Exhibit 2. Daftar Cloud, week of 5–11 October 2026. An occurrence is a firm-session in which the defect fired, from product telemetry. Modelled cost per occurrence is support contact rate × ₹340 loaded handling cost, plus the increment to non-renewal probability × lifetime value, which is annual contract × 0.80 gross margin × 4.4 years mean tenure: ₹3,87,200 for a practice and ₹46,464 for a business. D-114 is therefore 0.55 × 340 = ₹187 of handling plus 0.0090 × 3,87,200 = ₹3,485 of churn, or ₹3,672. Contact rate/increment/segment, other rows: D-131 0.40/0.0020/practice; D-142 0.70/0.0004/practice; D-150 0.25/0.0110/business; D-158 0.08/0.0001/business. The last column is blended, not summed.

Two things in that table matter. First, the ranking by exposure removed per engineer-day — D-150, D-158, D-142, D-131, D-114 — disagrees with severity at the bottom and in the middle. Both open on the same S1, D-150. But the other S1, D-114, comes last, at ₹7,344 against D-150's ₹61,587, a factor of 8.4, and a cosmetic S4 outranks both an S2 and an S3. Second, the blended ₹16,525 per engineer-day is not a target; it is what the week happens to contain.

Three steps sit implicit in almost every written triage policy, and Exhibit 3 depends on all of them. Deduplication: in the thirteen weeks to Sunday 4 October, Daftar received 3,887 defect-tagged tickets describing 1,274 distinct defects, 3.05 each, and severity attaches to the defect, not the ticket. Reach measurement, which needs telemetry the ladder never mentions. And re-triage: exposure moves when the occurrence rate moves, so a label set once has stopped tracking.

The rhythm itself is a queueing problem, and it is the part that drowns teams. Over those same thirteen weeks Daftar opened 1,274 distinct defects, 98 a week, and closed 1,196, or 92. But only 611 of the closures were code fixes — 47 a week, and 48.0 per cent of arrivals. The other 585 were administrative: duplicate, not reproducible, obsolete, or declined. Open defects therefore grew by 78 over the quarter, six a week, from 1,540 to 1,618. Closing backlog over arrival rate, 1,618 / 98, is 16.5 weeks; mean work in progress over throughput, Little's Law proper, gives 1,579 / 92 = 17.2. The median age of a fixed defect was eleven days. Both are correct. The queue is bimodal — a fast lane that clears inside a sprint, and a reservoir nobody will touch — so the mean describes no defect in the system. Any policy written against it will be met by closing old defects administratively, which moves the mean and changes nothing.

The second-order effect that catches boards hardest is composition, and Dhaara's rings are a specimen. Ring two carried 4.6 on 6,840 vehicles for four days — 27,360 vehicle-days, coincidentally the size of ring three — producing two cutouts, 0.073 per thousand. Ring three carried it on 27,360 vehicles for nine days, 2,46,240 vehicle-days, producing thirty-one: 0.126. Counts rose 15.5-fold against exposure 9.0-fold, so the rate rose 1.72-fold. But the ring's cold-weather population rose from 420 vehicles in 6,840 to 2,980 in 27,360 — a share of 6.1 per cent, then 10.9, a factor of 1.77 — while inside the cold set the rate went 1.19, then 1.16, a factor of 0.971. Their product is 1.72. The composition effect is real: the ring's cold share rose 1.77-fold. The 0.971 is not a finding. Ring two's 1.19 rests on two cutouts, and a Poisson interval on two events, 0.24 to 7.2, puts it between 0.14 and 4.3 per thousand cold vehicle-days. No detectable change is not the same as flat: these data cannot separate a rate that rose eightfold from one that fell to a quarter. The same thirty-one reports fed Tatachari's rollback request and Tanguturi's refusal, because 4.6 also carried a handshake fix that would save 1,240 failed charge sessions a week fleet-wide once fully rolled out, 496 in the 40 per cent that has it.

4. When the distinction earns its keep, and when it misleads

Three conditions can be stated as testable claims. First: the split pays only when the labelling party and the scheduling party differ and both have standing. At Daftar this holds: Lalit Tammineni's quality team sets severity, Tatineni sets priority, and neither overrules the other without a written reason. At Dhaara it does not: Tatachari's safety veto means calling a defect critical is a scheduling decision, so the fields collapse and arguments about labels become arguments about stopping the line.

Second: exposure-ranked triage is safe only when per-occurrence cost varies modestly across the queue. Daftar's five span ₹32 to ₹3,672, or 2.06 orders of magnitude; at that spread the expectation is dominated by the tail and a point estimate carries weight it cannot bear. Daftar fails this test; Dhaara, where almost every field defect costs a service visit, passes it.

Third: a rhythm survives only if code fixes close roughly half of arriving defects. Code fixes, not closures of any kind: Daftar runs at 611 of 1,274, or 48.0 per cent, marginally under the line, and Dhaara's board, 19 fixes against 23 arrivals a week, at 82.6 per cent. The half is a rule of thumb, not a derivation: the arithmetic forces only that the shortfall go somewhere, and Daftar's goes to 45 administrative closures and six backlog additions.

It actively misleads in two places: pure availability failures, where one error budget answers everything a ladder was built for, and probabilistic systems, where "wrong output" is not a defect class.

5. The hard edges

In a multi-product company a defect in a shared component has a severity that depends on the consumer, and no single board owns it: at Daftar the PDF renderer serves returns, invoicing and the audit trail, and the same fault is S3 on an invoice and S1 on a filed return. The mature answer is not a shared ladder but a named owning board per consumer, obliged to report the maximum severity upward.

On a marketplace or two-sided product, severity is asymmetric by construction. A listing-sync defect that mildly annoys ten thousand buyers may end a seller's week. Scoring severity on the worse-off side produces stop-ships nobody can justify; scoring it on the larger side underweights supply, usually the scarcer resource. Experienced teams keep two severity readings and let the priority decision reconcile them, which looks like indecision and is not.

In regulated products a reporting defect carries severity by statute regardless of impact. A GST filing that goes out wrong is wrong whether it reaches one firm or a thousand, and the DPDP Act's breach-notification clock starts on discovery, not on assessment. Such defects do not belong on the ladder at all; they belong in an override lane with its own clock.

Hardware plus software breaks the assumption that fixes are cheap and reversible. Severity attaches to defects, rollback attaches to releases, and a release is a bundle: Tanguturi cannot withdraw the regen defect without the handshake fix. AI-native products break the ladder differently, and that case is worked below.

6. Eight distinctions an expert makes and a competent practitioner does not

Severity must be stable or it measures nothing. The tell is a ticket whose severity changed while the defect did not — downgraded because the sprint was full, upgraded because a customer escalated. It looks like refinement, and it destroys the one field on which escaped defects can be trended: last quarter's S1 count then means something different from this quarter's.

The workaround discount is where severity inflation hides. The expert asks who executes it. If the user does, the defect genuinely does less harm. If a support agent does it for them, the harm did not shrink; it moved to a cost line nobody on the board owns. D-142's contact rate of 0.70 is the highest of the five precisely because support fixes it by hand.

Frequency belongs in priority; blast radius per occurrence belongs in severity. Both sound like "how many", which is why they are conflated. The diagnostic case is a single-tenant data exposure that happened once: frequency one, blast radius total. A team calling it S3 because it is rare has put a priority input in a severity field.

The S1 count is a capacity statement before a quality statement. The tell is an S1 count that does not move when everything around it does. Daftar logged six S1s among 374 distinct defects in March and six among 418 in October — 1.6 per cent, then 1.4 — while the lane clearing them doubled. That is not proof the threshold drifted to hold it, but it is what drift would look like.

Deferral has to be a decision with a name and a date. "Backlog" used as a verb is the warning sign. A defect declined by a named person on a named date can be revisited when its exposure moves; one that merely stopped being discussed cannot.

Safety and compliance need an override lane, not a severity level. The tell is a long argument over whether a regulatory defect is S1 or S2. It is unresolvable: the ladder measures harm, the statute does not care about harm, and putting statutory defects on the ladder corrupts both.

Reopen rate is a sharper diagnostic than escape rate. Of Daftar's 611 code fixes in the quarter, 58 were reopened within thirty days — 9.5 per cent. Escapes tell you what testing missed; reopens tell you the board authorised fixes against a diagnosis nobody had finished making, which is what a board under volume does.

Whoever writes the severity definition should not be whoever is measured on it. The obvious reading is that engineering should own severity because engineering understands impact. The expert reading is that whoever is measured on the S1 count will, with no dishonesty at all, write a definition producing fewer.

7. How much of this actually varies

Less than the literature suggests, and where it varies it varies specifically. In consumer products per-occurrence cost is small and occurrence counts enormous, so exposure ranking works well and ladders degenerate into three levels nobody argues about. In B2B and enterprise the opposite holds: Daftar's practice tier carries ₹3,87,200 of lifetime value per account, so a defect reaching twelve accounts a week can outweigh one reaching five hundred, and the severity definitions written into enterprise agreements become the real ladder.

On platforms the distinctive problem is that severity is assessed by a party who cannot see the harm: a deprecated API field is S4 to the platform and S1 to the integrator who built a billing flow on it. Marketplaces add the asymmetry described above. Hardware changes the economics, not the concepts: fixes cost service visits, so far fewer defects clear the bar, as Dhaara's ₹1,450-a-vehicle campaign shows. AI products are the one category where the concept itself needs rebuilding, because severity assumes a specification against which output is wrong.

By stage the pattern is cleaner. Before product-market fit a triage rhythm is overhead: one ordered list and a weekly glance. From the first enterprise contract, severity definitions arrive from outside and the ladder stops being yours. At scale the binding constraint is intake — deduplication, reproduction, telemetry — which is why Daftar's 3.05 tickets per defect matters more than any refinement of the ladder.

8. Three episodes, one of them a failure

Daftar, March 2026: severity-only triage. The quality lane then held two engineers over twenty-two working days: forty-four engineer-days. Six S1s consumed forty-one, 93.2 per cent, and all six were genuine. Eleven S2 defects that silently dropped rows on upload went untouched through the March year-end peak. In April, 2,340 firms filed amended returns; support handled 1,287 at ₹340 each, ₹4.38 lakh, against the nineteen engineer-days the eleven fixes would have taken. Severity-only triage was not wrong about severity; it was wrong about the queue, and it spent ₹4.38 lakh defending a correct label.

Dhaara, May 2026: scoping a critical defect. A cell-balancing fault produced nine field reports in three weeks, all on vehicles carrying battery lot BF-21 — 4,180 in a 54,600 fleet, or 0.103 per thousand lot-BF-21 vehicle-days. The severity reading was critical. Because lot identity sat in the telemetry, Tanguturi scoped the campaign to the 4,180 at ₹1,450 a vehicle, ₹60.61 lakh, against a fleet-wide ₹7.92 crore — a ₹7.31 crore difference resting on an identifier logged two years earlier.

Dhaatu Labs, 2026: the ladder that broke. Dhaatu builds an AI contract-review assistant for enterprise legal teams in Bengaluru. Its ladder, inherited from deterministic software, defined S1 as incorrect output. Because every output is probabilistic, 712 of the 1,180 defect tickets in the June quarter arrived as S1 — 60.3 per cent — and median first response on true S1s went from four hours to sixty-one. Nothing was mislabelled; the definition admitted everything. Lavi Tadimeti's recovery split defects from model-quality regressions, measuring the latter as movement in extraction F1 against a frozen 2,400-clause set and routing anything that moved it more than 0.8 points to an evaluation lane. Reclassifying the 712 put 29 in the defect lane and 683 — 95.9 per cent — in the evaluation lane. Live S1s next quarter numbered 34; first response returned to five hours.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Severity inflation. Early sign: the S1 share of intake rises while the escaped-defect rate stays flat. Diagnostic question: what changed about the defects, or about who may label them? Caught late, the stop-ship signal means nothing and the next real emergency cannot announce itself.

The silent-corruption blind spot. Early sign: a data-repair script appears in the release notes. Diagnostic question: which of our S1s was found by a monitor rather than a customer? Daftar's D-150 is the archetype — it threw no error, and 310 firm-sessions a week lost rows unnoticed. Caught late, the cost is not the fix but reconstructing months of wrong data.

Triage theatre. Early sign: meeting length scales with inbound volume. Diagnostic question: how many defects left yesterday's board with an owner and a date? Caught late, the board becomes a queue of its own and senior people route around it.

The deferral graveyard. Early sign: median age of open S2s exceeds a release cycle. Diagnostic question: name who declined this defect, and when. Caught late, the backlog is written off wholesale, taking real defects with it.

The reopen loop. Early sign: reopen rate above roughly eight per cent. Diagnostic question: did we fix the defect or the reported symptom? Caught late, the same defect consumes capacity three times and the exposure model understates it by the same factor.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Should severity include reach? The reach-free position rests on measurement discipline: severity is the one attribute that does not move when the population moves, so folding reach in destroys comparability across quarters. The reach-inclusive position rests on behaviour: boards keeping the fields separate reliably under-prioritise high-frequency, low-severity defects, and Exhibit 2's D-158 — an S4 outranking an S2 and an S3 on efficiency — is offered as proof that separation forces a second, undocumented reconciliation. The first fails if escaped-defect trending proves robust to a composite severity; the second fails if boards reconcile reliably without it.

Do error budgets supersede severity? The service-level position is strong where failures are availability failures and users fungible: one number, one owner, no arguments. It is weakest on correctness, where a defect produces confident wrong answers and burns no budget, and on compliance, where one occurrence is actionable. It fails if correctness defects can be instrumented as budget burn; the severity position fails if availability data shows budgets making worse stop-ship calls than ladders.

Is a standing backlog a liability or an asset? The zero-bug school's evidence is the seventeen-week residence time: a queue nobody will clear is a lie told to stakeholders. The managed-backlog school's is that exposure moves: a defect declined in March at ₹9,000 a week may be worth fixing in October at ₹90,000. It fails if re-triage almost never promotes anything.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this argues about denominators rather than labels, and asks what an occurrence is before asking how bad it is. They can say without looking it up what a week of engineering capacity is worth and what their top defect costs, and notice when the two are within a factor of two. They treat their S1 count as a statement about their own thresholds, and they know which of their numbers is a point estimate with a fat tail. And they defend deferral in writing, with a name and a date, because the alternative is not fewer declined defects but undocumented ones.

12. What they decided

Tatineni fixed D-150 first: three engineer-days, ₹1,84,760 a week removed. D-114 went second, behind a one-day validation banner shipped on 15 October, with the real fix set for Thursday 22 October — because ₹3,672 is a mean over twelve occurrences and prices nothing for a practice with four hundred filings blocked on the 20th. D-158 was declined in writing.

Tanguturi held 4.6 at 40 per cent and shipped 4.6.1 to the 2,980 cold-set vehicles on Monday 2 November. The nineteen days of waiting carried 56,620 cold vehicle-days at 1.16 per thousand: some 66 cutouts at ₹2,850 of roadside assistance plus a one-in-forty chance of a ₹46,000 claim — ₹4,000 each, ₹2.64 lakh in all.

Three questions

1. Daftar's model prices churn through lifetime value but nothing for the practice-tier tail. What measurement would Tatineni need to price that tail, and would having it reorder the five fixes?

2. Dhaara's cold-set rate is flat across two rings, which Tanguturi treats as evidence the rate is known. Under what sampling of the next ring would that inference fail, and what must the ring design add?

3. If a board adopted exposure per engineer-day as policy, which of the eight distinctions in section 6 would it violate first, and what guardrail would keep it honest for a quarter?

13. Going deeper

  • Testing and quality basics — triage handles only what testing finds.
  • Quality metrics and escaped defects — turns severity into a trend, exposing inflation.
  • Release management and launch readiness — where the stop-ship threshold is set.
  • Staged rollouts and rollback — Dhaara's rings are a measurement instrument, not a safety net.
  • Incident management and postmortems — takes over when severity stops being a queueing question.
  • SLAs, SLOs and error budgets — the strongest rival to ladders, and its limits.
  • Support and operational readiness — owns the contact rate exposure rests on.
  • Beta and early-access programmes — moves discovery earlier, changing the occurrence counts.
exp20v2-qo.bug.triage:
Bug Triage and Severity

1. Four days, five bugs

On Thursday 5 November 2026, Kirthika Sundaram, head of product at Coracle, a Bengaluru bill-payment and UPI autopay app, opened a spreadsheet that her engineering lead, Kishore Sankaran, had exported overnight. It listed 412 open bugs. Three weeks earlier the count had been 391. Each week 38 new reports arrived and 31 were closed (7 as duplicates, 10 as will-not-fix and 14 as fixed), so the list grew by seven a week and, at that pace, would reach 496 by 28 January.

The release branch would be cut on Monday 9 November. Festival-week leave left the team four engineer-days across the five engineers still at work for bug work, and five bugs had accumulated noise: Kanagaraj Somasundaram, who ran customer support, wanted the double debit fixed because his agents handled it daily, while app-store reviewers kept naming an Android crash. Fixing all five needed 10.5 days. A payments app that debits twice teaches users to distrust autopay; a team that spends its four days on the loudest complaints rather than the costliest ones pays for that twice. Kirthika needed a way to choose, and a routine that would not repeat this argument every Thursday.

Figure 1 shows why the problem is not the five bugs. The backlog adds 28 every four weeks whatever Kirthika picks on Thursday, so a decision made bug by bug cannot keep up; only a repeatable rule can.

2. The idea

Bug triage is the routine of examining each newly reported defect, deciding how bad it is, and deciding what the team will do about it and by when. The word comes from battlefield medicine, where limited surgeons forced a sort of casualties by need and chance of benefit. Software borrowed it as bug trackers spread in the 1990s; the Bugzilla tracker, built at Netscape in 1998, popularised keeping two separate fields on every bug, one for severity and one for priority. A formal vocabulary had arrived earlier: the IEEE's standard classification of software anomalies, published in 1993, which asked organisations to record how serious each defect was before deciding anything else. The problem both solved was the same: teams that rated bugs with a single number kept arguing about the number rather than the bug.

Severity is how much damage the defect does when it occurs. Priority is the order in which the team chooses to fix it. Severity is a property of the bug, assessable by anyone who understands the product. Priority is a decision about the team, combining severity with how many users meet the bug, what fixing it costs, what deadlines loom and what else is competing. Coracle's severity scale has four levels: S1, money wrong or data lost; S2, a core task fails for some users; S3, the task completes but wrongly or awkwardly; S4, cosmetic.

The sentence Kirthika could repeat in a meeting: severity is how bad it is when it happens, priority is when we have chosen to fix it, and only one of those is a fact.

The grid is why two fields exist. Bug A, a double debit, sits top-left: terrible and uncommon. A single "priority" collapses that distinction and the team loses the ability to say why it is working on something.

3. How it works

Coracle's rhythm has two meetings. A daily twenty-minute session handles only reports from the last day; a weekly forty-five-minute sweep revisits what daily deferred. Each report passes through six steps.

Steps 2 and 3 are the ones practitioners leave implicit. Duplicates matter because ten reports of one bug are one defect with a reach of ten, not ten defects. Reproduction matters because a bug nobody can reproduce cannot be severity-rated, only parked with a named question and an expiry date.

Step 4 assigns severity from the written scale, without looking at who complained. Step 5 measures reach, the distinct users who hit the bug in the past seven days, usually from logs rather than tickets, and estimates the engineer-days to fix. Step 6 is the one most often skipped: every report must leave with an outcome, an owner and a date, and "will not fix" counts as an outcome. Of the 31 weekly closures, 10 are closed that way, which is what keeps the list from being a graveyard. A third rule governs time: a bug waiting for information is closed after fourteen days of silence, with the reporter told exactly what would reopen it.

4. A worked example

Finance estimated the cost of one affected user at the figures in the table: support handling, held money, and an allowance for churn. Weekly harm is users affected a week multiplied by that cost. Priority is harm removed per engineer-day, because days are the scarce thing.

BugSeverityUsers a weekCost per user (₹)Weekly harm (₹)Fix daysHarm per day (₹)
A Double debit on UPI retryS11409001,26,000342,000
B Crash on Android 8 statementS22,4003072,000236,000
E Autopay reminder SMS missingS23004001,20,000430,000
C GST invoice off by ₹1S39002018,000118,000
D Logo misaligned on iPadS46053000.5600
Total3,36,30010.5

Ranking by harm per day gives A, B, E, C, D. Filling four days in that order: A takes three (cumulative 3); B needs two and would reach five, so it is skipped; E needs four, skipped; C takes one (cumulative 4). The team fixes A and C, removing ₹1,44,000 a week, or 42.8 per cent of the ₹3,36,300 total. No other combination that fits four days removes more; the next best, A with D, removes ₹1,26,300.

Now change one input. Coracle's campaign to first-time smartphone buyers starts on 9 November, and most of them use Android 8 handsets, so B's reach doubles to 4,800 users a week. B's weekly harm becomes ₹1,44,000 and its harm per day ₹72,000, the highest in the table. Order becomes B, A, E, C, D.
