Table 1 note: the rollback cost is the growth team's estimate of conversions lost with version 15's faster answers. Cost per answer avoided is cost ÷ avoided, for example 90,000 ÷ 108 = 833.

Average cost is the wrong yardstick for the last rung. Chittilappilly had set a rule months earlier: containment is justified while the extra cost of each extra unsafe answer avoided stays under ₹10,000. Going from the narrow switch to feature off avoids 12 more answers for ₹3,90,000 more, which is ₹32,500 each. The switch passes and feature-off fails, though its average of ₹4,000 looks cheap. Chemmanur turned the narrow switch on at 22:00.

The second pass changes one input. Next morning Chalissery re-measured the classifier on photographed reports, which it handled badly; recall across all critical reports fell to 70 per cent. The switch now routes 560 reports (₹70,000) and misses 240, leaving 240 × 0.15 = 36 unsafe answers, so it avoids 84. Figure 3 compares the residual harm.

At recall 70 per cent the switch alone leaves 36, worse than a rollback's 20, and costs ₹70,000 against ₹35,000. The ordering flips: roll back first. Layering the switch on the rolled-back version leaves 800 × 0.30 × 0.025 = 6, at a combined ₹1,05,000. The extra 14 answers avoided cost ₹70,000, or ₹5,000 each, under the limit, so both stay on. The switch's price per answer avoided stayed at ₹833 in both passes, since ₹125 ÷ 0.15 does not depend on recall; recall changed how much harm remained, and that moved the decision.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Containment is not diagnosis

A model's behaviour often cannot be reproduced on demand, and the cause may be a prompt change, a data shift or both. Contain on the pattern you can measure, find the cause afterwards.

A kill-switch is not a rollback

A switch removes a behaviour; a rollback restores a state, which requires that the earlier model, prompt and data version were all kept and still work together. Teams often keep the weights, lose the prompt, and find out at 22:00.

Severity follows harm, reach and reversibility

The severity came from roughly 780 unsafe critical-value answers, not from 4,200 reposts. A quiet failure harming thousands outranks a loud one that embarrasses; count affected people from logs first.

The three failure types need different levers

Harmful outputs respond to switches and rollbacks. Drift is slow, so the lever is detection and retraining, and an old model may itself be stale. Leakage is hardest: no switch retrieves information that has left, so containment means closing the channel and the response shifts to notification.

Disclosure runs on clocks that are not yours

If personal data leaked, India's CERT-In directions of 2022 require reporting specified incidents within six hours of noticing them, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 requires intimation to the Data Protection Board and affected persons; check current text with counsel. A harmful answer alone may carry no statutory deadline, yet those who received it are owed notice.

Monitors catch only what someone measured

Jeevadhara tracked latency, refusals and thumbs-down; none moves when a confident wrong answer pleases the user. Only a sampled audit or a targeted monitor would have seen the 15 per cent.

What the playbook cannot tell you

It cannot say whether 2.5 per cent unsafe after rollback is acceptable; that is a clinical judgement, and the ₹10,000 threshold only encodes an earlier one. Before relying on a switch, ask who may press it and when it was last tested.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace

The levers are the same; what changes is who must be told and what a pause costs. Table 2 sets out the difference.

ContextWhat an incident looks likeWho is owed noticeTypical lever
ConsumerPublic screenshot, fast spreadAffected users, the publicNarrow switch, public note
B2BA client's workflow quietly wrong; contract breachClient contacts, within contract termsPer-client flag, direct call
MarketplaceOne side harmed by the model's ranking or messageBoth sides, sometimes the regulatorFreeze the ranking rule

Scale matters as much. An early-stage company has few people: the commander is often the founder and nobody has rehearsed the switch, so the fix is a written page and one drill. A large company has lawyers but ten teams owning pieces of the system and no one able to press the lever, so the fix is a named owner with authority.

7. Common mistakes

The playbook that is a document. Symptom: hours pass and the statement is vague. Misunderstanding: writing a plan equals having the capability. Diagnostic: ask an on-call engineer, unannounced, to flip the staging switch and time it.

Waiting for the root cause. Symptom: "cannot reproduce" while harm continues. Misunderstanding: you must understand a failure to stop it. Diagnostic: ask which narrowest lever works without knowing why.

Severity by virality. Symptom: a quiet failure closed as minor while a loud, harmless one consumes the week. Misunderstanding: attention measures damage. Diagnostic: count affected users from logs before the first status call.

8. What good looks like

Picture the same Tuesday at a well-prepared Jeevadhara. A weekly audit of critical-value answers would have shown version 15's rate within days, so the screenshot would be the second sign. The switch is drilled quarterly. Legal has pre-approved a disclosure notice, and the ₹10,000 threshold is pinned in the on-call runbook, not left in one head. The commander applies a decision rather than improvising one.

9. What Chemmanur decided

At 22:00 she turned on the narrow switch, the narrowest lever that stopped most of the harm in four minutes. On Wednesday 14 October, with recall at 70 per cent, she ordered the rollback to version 14 and kept the switch as a second layer. Chittilappilly's team replayed the logs for their own count of unsafe answers, expected near 780, Chekkutty's staff contacted those users that day, and a public note followed at noon. Her reasoning: each step was reversible, passed a threshold agreed beforehand, and did not wait for the cause.

Read next on incident management and postmortems, which supplies the command structure and review habits used here, and then supervised learning in production, whose monitoring would have shortened Figure 1's bar.

Two questions to sit with. Which failure at your company would leave every dashboard flat, and who would find it first? If you had to put a rupee figure on one unsafe answer, whose judgement would you want in the room?
exp40v2-qo.ai.incidents:
AI incident response

What is our playbook when the model does something harmful in public?

1. Two decisions, ten days apart

At 19:04 on Tuesday 13 October 2026, Thushara Devapoojari, head of product at the Kochi news app Kazhcha Media, was sent a screenshot by a stringer in Thrissur. Kazhcha serves roughly 1.8 crore monthly users in Malayalam and Kannada, and since February every article had carried an AI brief. The brief on a district court report named a timber merchant — a bystander quoted in the eleventh paragraph, never charged with anything — as the man the court had remanded. It came from model version 4.2, released at 11:00 on Thursday 8 October.

Devapoojari had four levers, an intermediary-rules complaint arriving within the day, and no idea how many briefs looked like this one. No monitor had told her: the company learned from a stranger, 128 hours after release. Ten days later Thejus D'Mello faced its mirror image.

At 11:05 on Friday 23 October, D'Mello of Krithi Systems in Bengaluru read a message from a customer's security team. Krithi sells one product, an assistant drafting replies to customer correspondence for 38 banks and insurers: ₹96 crore of recurring revenue, an average of ₹2.53 crore a customer. A bank's agent had opened the "similar past cases" panel and found a letter belonging to a different bank, because a retrieval filter shipped at 14:20 on Monday 19 October had lost its tenant predicate on that path. He knew within forty minutes what had broken, his customer's logs being better than his monitoring; what he did not know was what to say, to whom and by when, with a six-hour CERT-In clock running and 38 contracts specifying three deadlines.

2. The idea, and the three positions on it

AI incident response is the organised practice of detecting a model's harmful behaviour in production, containing it with the narrowest lever available, disclosing it to those owed the truth, and changing the system so the class of failure cannot recur unnoticed. The canonical classes are harmful outputs, drift and data leakage: Kazhcha had the first, Krithi the third, Kadal in section 8 the second.

The practice is borrowed. California's fire services formalised the Incident Command System in the 1970s to end confused authority: one commander, defined roles, one picture. Web operations adopted it, and Google's 2016 reliability-engineering book spread the blameless postmortem. Safety engineering supplied the other parent — Leveson and Hollnagel, who place accidents in the interaction of controls rather than one component.

Why a separate name? Conventional software fails deterministically and one passing test retires a bug; models fail statistically. A model that mis-attributes a name in 3.2 per cent of court reports has no reproducible failure, and "is it fixed?" has no yes-or-no answer, only a prevalence and an interval. Three positions on what follows are irreconcilable.

The continuity position: an AI incident is an incident. It signs that every model failure gets a severity, a commander and a postmortem inside the existing on-call system; it refuses a separate safety function able to stop a shipping product.

The sociotechnical position: the unit of response is the failure class and its prevalence, not the ticket. It signs that nothing is resolved until the class is measured below a stated threshold; it refuses the claim that an incident ends when the error rate returns to a baseline never measured against harm.

The obligation position, usually counsel's: the binding constraint is what the firm must say and when. It signs scoping disclosure to the legal duty, on the clock; it refuses publishing a prevalence estimate nobody obliges you to publish, because an estimate is a stick handed to every plaintiff.

3. Mechanics: the ladder, the clock and the arithmetic

Expert practice runs seven steps — detect, declare, contain, preserve, measure, disclose, remediate — and the implicit ones decide the outcome: who may press the switch at 02:00 without a deploy, and snapshotting first, because a rollback destroys the scene. Every number below exists because Kazhcha copied its logs at 21:50.

Containment is a ladder: climb no higher than the harm requires. Devapoojari's four rungs are priced in Table 1, and pricing them needs one base. An August holdback test on 5 per cent of users measured briefs worth ₹0.15 more of advertising per session; across 1.20 crore sessions a day that is ₹18.0 lakh a day of attributable revenue. Court and crime work is 9 per cent of the 12,000 articles summarised daily — 1,080 briefs — and the advertising team attributes 9 per cent of brief revenue to it, ₹1.62 lakh a day.

Prevalence came from an audit: of 500 sampled version-4.2 court briefs, 16 carried a false attribution — 3.2 per cent, standard error 0.8 points, 95 per cent interval 1.7 to 4.7 per cent. The same sample against version 4.1 gave 4 of 500, 0.8 per cent. The 2.4-point difference carries a standard error of 0.88 points, so it sits at 2.7 of them: a finding, not noise. At 3.2 per cent of 1,080 briefs, version 4.2 produced 34.56 false attributions a day; over the 5.49-day exposure window, about 190 briefs, each served around 500 times — roughly 95,000 impressions.

Each rung leaves a residual. Name-stripping relies on an entity tagger with 94 per cent recall, so it leaves 34.56 × 0.06 = 2.0736 attributions a day, carried below as 2.07. Rolling back does not stop the class; it reduces it to version 4.1's rate, 1,080 × 0.008 = 8.64 a day. Only the switch-off rungs leave nothing. Counsel priced one false attribution reaching the named man's locality and producing a formal complaint at ₹9.5 lakh, with probability 0.08, so each residual attribution carries ₹76,000 of expected harm.

4. When the practice applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions make the frame the right one; state each as a testable claim, then test both firms.

C1: the failure class is detectable at population level before an outsider reports it. Both fail, for different reasons. Kazhcha's dashboards held latency, cost per brief and read-through, nothing counting name attributions, and Figure 1's 128-hour lag is that absence measured. Krithi had the machinery — a nightly tenant-isolation canary — but it exercised the main retrieval path only, so the broken panel ran 92.75 hours until a customer called.

C2: a lever exists narrower than switching the product off. Kazhcha passes with four rungs; Krithi half-passes, because the panel disables in two minutes but is what customers renew for, so its narrow rung is commercially broad.

C3: the harmed party is identifiable. For Kazhcha the named merchant is identifiable and the 95,000 impressions are not. Krithi's harmed individuals are the banks' customers, whom it cannot name or contact, so disclosure runs through the tenant — a technical duty becoming a commercial negotiation. C4: a rollback target exists that is warm and better. Kazhcha's is still wrong 0.8 per cent of the time; Krithi's costs 40 minutes and gives back a latency regression.

Two situations make the frame misleading. First, when the incident is the product's designed behaviour: a classifier sold at 94 per cent accuracy that is 6 per cent wrong is not failing, and declaring an incident substitutes ritual for the conversation about what was promised. Second, pure drift, where the declare-contain-resolve cadence has no declaration point and so manufactures false closure; drift becomes an incident only when it crosses a threshold set in advance, as a margin-floor alert would have been — Kadal's weekly report only approximated one.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Where one model serves several products, the granularity that matters is per capability: the blast radius sits with the platform team while the harm lands on product teams, and the predictable failure is a platform owner who stops one product's harm and breaks four others. Two-sided businesses face the mirror problem — Kazhcha's section switch removed briefs from the court reporting of 40 publishers who had done nothing wrong, and their traffic loss appears nowhere in Table 1.

In regulated B2B the clock is not yours. Krithi's banks must themselves report material incidents to the Reserve Bank of India on a six-hour clock from their detection, so Krithi's latency is consumed by someone else's duty before it begins. Mature vendors pre-negotiate the schedule and keep a drafted letter in the runbook.

Hardware differs in kind: rollback is a reach curve, not an event. A tractor-telematics vendor rolling back an on-device vision model reached 5,254 of its 7,400 units within 48 hours — 71 per cent — and 92 per cent within a fortnight, so the real decision concerned the 2,146 units still running the bad model on day three. AI-native products have the sparsest ladder: with no narrow rung, they contain by refusing a class of input.

Two seams decide how this goes. An unpinned third-party model gives you no rollback, only a support ticket. And privilege stops the blameless postmortem circulating, so mature firms split it: a privileged legal record and a published technical one.

6. Eight things that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Detection time dominates total harm, and nobody budgets for it. The tell is a postmortem timeline beginning at "incident declared": Kazhcha ran 128 hours undetected and 3.8 hours more before the switch took effect, so halving the response would have saved under two hours and halving detection would have saved 64.

Severity scales built for availability under-rate harm. An availability ladder keys on users affected and minutes down, so 190 briefs triages as a Sev-4; the tell is a top row reading "complete outage" rather than "irreversible harm to an identified person". Experts add an orthogonal harm axis.

A rollback is a reduction, not a stop. Test every member of the class "levers that end the harm" against its definition: name-stripping leaves 2.07 a day, rollback leaves 8.64, only the switches leave zero. Rollback feels like a stop because "known-good" is a claim about the past, not about the failure class.

The denominator in the disclosure letter is a decision, not a fact. Krithi's replay produced three defensible numbers for one event, differing by a factor of 6.6; the tell is a letter quoting one. Experts quote all three and name the one they rely on; the rest pick the smallest and are asked why in a deposition.

Expected value must be expected on both sides. The ₹10,000 rule above is one common shape of this error: a certain cost on one side, a weighted harm on the other, and a recommendation that inverts when you fix it. The tell is any rule stated as cost per unit of a count.

A switch you have not exercised is a belief. The tell is a runbook naming a kill-switch with no date of last exercise, and section 8's freight case is what that belief costs.

Every guardrail creates a new failure class and a workaround. Name-stripping made court briefs vague, and within two days three desk editors were re-inserting names by hand into the brief field, outside the tagger, restoring the original risk by a path no monitor watched. The tell is a guardrail with no measurement of what users did next.

"Resolved" needs a threshold and an interval. Zero recurrences in a week proves little when the base rate is 3.2 per cent and the sample is 60 briefs: an upper bound that loose is consistent with the original rate. Experts close against a written prevalence target and size the sample first.

7. How it differs by product type and by stage

Five differences are real. In consumer products the clock is set outside the firm by how fast a screenshot travels and disclosure is public, so the drafting problem is tone at scale. In B2B the clock is contractual and disclosure runs through a customer with their own regulator, so the problem is consistency across 38 letters. In marketplaces containment harms a third party who caused nothing, and the duty to notify them is usually missing from the runbook. In hardware the lever is a reach curve, so containment is a schedule; in AI-native products the ladder has no middle rung. Said plainly, the seven steps and section 3's arithmetic hold everywhere, and detection time dominated for both protagonists — though not where the lever is a reach curve.

Stage changes what to build, not what to believe. At seed the practice is a kill-switch anyone can reach, a logged record of what the model was given and returned, and one named person; a severity taxonomy then is theatre. In growth — Kazhcha's stage — the binding constraint is usually detection, because the product has outrun its instrumentation. At scale it moves to disclosure consistency, and the control is a single exposure measurement from which every letter is written.

8. Three worked examples

Kazhcha, 13 October. Covered above: detection by a stranger at 128 hours, containment 3.8 hours later, a ranking that inverted when both sides were weighted.

Krithi, 23 October. Replaying 61,400 logged panel calls against an index snapshot gave three figures. In 1,782 calls — 2.9 per cent — the retrieval set held a document belonging to another tenant. The panel renders three results, and a foreign document sat in the rendered three in 1,104 of those 1,782 calls, 62.0 per cent. An agent expanded the panel, the only logged evidence of a human reading it, in 268 of the 1,104, 24.3 per cent. The rendered 1,104 drew on 737 distinct documents from 11 source tenants, 204 of them carrying a customer name beside an account identifier.

The expensive mistake was not arithmetic. Krithi's draft letter told 29 customers they had nothing to report, a figure reached as 38 minus the 9 tenants whose agents had seen foreign material. But 11 tenants were sources, and 5 of those were also receivers, so the affected set is 11 + 9 − 5 = 15 and the untouched set is 23, not 29. Six customers were nearly told their data was safe when it had been served to another bank: the class admitted two ways of being affected, and the count used one.

Kadal Freight Systems, where the approach failed. This is the drift case, though not a pure one: the inputs stopped moving while the world did, and the freeze had a date, even if nobody read it. Kadal's pricing agent quoted 14,200 truck-freight lots a day, 23 per cent accepted, 3,266 bookings at an average ₹18,400 and a 9.1 per cent margin — ₹1,674 a lot. On Friday 28 August 2026 the diesel-and-toll index feed stopped updating. Quotes drifted 11 per cent low, ₹2,024 a lot, turning the margin to minus ₹350, and cheap quotes lifted acceptance to 29 per cent, so volume rose to 4,118 lots a day. The weekly margin report caught it on Tuesday 1 September, by which time Kadal had booked 16,472 lots at minus ₹350, losing ₹57.65 lakh against the ₹2.19 crore the counterfactual 13,064 lots would have earned: a shortfall of ₹2.76 crore, or ₹69.1 lakh a day.

Kadal had a kill-switch, which is why this is the failure case. Nobody had exercised it since July, and the engine behind it had lost the lane-weight table when a warehouse database was retired on Friday 24 July. The switch worked as designed: it fell back to an engine that could price only 38 per cent of lane-and-weight combinations, so 62 per cent of requests got no quote for 31 hours, costing 2,616 bookings and ₹43.8 lakh of margin. Against a ₹69.1 lakh daily bleed it still paid for itself in 15.2 hours, but the nine hours spent arguing about whether the fallback worked cost ₹25.9 lakh, and they argued because nobody could answer. Recovery was manual: eleven people quoted from a spreadsheet for two days while a feed check was built. The written lesson was that an unexercised fallback has a decaying option value nobody carries on the books.

9. Failure modes, their early signs and the cost of lateness

No owner of the switch. Early sign: the runbook says "notify the ML team". Ask who can disable this capability at 02:00 on a Sunday without a deploy. Late cost: 3 hours 36 minutes passed between Kazhcha's screenshot and the switch being thrown, most of it spent finding who could.

Monitoring the model instead of the harm. Early sign: dashboards of latency, token spend and refusal counts, nothing counting what would embarrass you. Ask which chart would have moved on this incident. Late cost: Figure 1's 128 hours.

Fallback decay. Early sign: no date of last exercise. Ask when real traffic last came from the fallback, and what fraction it covered. Late cost: ₹43.8 lakh and nine hours of hesitation.

Disclosure drafted from the wrong set. Early sign: a customer list produced by subtraction. Ask what the ways of being affected are, and whether the list covers each. Late cost: Krithi's 29 against 23.

A postmortem that yields a model fix and no control. Early sign: every action item begins "retrain" or "add to the prompt". Ask which item would catch the next member of this class. Late cost: a second occurrence, found externally again, the first now documented.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The continuity position's strongest form is empirical: incident competence is a muscle, and firms that route AI failures through a separate process get worse at both. Every number in section 3 came from ordinary reliability machinery — logs, replay, a severity call, a commander — and most model incidents start with a deploy, a config change or a feed. It would be wrong if harmful behaviour routinely arrived with no change on the firm's side, which a deploy-centred process cannot see.

The sociotechnical position's strongest form is that its rival cannot define "resolved". A deterministic incident ends when the bug is gone; a statistical one ends at a prevalence, which needs standing measurement, sampling design and an interval — none of which an on-call rotation produces, and Kazhcha's 3.2 against 0.8 per cent exists only because somebody built a sample. It would be wrong if cheap automated evaluation made prevalence measurement a commodity, making the specialist function a tooling choice.

The obligation position's strongest form is that voluntary disclosure is not free and firms under-price it. An estimate with an interval is a discoverable admission repeated in every later claim, and the asymmetry is real: candour's benefit decays in weeks and the legal exposure does not. It would be wrong if disclosure measurably reduced total cost — but nobody has a clean comparison: disclosing and non-disclosing firms differ in a dozen ways.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this writes a severity matrix. Someone who has internalised it can tell you, without looking, when the kill-switch was last exercised and what fraction of traffic the fallback covered. They ask what the denominator is before they ask how bad it is. They snapshot before they contain, even at 22:00 with a screenshot going round. They refuse to compare a certain cost against an unweighted count, they close against a written prevalence target rather than a quiet week, and they treat each new guardrail as a new failure class. Most visibly, they spend on detection, having done the arithmetic in Figure 1.

12. What they decided

Devapoojari turned briefs off for the court and crime sections at 22:40 on 13 October, in effect by 22:52 — the ₹1.62 lakh option, against her own ₹10,000 rule — because once both sides were weighted it was cheaper as well as safer, and because the residual she would have accepted was a person's name. Treesa Dantas's team shipped name-stripping on 15 October and Titto D'Sa published the prevalence with its interval. D'Mello notified all 38 customers inside the 24-hour clause, not only the 24 bound by it, with three letters keyed to the source, receiver and untouched sets; each reported 1,104 rendered exposures and 268 confirmed human views rather than 2.9 per cent. Tavishi Darbe's canary covered every retrieval path by 27 October.

Three questions. First: Kazhcha's ₹10,000 rule was overridden by the lead who wrote it — was the rule wrong, or was the override an unpriced change of appetite that belonged to the board? Second: had Krithi disclosed only the 268 confirmed views, which of section 2's three positions would have been satisfied, and at what cost next time? Third: Kadal blamed an unexercised fallback — what would you measure monthly to make that a control?

13. Going deeper

Supervised learning in production — these classes are pipeline properties, so it sets which monitors exist. Incident management and postmortems — the parent practice, and the machinery not to rebuild. Testing and quality basics — what a passing test can and cannot retire. Bug triage and severity — where section 6's harm axis belongs. Release management and launch readiness — the gate at which a kill-switch and a log become preconditions. Staged rollouts and rollback — the mechanics behind Table 1's rungs. SLAs, SLOs and error budgets — where a prevalence threshold gets enforced. Support and operational readiness — the channel that found both incidents.
